text: Case Study Assignment (Case study, 30%, Individual). Students will develop and present analytical case studies of technological innovations in financial markets or financial services, including Compliance, Anomaly, and Fraud Detection applications.

subject_name: AI-Driven Compliance, Anomaly and Fraud Detection
text: AI Application Proposal (Report, 45%, Individual). Part A: AI application proposal (30%) Students will develop an industry-focused proposal for the practical application of AI-driven compliance, anomaly detection, or fraud prevention in a specific area of the finance industry. The objective is to bridge academic knowledge with real-world applicability. Part B: Critical reflection (15%) AI tools often rely on previously collected data to train the model, and/or continue to collect data throughout the use of the tool to improve modelling. This includes data from Indigenous peoples. Consider how your selected tool would collect data and any potential ethical issues with this collection. Then consider how you would collect and analyse data on Indigenous peoples in the future to ensure respect for data integrity, data sovereignty, and self-determination principles are considered. Critically reflect on how this learning will influence your future professional practice to work with and for Indigenous Australians. This assessment assures the following course intended learning outcome(s): Ensure ethical AI practices in finance that are inclusive, fair, and transparent Critically reflect on the rights to consent, privacy, data sovereignty and self determination to work ethically with and for Indigenous Australians across finance professions

Sustainability Reflection (Individual) (Reflection, 25%). In this task students will investigate the relationships between ecological footprints and sustainability theories to reflect on the difference between espoused and actual behaviours that characterize the adoption of sustainability at individual, organisational and societal levels. They will then articulate their approach to direct future organisational action to reduce or eliminate this difference between espoused and actual sustainability behaviours. This assessment addresses weeks 1 & 2, and is due at the end of week 2.

Implementing Sustainability Report (Individual) (Report, 45%). In this task students will critically analyse the application of sustainability business models within an identified organisation or industry. Using established organisational and sustainability theories students will critically analyse the organisations business model and evaluate how effectively sustainability has been implemented . Finally students will determine the possbile next steps to enable this organisation to improve its sustainability implementation. Students can select their current organisation or any ASX-listed company. This assessment addresses weeks 3 & 4,and is due at the end of week 4.

Sustainability Governance Analysis Report (individual) (Report, 30%). Students will build on their sustainability implementation report to design a sustainability governance framework to support the implementation and evaluation of identified sustainability improvements to achieve net-zero by 2030 for their selected organisation. Students will then critically reflect on the potential impact of their sustainability governance approach and consider the change effort required to ensure it functions successfully. This assessment addresses weeks 5 & 6 , and is due at the end of week 6.

Regular quizzes (Quiz/test, 25%, Individual). There are 6 quizzes to be completed in tutorials, each with randomised questions of multiple choices or fill in the blanks. The best 4 out of the total 6 quizzes will count.

Report (Report, 25%, Group, group assessed). In modern day business environment, decision-making hinges on data analytics that allows users to extract statistical information from data and interpret statistical results. Therefore, the assignment requires students to demonstrate their ability to locate, select and analyse data using appropriate resources and analytical tools. The assignment requires students to access and critically analyse data. But students will also be the source of the data. In this way students will be able to see the 'objective' side of data analysis, but also the subjective side of data creation - much data for individuals, businesses and governments comes from people. Further details will be provided on Canvas. This is a groupwork assignment. You may form groups yourselves before the end of week 5. After week 5, those who havenât found a group will be randomly assigned to existing groups or be assigned to a completely new group.

Final Exam (Examination, 50%, Individual). The final examination assures objectives 1, 2 and 3. The examination tests the student's ability to correctly identify and use statistical tools and to interpret output within related contexts. The exam tests the student's ability to be able to critically interpret statistics and business information. The final exam assures the Bachelor of Business learning goal that students should have well developed critical and analytical skills and be able to access and interpret statistics and business information. It will assess material from the entire semester.

Internship Plan (Learning contract, 25%, Individual). This assessment is designed to help you define your internship's project scope, including your professional development goals. These elements should be collaboratively negotiated with your industry partner or organisation.

Internship Project (Project, 40%, Individual). As part of your internship, you will complete a project. After your internship, you will submit your project for evaluation. Ensure that your submission effectively reflects the knowledge and experiences you gained throughout your internship.

Mock Interview (Presentation, 35%, Individual). In this assessment, you will conduct a video interview reflection to demonstrate your learning and insights gained during your internship. This task will help you articulate your experiences and professional development effectively.
Quizzes (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). Quizzes are presented as multiple choice, 2-4 questions per week for ten weeks. These are completed in class and students receive immediate feedback.

Algorithm Implementation and Journal Reflection (Project, 50%, Individual). The goal of this assignment is to develop your hands-on skills in performing learning from data, as well as further understanding of the practical technical details of the learning procedure. For this assignment, your program should perform one of two tasks: Option 1: Demonstrate your understanding of a specific machine learning model within the context of the learning theory framework introduced in the subject. Your program should be designed to explain and illustrate the principles and functioning of the chosen algorithm, highlighting its benefits, drawbacks, and appropriate use-cases. Option 2: Propose a learning-based system to solve a practical task. This task can be anything from predicting stock prices to identifying patterns in images or text. Your program should implement the learning system, demonstrating its ability to learn from data and make accurate/useful predictions or decisions. Remember, the focus here is not merely on the practical problem, but also why you believe a learning-based system is an appropriate solution to it, and how. In both cases, you should tie your work back to the concepts and frameworks we've discussed in class. This task is AI open. You are encouraged to employ AI assistance tools to accomplish this task. You are required to explain the process of accomplishing the goal of the task. Therefore, the assessment of the submission will be according to the following procedure. Submission The assignment should be completed in three parts: a computer program implementing a machine learning model, an implementation memo and a presentation. The program and the memo will be submitted to fulfil this task: Computer program of a machine learning model. The implementation should be ready to run on a cloud-based platform. Project Implementation Journal. This is a detailed account of the entire journey of the project, including the design, implementation, log and reflection. Please pay special attention to account how you have utilised AI-tools to assist in each step. The submissions will be assessed during an interactive peer-review process according to the following criteria . The procedure of running the process is specified in Assessment Task 3 (where the aforementioned presentation is used). Important criteria: âCompleteness of Explanationâ: 1) you are able to independently explain a concept is considered as full understanding. OR 2) you are able to show evidence in the memo report that an issue has been queried with an AI-assistance, and the result has been critically studied is also considered as FULL understanding. âLinking Machine Learning Concepts with Program Componentsâ: you should be prepared to illustrate, upon request, how certain theoretical concepts have been designed, implemented, or reflected within your program. This demonstration should ideally be reflected within your memo report, drawing clear connections between machine learning theories and the practical aspects of your project. âFunctionalâ: the program runs without exception in anticipated cases. For edge cases, e.g. size of data being large for the complexity of the program, the issue has been expected and explained. More details will be released in specification documents on Canvas site.

Presentation and Peer Review (Presentation, 20%, Individual). This task requires you to both present your own work and to review the work of your peers. This will involve small group discussions including a tutor, allowing for deep dives into the material, and the provision of and response to constructive feedback. Part 1: Presentation of Your Work For the first part of this task, you are required to present the work you completed in Assignment 2. Your presentation should be succinct yet comprehensive, detailing the algorithm you implemented, the rationale behind your decisions, and your experiences and reflections during the implementation process. You should also discuss how you utilized AI-assistant tools (if any) and your approach towards data handling. Part 2: Peer Review In the second part of this task, you will switch roles and act as the reviewer for your peer's presentation. As you listen to their presentation, take notes on their approach, their algorithm choice and implementation, as well as any unique insights or methods they employed. Once they have finished presenting, provide them with constructive feedback and relevant comments. Part 3: Interactive Session Commentary Finally, comment on your peers' contributions during the interactive session. Consider their engagement in the discussion, clarity of explanations, ability to ask relevant questions, and responsiveness to feedback. NOTE : At the end of the review process, you will get a grading of BOTH Assessment Task 2 and 3.

Project Proposal & Learning Contract (Report, 0%, Individual). Each student must develop a project proposal which includes a learning contract and details of the project deliverable with their supervisor. The learning contract of the proposal must be approved by the subject coordinator.

Project Deliverable (Portfolio, 100%, Individual). Each student will produce the project deliverable - as specified in the project proposal. This portfolio must include a personal reflection report of 1 page on the competencies, skills and knowledge gained from the project.

Learning Journal (Exercises, 50%, Individual). This task is designed to help you capture and reflect on your learning through the semester.Â A range of 7 creative coding tasks will be assigned during the workshop. You will complete and present these tasks collaboratively in the workshop class, based on the preparation you have undertaken in response to the online lecture, and will describe your coding approach to your peers in detail, seeking and responding to critical feedback, and answering thoughtful questions. Some of the presentations will be peer-marked while others will be marked by the tutor. Your top 5 tasks will form the basis for your mark and the bottom 2 (including any non-submissions) will be dropped from your mark.Â Please note that attendance at the workshop is required to present these tasks to your tutor and your workshops class.Â

Individual Project (Project, 50%, Individual). This project allows you to develop an individual creative approach to a design task that encapsulates the topics discussed in this course, while exploiting your new knowledge of interactive media. Several detailed design briefs will be made available on the Canvas site, and students will develop a software tool that responds comprehensively and creatively to one of those briefs. Â Students who do not address one of the briefs supplied will be marked down proportionally to the relevance of their submission.Â The mark will reflect several progressive stages of development and their associated submission and discussion with peer feedback.Â Additionally, you should reflect on the design development, and relate the methods you decided to use to the creative outcome achieved. Students are reminded to review the assessment criteria and the marking rubric on the Canvas site.Â The final part of this assessment will be marked as an interactive oral assessment. This will mean that you will need to physically attend a location at Campus during the assessment period, and you will need to present and discuss the decisions you have made during your creative development of this project, as defined by the assessment rubric.Â

Business Proposal (Report, 30%, Individual). Comprehensively argue a business case for IT investment. The task is to write a business proposal to present to an organisation's Investment Review Board in relation to a set case study. The proposal should argue the case giving both arguments for and against the proposal and should examine some alternatives. Full details can be found on Canvas.

Management Report (Report, 30%, Individual). Raise awareness to senior management level about possible impacts of IT issues on overall company performance in view of mitigating those issues. The task is to prepare a report for senior management identifying an IT problem and suggesting a solution and its effect on technology, HR and change management. Full details can be found on Canvas.

Case Study Portfolio (Portfolio, 30%, Group, group assessed). Assess the scope and impact of an IT departments challenges in a wider commercial context. Students will work in teams throughout the semester and the tutorials to cover all aspects of the case study in a consistent way. This will be consolidated into a consistent and comprehensive portfolio representing the teamâs full understanding of the case study. Full details can be found on Canvas.
Contribution to discussion and engagement (Laboratory/practical, 10%, Individual)

Team Project (Project, 75%, Group, individually assessed). Putting theoretical skills to practice You will work on a major game project as a team. The work will be divided into 4 Sprints. Sprint 1: 15% Sprint 2: 20% Sprint 3: 20% Sprint 4: 20% For each Sprint, you will be required to set tasks to be completed by the end of the Sprint, estimate the amount of time you expect the tasks to take, record the tasks as they are completed and submit a Sprint report. Also, you must write a group and an individual reflection following the Recount-React-Analyse pattern. Sprint report templates with samples will be provided via Canvas. Intermediate deliverables: Sprint reports and demos of work in-progress. Final deliverables: Presentation and report.

Lab Exercises (Exercises, 25%, Group, group and individually assessed). Continuous building on skills. There are 4 separate deliverables for this assessment: 1- Build an Arcade Game from the 80s (from Scratch) and document the process (includes reflection) (5%); 2- Build an Arcade Game from the 90s (from Scratch) in teams using SCRUM (includes reflection) (5%); 3 - Build a Game to Client Specifications (Part 1). Design a Simple Game, Write User Stories and Find a Team that Builds your Game (5%); 4 - Build a Game to Client Specifications (Part 2). Implement a Game Following the User Stories written by another team (10%).

Game Production Project (Project, 100%, Group, individually assessed). Putting Theoretical Skills into Practice You will work collaboratively in teams on a major game development project across the semester. Where possible, you will also collaborate with Music and Sound Design students to support the integration of original audio assets into your game. The project will be organised into five Agile development sprints: Sprint 1: Game Design Document Sprint 2: Playable game prototype without sound Sprint 3: Game implementation with approximately 50% of audio assets integrated Sprint 4: Game implementation with approximately 75% of audio assets integrated Sprint 5: Final game build with complete audio integration For each sprint, teams will be required to define and allocate tasks, estimate development time, track progress as tasks are completed, and submit a Sprint Report and Game build. In addition, students must complete both group and individual reflections informed by Agile and SCRUM methodologies for Games Development. Sprint Report templates and sample submissions will be provided via Canvas. Intermediate deliverables include sprint reports and demonstrations of work-in-progress. Final deliverables include the completed game build and final Sprint Report.
Exercises (Exercises, 40%, Individual). To become familiar with the lecture contents Small practical exercises with Unity.

Storyboarding (Laboratory/practical, 10%, Group, individually assessed). Sketch the storyboard, character design, and environment design with a 2D sketch. Students can choose between animated sequences or interactive projects. Submission can be made in PDF or PowerPoint format (approx. 10-15 slides), with an optional 5-minute presentation video. If no video is submitted, a live online presentation is required. Storyboards contain a shot-by-shot visual plan, including camera angles, actions, characters, and interactions for interactive adventures. For interactive projects, explain planned interactions. Further details on the Canvas site.

Final Presentation with 3D characters Animation, Lighting and Written Report Objectives (Project, 50%, Group, individually assessed). To present the final animation and get feedback from an expert panel. To create a complete document for the final animation. Students are required to create and present a near-completed version of their final project on week 12, and submit the finalized version online by the end of week 14. The project is allowed to evolve from its storyboard version. During week 12, students should showcase a 30 to 90-second animation preview of the final project in class, which can be either an animated sequence or interactive. In addition, students are expected to deliver a brief 15-minute presentation in class using either a prerecorded video or live PowerPoint slides. This presentation should cover technical choices made and individual contributions to the project. By week 14, the final version of the project must be submitted, accompanied by a document outlining the changes made from the version presented in class and detailing each student's individual contributions. Further details on the Canvas site.

Research Diary/Project Logs (Reflection, 20%, Individual). This assessment task is to assess studentsâ ability to keep trace of project progress and carry out reflective practice. Students make regular entries to the research diary/project logs (minimum 2 entries per week) to record activities, meetings, progress, lessons learned and reflections (attach regular project meeting minutes which should be signed by the mentor). Detailed marking rubric will be provided in Canvas Assignments.

Project Report (Written submission, 40%, Individual). This assessment task is to assess studentsâ ability to report on what they have achieved in completing the project in a written format to general audience. Students need to develop a professional report to present the motivation behind the topic choice, a brief literature review / background study and a detailed description of the methodology used with justification, the research /development undertaken, the results and conclusions, and an outline of future research in the area or limitation of the solution. The report will be assessed for the quality of its written presentation (30%) and the quality of its content (70%). The quality of written presentation includes professional usage of English language and quality of presentation of project context. The quality of project content includes articulation of significance of the problem, clarity of problem statement/project objectives, suitability of methodology used, the amount of work, elegance and correctness of results/solutions, fairness of testing or evaluation, generality/applicability, and future work/limitations. Detailed marking rubric will be provided in Canvas Assignments.

Oral defense (Presentation, 40%, Individual). This assessment task is to assess studentsâ ability to present what they have done to achieve the project objectives and defense themselves for their claims, such as solving a problem using DA/AI solution. Students need to give an oral presentation of their projects and defense themselves for what they presented. The assessment panel may ask questions related to the originality of the work, problem/issues addressed, methodology used, results, evaluation and applicability of solutions, difficulties / challenges encountered, decisions made and why, lessons learned and future improvements, highs and lows in the project progression.

Topic review and discussion (Exercises, 25%, Individual). To demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the concept of IT strategy and business processes based on scholarly articles and real-world case studies. Online discussion (Part A) and analysis of relevant articles/real-world examples during tutorials (Part B). These topics will explore key topics supporting/complementing the subject matter. Students are required to participate in online discussion board forum and review/ analyse/complete the required articles, real-world scenarios, problem cases, and hands-on activities during tutorials

Group Project (Report, 45%, Group, individually assessed). To apply knowledge and theories gained during lectures and tutorials to develop an optimal strategic business & IT plan. Apply knowledge, theories, and insights gained during lectures and tutorials to a chosen case study. This is a group assessment. Students will be asked to prepare a report and present their understanding. Students will work in a project group to develop a business and IT strategic plan in response to a proposal request. Based on the provided scenario and additional research, the groups will be required to formulate/present a report for a business. This report will include an analysis of the company using Information Systems Strategy Triangle (business strategy, organisational strategy, and IT strategy), social business strategy, information resources strategy and other topics discussed in the subject. This assessment task includes the following components: (1) Report, (2) Presentation and (3) Peer Assessment.

Quiz 1 (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). To assess studentsâ knowledge, understanding, and insight gained during lectures and tutorials using MCQs and real-world scenario questions. This assessment includes in-class/tutorial quiz. Quiz questions contain multiple choice questions, fill in the blanks, matching words, true/ false and/or a realâworld case study with a set of questions about the topics covered in the lectures.

Quiz 2 (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). To assess studentsâ knowledge, understanding, and insight gained during lectures and tutorials using MCQs and real-world scenario questions. This assessment includes in-class/tutorial quiz. Quiz questions contain multiple choice questions, fill in the blanks, matching words, true/ false and/or a realâworld case study with a set of questions about the topics covered in the lectures.

Problem Formulation and Understanding the Domain through Literature and Data Review (Project, 30%, Individual). To formulate problem, and also to understand the problem domain and tools, learn about designing participatory modelling processes, identify limitations clearly and deeply before generating ideas or solutions. Students are to: Formulate Problem Individually, Represent the Problem Collect, Review and Incorporate Evidence in the form of Literature and Data Discuss the problem and receive feedback from students in the tutorial for collaboratively synthesising multiple viewpoints Individual Sections: Problem Representation Diagram, and Literature and Data Analysis.

Develop a Solution Evaluate Potential Change and Demonstrate Benefits Develop Prototype Proposal Development Develop Portfolio Report Groups will submit a report for grading. Collaborative Project Evaluation and Reflection (Reflection, 40%, Individual). To reflect on the effect of whole experience associated with peer review and evaluation of work of peers to oneself. This assignment consists of 3 parts, as shown below: Part 1: Reflection Weight: (Individual: 10%, Group: 0%) The students are encouraged to keep a Journal describing, and reflecting on, personal experience in a Collaboratory process that they undertook during your project work. Using this, the students will use reflection strategies to enhance studentsâ personal contributions to the workplace. In this reflective task, the students ask themselves questions such as what went well, what did not go well, how they could improve these in the future etc. It is understood that the reflection would be subjective. The marking will be for the quality of questions they ask themselves, and/or the responses that they would give to questions suggested by the instructors. Rubric will be provided separately. Part 2: Intra Team Evaluations Weight: (Individual: 10%, Group: 0%) Intra-Team Evaluation: The students would provide feedback about the performance of their peers as well as themselves. The responses would be submitted on SPARKPlus. Part 3: Presentation Weight: (Individual: 20%, Group: 0%) Groups will present and defend their problem formulation and solution in class and respond to questions raised by their lecturer and peers. Every student in the group must present their contribution to the group project. Rubric and specific instructions will be provided separately.

Serious Games Studio Project (Project, 100%, Group, individually assessed). You will work in a team to design, build, and evaluate your own serious game across the whole semester. Everything connects into one continuous project that develops step by step, like a real game studio. You will start by coming up with a game idea that addresses a real-world issue such as health, education, wellbeing, or the environment. Early on, you will also reflect on how your design would need to change if you were working with an Indigenous Australian community, using established cultural and intellectual property protocols discussed in class. From there, you will develop a full research and design proposal. This becomes your project roadmap and includes your Game Design Document, background research, and a plan for how you will evaluate whether your game actually works as intended. Next, you will build a small proof-of-concept prototype. This is not about polish, it is about testing whether your core idea works in practice and learning from it early. After that, you will expand and refine your game into a more complete playable prototype, using feedback and testing to improve your design and systems. Finally, you will submit your finished prototype along with a short research report that explains what you built, how it evolved, how you tested it, and what you learned through the process. Sprint 1: Game Concept & Cultural ReflectionÂ (20%) Sprint 2: Research & Game Design ProposalÂ (20%) Sprint 3: Proof of Concept PrototypeÂ (20%) Sprint 4: Final Game & Research ReportÂ (40%) Sprint Report templates and sample submissions will be provided via Canvas.
Quizzes (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). Multiple choice questions

Data Exploration and Preparation (Report, 35%, Individual). Individual assessment. This assignment includes practical work on data visualisation, exploration and preparation (preprocessing and transformation) for data analytics.

Data mining in action (Report, 50%, Individual). Students will use several classifiers for a predictive analytics task. They will choose among the methods from class, but probably others of their own choosing. All the classification models should be submitted to Kaggle, and then select the best one to participate in the competition. Students must submit a report of about 15 pages discussing how they solved the problem and give results.

Programming Assignment 1 (Project, 20%, Individual). This assessment task allows you to demonstrate an understanding of some of the data structuresÂ and algorithms covered in the course to this point, and their implementation in C++. Students will gain a greater understanding of how data structures in the C++ standard library are implemented, and explore how algorithmic decisions affect the performance of a program. Given a specification, create a well designed and well tested command line program in C++.

Programming Assignment 2 (Project, 30%, Individual). This assessment task builds on the skills and knowledge you have developed through the subject and combines more complicated data structures and algorithms in a more sophisticated manner, allowing you to demonstrate ability in advanced programming and a higher level understanding of the main topics areas of the subject. Given a specification, create a well-designed and tested program in C++.

Final Examination (Examination, 30%, Individual). The final exam assesses your grasp of the discipline knowledge component of the subject. It also allows you to demonstrate your ability to communicate algorithm and data structure design ideas in short form. Take-home open-book exam format. The questions will include a mixture of multiple choice and short coding questions. The questions will cover the whole range of material presented in the lectures and the laboratories. The questions will test the students understanding of the material rather than how much they remember.

Weekly theoretical and practical exercises (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). Every week there will be short multiple choice quiz and a programming exercise. The quiz aims to provide regular feedback and basic assessment of your progress through the course by addressing key knowledge points. Programming is a skill that requires consistent practice which is provided by the weekly programming exercise. This allows you to interact with the material from lecture by coding it yourself, and to engage in algorithmic problem solving. This assessment forms the primary routine feedback channel for the subject. The quizzes and coding exercises will be administered through Ed.

Project Identification (Report, 20%, Individual). Identify and analyse an economic problem related to a current, real-world IT project within an organisation/start-up. You will research publicly available information, submit an analysis, engage with peers and form a group for future assignments.

Group Project: Financial Analysis and Presentation (Report, 30%, Group, group assessed). Building on the work completed in Assignment 1, this group project focuses on developing a financial model for the selected IT-related project/start-up business and analysing its current and future performance. This assignment encourages teamwork and applies the knowledge gained through tutorials, workshops, and online Canvas materials. Report (18%) + Presentation (12%)

Group Report and Presentation: Final Project Feasibility Analysis (Presentation, 50%, Group, individually assessed). Building on Assignment 2, where your group created a financial model and presented initial findings, Assignment 3 requires your group to produce a comprehensive written report and a final presentation evaluating the IT projectâs feasibility for expansion, replacement or investment. This assessment integrates detailed financial analysis with professional reporting and presentation skills. The video should be content presented in an appropriate format for the target audience. Report (35%) + (15%) presentation

Project Requirements and Specifications (Essay, 25%, Group, individually assessed). This assignment will require each group of 5-6 students to produce a written document containing requirements and specifications for an image processing and pattern recognition project. The project topic should be granted approval by the lecturer. The specifications must cover: analysis of the problem, including the availability of one or more suitable, public datasets; selection of the techniques that the students expect to solve the problem. This will include various, plausible alternatives; motivation for the approach based on the knowledge acquired during lectures and independent readings; a performance evaluation methodology which will be used to assess the approachâs performance. This will require conducting experiments on the chosen dataset(s) with the various alternative techniques and collate their performance; a list of references; the contribution of each student to the group will be described in a short table in the report.

Project Implementation (Project, 50%, Group, individually assessed). This assignment will require each group of students to implement the project described in their Assignment 1. The project will be developed as a Matlab program. The contribution of each student to the group will be described in a short table in the report. This assignment will consist of a written report on the outcomes of the project

Project Presentation (Presentation, 25%, Group, individually assessed). This assignment will require each group of students to present their project as a video presentation. The presentation will be based on PowerPoint slides describing the project and a demo of the program. Each member of the group will deliver a part of the presentation and the PowerPoint slides and one video for the entire team will be submitted by the students using Canvas.

Review Quiz (Quiz/test, 5%, Individual). To ensure pre requisites are well understood and ensure appropriate and tailored feedback is provided to enable catching up where required. This will be a review quiz consisting of short answer questions covering pre requisite knowledge for remainder of the subject.

Project Report Part A (Report, 10%, Group, group assessed). To ensure that the choices of an ISD project can be argued and justified. Prepare a report for the business case of a business system and a method engineered to support its development. Students are required to argue for their proposed approach by comparing aspects of methodologies and outlining the benefits and drawbacks of each.

Review Quiz 2 (Quiz/test, 5%, Individual). To ensure that students are up-to-date and provide appropriate and tailored feedback to enable catching up where required. This will be a review quiz consisting of short answer questions covering knowledge from the first 9 weeks of the subject.

Project Report Part B (Report, 25%, Group, group assessed). To ensure that a professional analysis and development report of an ISD project can be produced. Prepare a report for the development methodology of a business system. Students are required to argue for their proposed approach by comparing aspects of methodologies and outlining the benefits and drawbacks of each.

Project Presentation (Presentation, 15%, Individual). To ensure that a professional oral presentation can be delivered to describe the work done in an ISD project and to be able to defend design choices if required Presentations for Assessment 2 will take place towards the end of the session, and all students are expected to be present and participate in a formal presentation of the project.

Students will write a report on the elements to be included while developing a contract for outsourcing IT operations and IT management. Refer assignment instructions under âAssignmentsâ in Canvas.

Take-Home Examination (Examination, 20%, Individual). To demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the concepts thought at the lectures and tutorials by applying them in a case study. The examination will include materials discussed in the class, tutorials and assessment tasks. Take-home examination is maximum of 2,000 words.

Contribution to discussion and engagement (Laboratory/practical, 10%, Individual). To apply knowledge and theories gained during lectures and tutorials to discussions at online lectures and tutorials by engaging with the lecturer, tutors and students by asking questions and giving comments. Contribution to discussion and engagement in your tutorial will take various forms within the tutorials. Assessment will be made by your tutor only.

Journal Assignment (Journal, 20%, Individual). To develop studentsâ sensitivities and perceptions about how people use technology in their everyday activities and the ability to articulate various issues around the design and use of technology from the perspective of its usability and usefulness. Â Students will work individually to produce three journal entries describing and critiquing real-world digital systems in terms of their design and use, that are relevant to the interests of the subject. While students are provided with the actual digital systems they have to write about for entries #1 and #2, they will have to actively seek out their own example for entry #3. For these journal entries, students have to observe and documentÂ people's interactions with the systems as well as apply their understanding of various design/usability concepts, theories and principles to analyse and critique the experience people have during these interactions. These may include poorly designed systems that do not support the activity they are used for, as well as systems that work well within their situation of use. Design & Build a Board Game (Project, 25%, Group, group and individually assessed). This is a group assignment. Design and construct a board game in a randomly assigned group. Game Critique (Report, 30%, Individual). This is an individual assignment. Present a critique report on a digital game based on the concepts taught in class. Design a digital game as a group using a modern game engine. Programming Exercises (Laboratory/practical, 30%, Individual). Individual work on lab exercises. The weekly lab exercises are designed to instruct students on fundamental game development techniques. This promotes students to be proactive in their own learning and establish them as life-long learners in the constantly evolving game development industry.
Quiz (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). This is an individual in-class, open book quiz based on content taught in class.

Classic Game Recreation - Getting Started (Project, 20%, Individual). This assessment requires students to apply what they have learned to recreate a classic 2D game, drawn from the early eras of the games industry. At this stage, the project will need to have the scene for a single level set up, visual assets and animations created, audio files included and basic player movement functionality implemented. This will be a re-skinned game, meaning that all visual assets (sprites and animations) must be made by the student and audio files will need to be sourced from royalty-free providers, such that the game operates in the same way as the original while looking and sounding distinctly different to the original. Additional assessment details and marking rubric will be provided on Canvas.

Classic Game Recreation - Enhancing and Innovating (Project, 35%, Individual). This assessment extends upon Assessment 3 by requiring students to produce two scenes in their recreated game. While lower grade bands are achievable through knowledge and skills presented in the lectures, higher grade bands will require students to carefully plan solutions to previously unseen problems and be proactive in their learning to implement these. The second scene of the game will contain the student's own innovative twist to the core game mechanics and player experience, which exposes students to a design and development cycle of original content. Students are encouraged to push the boundaries of their skill in this second scene and seek new knowledge in order to implement their novel gameplay design. Additional assessment details and marking rubric will provided on Canvas.

Peer Assessment - Each individual member of the team will be required to assess each member of their team (including themselves) as per the assignment sheet and as discussed in the first lecture.. 3. The intent of this task is to help students understand how business problems can be identified and framed from a data analytics perspective. Students examine a business or organisational dataset to identify potential business problems that could be investigated using data analytics. They describe the dataset, key variables, business context, and likely stakeholders, then propose three business problems with relevant analytical questions and decision-making implications. Students must also use generative AI strategically and transparently to support at least one part of the task. Their reflection should explain how AI was used to refine, critique, justify, and communicate their ideas. The final submission should demonstrate strong human judgement, substantial refinement, and clear ownership of the work.

Data Exploration and Preparation (Written submission, 35%, Individual). The intent is to master basic data exploration and preparation skills for data analytics. This assignment includes practical work on data visualisation, exploration and preparation (preprocessing and transformation) for data analytics. The final submission should demonstrate strong human judgement, substantial refinement, and clear ownership of the work, if AI tools are used.

Data Analytics in Action (Combination, 50%, Individual). The intent is to utilise data analytics skills for problem-solving. Students will be allocated a group of classifiers to use for a predictive analytics task. They must use at least all classifiers within the group, but more probably several other methods of their own choosing to solve the problem.Â Students must submit a written report discussing how they solved the problem and give results. This will contribute to 60% of the marks.Â The final submission should demonstrate strong human judgement, substantial refinement, and clear ownership of the work, if AI is used. Each student will also undertake a short interactive oral defence of their work. This will contribute to 40% of the overall marks. At the interactive oral defence, students will answer questions about their classifier(s) showing the workflow or code depending on implementation tools.

Task 1 - Building Research Skills (Exercises, 15%, Individual). To become an independent researcher. To develop the skills of working collaboratively and talking informally about research. Demonstrate an independent approach to the mastery of foundational research skills. In-class exercises require students to undertake a series of practical activities aimed at building skills in conduction literature reviews and developing research proposals. Â

Literature Review (Literature review, 45%, Individual). To establish search skills and the ability to evaluate the appropriateness of the articles chosen. To develop the skills of critical analysis and synthesis, direct and indirect citation, referencing and the writing of a complete report. Students will select a topic and conduct a search of the literature relevant to their research topic and write a literature review, which includes title page, table of contents, introduction, critical evaluation of the sources, literature review, conclusion, reference list and appendix.

Project Proposal (Report, 40%, Group, individually assessed). To identify a significant research problem applicable to the industry context, to add depth to their knowledge and understanding of a field in which they are interested, and to design a method for addressing the question. Students will develop a project proposal in a group (up to three students) or individually for the industry or academic, demonstrating that the student engages in genuine enquiry and investigates something worthwhile. This industry-style or academic report will link the proposed research question and literature review, linking existing knowledge, ideas, facts, technologies, and relevant solutions. It should be suitable and feasible for the execution of the student's capstone project in the subsequent session. The report must contain the following elements: Cover Page, Executive Summary (or Abstract), Table of Contents, Introduction, Research Aims and Objectives, Background, Research Significance and Innovation, Research Methods, Indigenous Research Protocol and Assessment, Project Plan and Resources, Conclusion Reference List and Appendix.

Compare and evaluate different visualisations of a data set (Report, 30%, Individual). Collect a dataset, students apply a range of different visualisation methods. Students compare each method and evaluate their suitability for the data and for different users.

Create a data visualisation of a dataset that includes a range of complex data types (Project, 30%, Individual). Given a dataset containing a range of data types, students are required to verify dataset first, then to develop an effective data visualisation that successfully conveys key insights. Students will use a range of interactive data visualisation techniques to ensure users are able to comprehend, navigate and effectively explore the dataset.

Create an interactive data visualisation that enables users to discover and communicate data-driven stories (Project, 40%, Individual). Given a data set, each student is required to create an interactive data visualisation that supports the discovery and communication of narratives in the context of the data's business domain. Students will need to select and customise a range of interactive data visualisation techniques to enable this.
Quizzes (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). Quizzes are presented as multiple choice questions per topic out of 6 weeks. These are completed online and students receive immediate feedback.

Proposal on Real-world Data Analysis Project using Machine Learning (Project, 35%, Individual). You will propose a machine-learning solution for a business problem. In this assignment, you are required to demonstrate your understanding of the principles introduced in the subject and apply the principles in a practical scenario. The goal of this assignment is to develop your skills in applying the knowledge to real-world learning-based and data-driven projects, as well as further understanding of the practical techniques and methods. There are two business problems from which you can pick one. The detailed specification of each use case and an example template will be provided on the Canvas site.

Technical understanding of basic machine learning models (Project, 45%, Individual). Following on from Assessment Task 2, you will now move to the implementation stage of the machine learning project. You will be given the code skeleton with some missing parts for the selected project from Assessment Task 2 and then you will have two options: a) complete the code to get the results and then explain and translate model results into business criteria and how it is aligned with business objectives in Assessment 2 or; b) complete., extend and improve the code to get higher performance results and explain how you technically achieve better results and what can be done to improve it even further. The goal of this assignment is to develop your technical and programming skills to implement the ML solution to the business problem and translate the results back to business objectives.

SQL Lab Test (Laboratory/practical, 40%, Individual). Demonstrate SQL skills. In this lab test, students will be required to successfully translate the given question statements in English into SQL queries that run on a computer. The queries are single table queries. Each query will be marked as correct or incorrect. The database to be used in this lab exam will be provided.

MiniDatabaseProject (Report, 60%, Individual). Test all advanced database development skills. Students will create a script file to build a database. Minimum necessary conditions, such as minimum number of tables, and minimum number of relationship types, that will be specified in a separate document.

Quiz (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). The quiz consists of a small number (10 - 20) of multiple choice questions. The quiz will explore the extent of your knowledge and understanding across the weekly topics. The questions will be taken from: The Lecture slides and Readings for weeks 1 - 6. The Labs for Lectures 1 - 6. To answer the questions correctly you need to understand the question topic. To do this you will need to attend the weekly lecture/discussion sessions, perform the weekly lab and discuss the lab questions with your group and read the weekly readings. There will be a quiz Q&A document released two weeks before the quiz. There will be a practice quiz a week before the quiz.

Case Study (Case study, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Case Studies are designed for students to practice their skills their skill in locating digital forensic evidence in supplied logs and traces in a real world environment. The topic is chosen from a list provided. Students need to research the topic online, download and explore some apps/tools and prepare a report and short presentation. Students need to provide detail in depth so that others can replicate the work. Students need to submit a Proposal to confirm the assignment topic and plan in the middle of the semester. By the end of the semester, students need to submit a Report and give a Presentation. There will be a proposal guide and report guide in the assignment introduction. Feedback will be provided via Canvas.

Skills tests (Demonstration, 30%, Individual). Skills Based Assessments (SBAs) are designed for students to demonstrate their skill in locating forensic evidence on a digital device. Students are given an image file acquired from a suspect's laptop and asked to assess if allegations of failing to comply with company policies regarding the use of company time or intellectual property are proven. Topics are taken from the weekly labs.

Weekly Skills Test (Laboratory/practical, 20%, Group, individually assessed). For students to demonstrate mastery of weekly lab concepts. Students are given a small assignment to complete in each week's lab class. Students can complete the assignment in class or in their own time. There will be 10 weekly tasks, each worth 2%. Students upload their answers for tutor feedback prior to the next lab class.

Combined Module Tests (Exercises, 25%, Individual). This assessment consists of three separate online tests conducted via UTS Canvas under restricted open-book conditions. Each test evaluates the content covered from either the start of the session or the conclusion of the previous test up to the week of the current test. During the tests, students are permitted to useÂ one double-sided, A4-sized sheet of handwritten notes . No other printed or digital materials are allowed, including Canvas lecture slides, tutorial handbooks, and external websites. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited.

Skills Based Assessment (Laboratory/practical, 35%, Individual). The Skills-Based Assessments (SBAs) are designed for students to demonstrate their practical understanding of network security. This individual, restricted open-book assessment is conducted in class during students' scheduled tutorial/lab sessions using Packet Tracer software. Assessment questions will be released via Canvas at the specified assessment time. During the assessment, students are permitted to useÂ one double-sided, A4-sized sheet of handwritten notes . No other printed or digital materials are allowed, including Canvas lecture slides, tutorial handbooks, and external websites. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited.

End-of-session Quiz (Quiz/test, 40%, Individual). This individual, restricted open-book test consists of short-answer questions conducted via UTS Canvas. The test will be completed in class during the scheduled session time and covers the concepts and knowledge studied throughout the semester. During the test, students are permitted to useÂ one double-sided, A4-sized sheet of handwritten notes . No other printed or digital materials are allowed, including Canvas lecture slides, tutorial handbooks, and external websites. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited.

Quiz on subject (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). To provide students with an awareness of human-centred research methods as taught in this subject. Students are quizzed on their understanding of the subject matter, the way the subject itself is set up, and their responsibilities as ethical and people-focused researchers.

Poster on interviews (Report, 30%, Group, individually assessed). To provide students with the opportunity to put into practice and further develop skills in human-centred research. This includes literature research, developing relevant questions, performing interviews, qualitative data analysis, and communication of findings. The assignment requires students to work in groups of 3 or 4. They study and develop a research proposal, followed by contacting potential participants and performing in-depth interviews. Afterwards, students are encouraged to learn substantial methods for the analysis of data and its reporting. Online tutorials and class meetings give students the opportunity to receive guidance and feedback on their progress. SPARKPlus will be used to answer questions about groupwork after submission.

Short report on probe design (Report, 10%, Individual). To provide students with the opportunity to put into practice and further develop skills in human-centered research. Following the direction set out in task 2, this task approaches similar research questions with another qualitative research tool, namely probes. Students will learn its application and analysis, and communication of findings. The assignment requires students to independently design and develop a probe kit, explain the research goal of the kit and how each of the probe kit elements contribute to reaching this goal. Visual material, such as sketches or photos should be included of the draft probe design. A draft positive and respectful informed consent form needs to be attached. A description should be added of the participant the student has invited to participate in their research, without revealing their identity. Online tutorials and class meetings give students the opportunity to receive guidance and feedback on their progress.

Presentation of analysis, short paper and video on probe study (Combination, 50%, Individual). To provide students with the opportunity to put into practice and further develop skills in human-centered research. Following the direction set out in Assessment Task 2 (group work), this task approaches similar research questions with another qualitative research method, namely probes. Students will learn its application and analysis, and communication of findings. The assignment requires students to individually study and develop a research proposal, followed by contacting a participant and asking them some questions (intro interview), then handing them a self-made probe kit and after pick-up performing an in-depth face-to-face interview (exit interview). In the last tutorial before the Assessment Task 4 submission deadline each student will be required to present the outcome of their thematic analysis in-class.Â This is a compulsory item to be able to get marks for Assessment Task 4. Compared to Assessment Task 2, this individual task puts more emphasis on the quality of writing a paper and dissemination of findings in an academic way. Due to the visual and physical nature of the probes method, a video deliverable enables students to communicate that part of their work effectively. Students need to demonstrate awareness and implementation of positive and respectful ethical practices. This includes applying the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander (AIATSIS) Code of Ethics when working with and for Indigenous Australians; demonstrating that they have gained approval of free, prior, and informed consent; and attaching a completed ethics form.

Quiz 1 (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). This task assesses student knowledge on the content presented within the first half of the session, including ray tracing vs raster, coordinate systems, camera views, vector and matrix mathematics, lighting, and shading. This quiz is in an open-book / open internet format and is to be completed during the lab of the specified week. The quiz will be completed on Canvas and students will be provided with a code in the lab to access the quiz. This is an individual assessment and students are expected to complete the quiz without communicating with other students.

Quiz 2 (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). This task assesses student knowledge on the content presented within the first half of the session, including the OpenGL pipeline, 3D modeling representations, texturing methods, and shaders. This quiz is in an open-book / open internet format and is to be completed during the lab of the specified week. The quiz will be completed on Canvas and students will be provided with a code in the lab to access the quiz. This is an individual assessment and students are expected to complete the quiz without communicating with other students.

Exercises (Exercises, 20%, Individual). To become familiar with the lecture contents and acquire the coding skills needed to assemble the final project. Small practical exercises with the framework explained in class.

Group Project Presentation and Quality (Presentation, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). This task assesses individual contributions to the group project and the extent of each individualâs knowledge via a presentation and open dialogue with the lecturer. Students will work in 3-5 members to produce a substantial and authentic offline 3D web application prototype. Groups will choose to work on one of a small number of specified applications, otherwise groups may propose their application designs in discussion with the lecturer if they wish. The aim here is to produce an application that would have real-world value, which can be added to future employment portfolios. These applications will utilize knowledge learnt during the lectures and labs and require group members to broaden their knowledge through self-learning of relevant topics. Groups are required to present their project in week 12 to the rest of the class, with each group member talking about the project's contributions. Each group will have 10 minutes, including the time to present and time for the lecturer and peers to ask questions. Students will be assessed on the degree of their contribution to the project and the depth of their knowledge on their contribution areas. We will assess the individual contribution in week 12 through the presentation (30%). Group members are expected to contribute evenly to the project, and this is assessed via the âGroup Graphics Project - Presentationâ assessment task. The group will be assessed as a whole on the quality and technical difficulty of the application from a user experience perspective as well as a coding and solution design perspective. User Experience Journal Entries (Journal, 20%, Individual). To assess studentsâ understanding of different aspects of user experience. This includes both the conceptual and practical aspects of user experiences when people use interactive technologies in their everyday lives. These journal entries are aimed at developing studentsâ sensitivities and perceptions about how people experience their use of interactive technologies in their everyday lives, and the ability to articulate how various factors influence people's user experiences arising during-and-through their use of interactive technologies. See Canvas for details on the assignmentsâ formats and submission requirements.

Design Assignment (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). To provide students with opportunities to practise a Human-Centred Design methodology to focus on designing to support User Experience through combining user research, design and evaluation activities including theory, exploratory and experimental studies, prototyping and evaluation. Students will work individually and in teams of 4-5 to develop the interaction design for a system that supports good user experience . The project and the problem have been designed to provide opportunities to practise a human-centred design methodology in user experience design by combining user research, design ideation, prototyping methods and evaluation activities. Through this, students will develop personas, user stories, ideation, prototypes of the systems and evaluation of these prototypes in real life situations to refine the design of the system. Exercises during tutorials will provide students with opportunities to familiarise themselves with the various user experience techniques and tools used in this assignment. Work conducted during tutorials will also provide opportunities for students to familiarise themselves with the specific requirements of the assignment and more importantly, receive guidance and formative feedback on their understanding of the skills and evolving thinking about design. See Canvas for details on the assignments' formats and submission requirements.

Reflection and Personal Portfolio (Portfolio, 30%, Individual). To evaluate studentsâ capacity to collaborate and contribute to their own and their peers' learning as well as to reflect upon their own understanding and proficiency of the range of skills and tools used in user experience design. This is an individual assessment that contains two parts. In the first part, students will examine how they have engaged their audience in a positive and respectful manner. Students will critically reflect on how this knowledge will influence their future professional practice when working with, and for, Indigenous Australians. In the second part, students will create and present a Personal Portfolio which consists of a carefully chosen compilation of work samples the student has personally created during this subject. The portfolio is a valuable resource that students can use to demonstrate their work, their skills and their proficiency with various tools work to prospective employers. As such, it should be organised, accessible and purposeful without overwhelming the reader. Students should choose work samples that reflect and demonstrate the development of their skills in using various tools to support designing for UX. They could be related to sketches, personas, scenarios, user journeys, as well as stories and the re-creations of these stories through pictures and videos, and so on. See Canvas for details on the assignmentâs format and submission requirements.
Quizzes (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). Quizzes are presented as multiple choice, 2-4 questions per week for ten weeks. These are completed in class and students receive immediate feedback.

Algorithm Implementation and Journal Reflection (Project, 50%, Individual). The goal of this assignment is to develop both your hands-on skills and the capability to apply theory to analysis of practical problems in performing learning from data. For this assignment, your program should perform one of two tasks: Option 1: Demonstrate your understanding of a specific machine learning model within the context of the learning theory framework introduced in the subject. Your program should be designed to explain and illustrate the principles and functioning of the chosen algorithm, highlighting its benefits, drawbacks, and appropriate use-cases. You should present a clear map between your program and the core components of a learning system that will be discussed in the subject. Option 2: Propose a learning-based system to solve a practical task. This task can be anything from predicting stock prices to identifying patterns in images or text. Your program should implement the learning system, demonstrating its ability to learn from data and make accurate/useful predictions or decisions. Remember, the focus here is not merely on the practical problem but also why you believe a learning-based system is an appropriate solution to it, and how. You should provide a feasibility analysis regarding extending the implemented prototype system to production environments. In both cases, you should tie your work back to the concepts and frameworks we've discussed in class. This task is AI open. You are encouraged to employ AI assistance tools to accomplish this task. You are required to explain the process of accomplishing the goal of the task. Therefore, the assessment of the submission will be according to the following procedure. Submission The assignment should be completed in three parts: a computer program implementing a machine learning model, an implementation memo and a presentation. The program and the memo will be submitted to fulfil this task: Computer program of a machine learning model. The implementation should be ready to run on a cloud-based platform. Project Implementation Journal. This is a detailed account of the entire journey of the project, including the design, implementation, log and reflection. Please pay special attention to account how you have utilised AI-tools to assist in each step. T he submissions will be assessed during an interactive peer-review process according to the following criteria. The procedure of running the process is specified in Assessment Task 3 (where the aforementioned presentation is used). Important criteria: âCompleteness of Explanationâ: 1) you are able to independently explain a concept. OR 2) you are able to show evidence in the memo report that an issue has been queried with an AI-assistance, and the result has been critically studied. âLinking Machine Learning Concepts with Program Componentsâ: you should be prepared to illustrate, upon request, how certain theoretical concepts have been designed, implemented, or reflected within your program. This demonstration should ideally be reflected within your memo report, drawing clear connections between machine learning theories and the practical aspects of your project. âFunctionalâ: the program runs without exception in anticipated cases. For edge cases, e.g. size of data being large for the complexity of the program, the issue has been expected and explained. More details will be released in specification documents on Canvas site.

Presentation and Peer Review (Presentation, 20%, Individual). Task : This task requires you to both present your own work and to review the work of your peers. This will involve small group discussions including a tutor, allowing for deep dives into the material, and the provision of and response to constructive feedback. Part 1: Presentation of Your Work For the first part of this task, you are required to present the work you completed in Assignment 2. Your presentation should be succinct yet comprehensive, detailing the algorithm you implemented, the rationale behind your decisions, and your experiences and reflections during the implementation process. You should also discuss how you utilized AI-assistant tools (if any) and your approach towards data handling. Part 2: Peer Review In the second part of this task, you will switch roles and act as the reviewer for your peer's presentation. As you listen to their presentation, take notes on their approach, their algorithm choice and implementation, as well as any unique insights or methods they employed. Once they have finished presenting, provide them with critical and constructive feedback and relevant comments. Part 3: Interactive Session Commentary Finally, comment on your peers' contributions during the interactive session. Consider their engagement in the discussion, clarity of explanations, ability to ask relevant questions, and responsiveness to feedback. NOTE : At the end of the review process, you will get a grading of BOTH Assessment Task 2 and 3

Dynamic Web Interface to a Database System (Project, 40%, Individual). This is an individual programming assignment where students have to demonstrate the use of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and MySQL/MongoDB to design and implement a single-page dynamic website for a real-case application.

This is a group programming assignment where students have to demonstrate the use of JSON and ReactJS (or comparable alternative libraries/frameworks) in the development of a relatively complex website. The required submissions include a demonstration of a fully functional multi-page website, relevant source code (preferably with GitHub traces), and a clear statement of the workload allocation among group members to assist the assessment of individual contributions in the assignment. The group component (website design, functional completeness, consistent layout, intuitive navigation,Â speed, unified version control, and statement of workload allocation) and the individual component (individual coding of the allocated portion of the website) account for 15% and 25%, respectively.Â Details about the assessment criteria across the group and individual components will be available on Canvas.

Online Quizzes (Quiz, 20%, Individual). There will be two multiple-choice quizzes regarding the content of the subject: one in the middle and one at the end of the session. Each quiz will be worth 10%, and students have 20 minutes to complete all questions and submit their answers. Late submissions won't be accepted, and no make-up quizzes are available.

Networking Skills Test (In session exam, 20%, Individual). This is a lab-based skills test. It will provide the opportunity for students to demonstrate their system administration skills and record keeping techniques. Be able to set up initial system configuration including network configurations.

Lab-based group Q&A discussions and individual Quizzes (Combination, 30%, Individual). To allow students to gain feedback on their understanding of lab activities and key topics taught in this subject. This task includes five lab-based Q&A activities, which account for 15% of the total grade, and three lab-based quizzes, which account for 15%. For the Q&A component, students work in groups to answer questions related to the laboratory experiments (e.g., "What happens if a variable in a function is changed?") and submit their observations and results in writing. This component isÂ group-assessed . For the quiz component, students complete online tests individually during the laboratory sessions. This component isÂ individually assessed .

Final Skills Test (In session exam, 40%, Individual). The assignment provides students with the opportunity to demonstrate their learning outcomes and to evaluate the techniques they have acquired through the lab sessions. This is a lab-based skills test that assesses studentsâ technical skills developed in the lab sessions, focusing on system administration and network servers. Students are allowed to refer to their learning journals, use the LinuxÂ man Â andÂ info Â commands on their virtual Linux servers, and use their Windows servers to assist them during the test.

Learning Journal (Reflection, 10%, Individual). The use of a learning journal (also called an Engineering journal) will encourage students to keep good logbooks for systems under their control and to foster reflective learning by conducting further research on related knowledge. This should be developed over the entire semester and will be used in the skills test and assignment. The assignment will ask students to demonstrate their skills to summarise lecture contents, lab practices, and their findings during practice.

Mid-session Assessment (In session exam, 10%, Group, group and individually assessed). The purpose of this early session assessment is to provide students with early feedback, enabling them to adjust their learning strategies and enhance their learning efficiency. This assessment consists of twoÂ equally weighted tasks: Part I Subnetting QuizÂ (50%): is anÂ individualÂ assessment task that requires each student to subnet an IPv4 network with VLSM to meet the specified requirements within a set time limit. This is a closed-book assessment. No references, calculators, mobile phones, smartwatches, or any electronic devices are permitted during the assessment. Part II SBA1 Â (50%): is a group-based, hands-on practical task assessed as a group. In this task, each group is required to build a small network using the allocated hardware and perform basic configurations to establish end-to-end connectivity within a set time limit.Â Handwritten notes are allowed for this task, but they must not include the full network configuration script of any network. Students who miss their scheduled session due to illness or other documented legitimate reasons may be rescheduled for a later or alternative time within the same week, as much as practically feasible. However, if this rescheduling is not possible, the student will receive a zero for this component.

Case Study (Project, 20%, Group, group and individually assessed). As an authentic, comprehensive assignment, this assessment task provides an opportunity for students to integrate individual topics covered in each week into a real network. This assessment task is a comprehensive project that covers all the main topics for this subject. It is to be completed as a group activity outside of scheduled class time, with 75 percent of its total marks being awarded individually. The task involves designing, implementing and testing a small-to-medium-sized network based on the requirements specified in the Case Study document that will be issued in Week 3. Groups are to read the requirements, and design, build and test the network progressively as the topics required are covered during lab sessions. The Case Study will be assessed as a group-based assignment and consists of the following two-stage submissions: Part A: IPv4 Addressing Milestone Submission (25%): Each group as a whole is required to submit their IPv4 addressing scheme to their instructor before the milestone due day for feedback. A copy of the PT file completed by the group should also be submitted for feedback. Late Submission: Please note that since feedback and detailed solutions will be provided in Week 11, late submissions will not be accepted. It is worth noting that the workload for properly completing this assignment is not trivial. The preparation for this task will help students prepare for the final assessments.

Final Skills-based Assessment (Practical test, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). As a final practical assessment, this assessment task evaluates students' competency on their hands-on skills. This is a hands-on practical assessment based on group work. For a typical group of three students, 80% of the marks are awarded for items on which each student in the group is assessed individually and the remaining 20% is group assessed. In case of other group sizes, the task will be adjusted to match the group size. Given the network specifications and detailed tasks, each group will have approximately one hour to build a small-to-medium-sized network using real equipment allocated by the instructors. Students are expected to apply their knowledge and skills to cable the network, configure devices, and troubleshoot as necessary to demonstrate the network's connectivity and functionality. Students may use their handwritten Engineering Journals/notes, subject to the instructors' inspection.

Final Exam (Final exam, 40%, Individual). This assessment is to evaluate students' overall performance of achieving the subject learning objectives. This task is a restricted open-book, individual assessment held on campus during the exam period. Students are permitted to use one double-sided A4 page of handwritten notes. Each student will have two hours to complete up to fifteen short-answer questions. The questions will be based on the key concepts presented during weekly lectures, as well as labs, during the whole session. Sample questions will be made available towards the end of the session.

Individual Report (Report, 20%, Individual). The report will help students gain a deeper understanding of Global Information System issues, both theoretically and practically through a critical examination of literature published in books, refereed journals, conference proceedings etc., published after 2010. A minimum of 20 separate articles and/or books should be accessed as a basis for the report. Report on the trends in globalisation. It will be greatly beneficial for students to be present during the lectures to understand what is going on and to write their Report.

Group Assignment Report (Report, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). The report helps to gain a general understanding of global information systems and how organisations attempt to leverage business performance and even deliver new business directions. Assignment 2 Report (30%) is a group work, wherein students are expected to work on a substantial problem related to global information systems and global business. Creation of a project report and presentation of the project will be done in a group. All presentations will take place towards the end of the semester, and students are expected to be present and participate in the formal presentation of the project. Soft copies of both the report and presentation are required.
