If you have trouble with the operation of your group, ask the Subject coordinator for advice (preferably ask as a group). If some of the groups feel that other members are not contributing, the Lecturer should be informed and a group meeting held to produce a solution. In extreme cases a group member may be asked by the lecturer to do extra work or accept a lower mark. No complaints about group operation will be considered after the assignment has been handed in to the lecturer.

Take-Home Examination (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). To demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the concepts thought at the lectures and tutorials by applying them in a case study. Based on topics covered in the class, reading material provided and research expected of the students.

Contribution to discussion and engagement (Laboratory/practical, 10%, Individual). To apply knowledge and theories gained during lectures and tutorials to discussions at tutorials by engaging with the tutors and students by asking questions and giving comments. When evaluating your contributions, your lecturer/tutor will consider the following criteria in calculating the engagement: 1. Weekly verbal test on the weekâs content: â¢ Evidence of learning and required preparation for the session, responding to questions from the modules, assigned work, cases or readings for the week (when cold called or asked to volunteer). It should be set in the context of the existing literature and theory relating to your thesis topic. Within the document, you should seek to explain or resolve a particular problem or several issues through your knowledge and skills in the mathematical sciences. This may be through the development of novel mathematical theory, may be new applications of existing theory, or may be an in-depth discussion and review of the literature of an advanced field of the mathematical sciences. If you have novel findings, whether in terms of the development of new mathematical theory or of a new application for existing results, the importance of these in the wider field should be noted and critically assessed. If your thesis is an exploration of the existing knowledge of an advanced field of study, you should provide a detailed discussion of the importance of the key theory and results, identifying some of the likely directions of future development in the research area. You are encouraged to use citations of other published work for methods and existing theory used in your project that are well known and well accepted within their field of study. Citations should be made according to the style format of an appropriate journal (usually either sequential numbering or as âsurname (year)â) within the main text. An accompanying References list should be included at the back of the thesis, before any appendices. Where large amounts of data or computer code are included in a thesis, these should be placed in electronic appendices, and not in the main body of the thesis. These appendices need only be included in the electronic submission of your Thesis, and not in the hard copies. The tone and clarity in the writing should be equal to that of published journal papers or commercial consultancy reports.

Project overview (group 3-4 students) Stage 1 (20 marks, due week 5): The objective of stage 1 is to explore a data set and define a research question based on a research/business requirement. Activities include: (1) selecting a data set; (2) defining the problem and project requirements; (3) completing literature review and (4) exploring, summarising and preparing the data. Report The three-page report (not counting title page and references or appendix) should describe the problem, proposed approach and your data: Section 1: Problem Describe the problem from a general perspective, highlighting the business/research need. List the research question(s) you will answer in stage 2 of the project. Section 2: Literature review Describe 5-7 papers related to the problem listed in Section 1 Section 3: Approach Describe the approach you will take to solving the problem and any requirements. This is your plan for stage 2 Section 4: Data Describe the data from a general perspective e.g. source, size, fields of interest. How did you acquire the data? Describe any exploratory analysis you have done to refine your understanding of the data and research question. One or two supporting figures/tables would be great. Describe any data preparation e.g. transformation, sampling, cleaning. Which tools did you use to clean and explore the data set? The report is worth 20% of the overall mark. It will be marked on data relevance, problem definition, data preparation, data summarisation and report completeness. The report should use the high-level headings above (problem, approach, data). It should use line spacing of at least 1.15 and body font size of at least 10pt. The goal is to convey the problem clearly and concisely. Stage 2 (30 marks, due week 12): The objective of Stage 2 is to complete the analysis or model building to solve the problem you defined in Task 1. Activities include: (1) Literature review related to your approach; (2) defining an experiment setup; (3) implementing your proposed approach; (4) evaluating and analysing your approach; and (5) Conclusion and any future work . Report Your report, no more than four pages in length, should describe the experimental setup, approach and results: Section 1: Literature review Describe 3-5 papers related to your proposed approach. Section 2: Setup State your research question(s). State null and alternative hypotheses. Describe how you will quantify reliability e.g. significance testing, confidence intervals. If appropriate, describe how you will measure effectiveness e.g. regression r-square, clustering V-measure, classification f1-score. Identify datasets and the data you derived from them. Section 3: Approach Describe your proposed model and any benchmark models for comparison: Machine learning projects could focus on e.g. learning techniques, features, model tuning, parameter selection Analysis projects could focus on e.g. how the analysis will answer your research questions, operational variables for analysis, method of analysis Section 4: Results Summarise results, reliability and comparison to any benchmark analyses or models. Critically analyse results e.g. limitations of data, setup or approach, characteristic errors, possible improvements Section 5: Conclusion Conclude with what you have learned from this study which would improve yourself as a data analyst. Would you recommend this as a solution to your problem? Provide reasons. Â The report is worth 30% of the overall mark. It will be marked on clarity of research question, evaluation framework, approach/implementation, discussion of results and quality of analysis. The report should use the high-level headings above â setup, approach, results and conclusion. It should use line spacing of at least 1.15 and body font size of at least 10pt. Stage 3 (10 marks, due week 12): Presentation Prepare ppt slides which summarise stage 1 and stage 2. Submit a video presentation (2-3 mins per member)

text: Oral Presentation (Presentation, 30%, Individual). This is a 10-to-15-minute oral presentationÂ summarizing your work throughout the session. The presentation must briefly discuss the chosen quantitative finance problem and the proposed methodology, including the required computational/numerical techniques required to solve the problem. You must discuss relevant results and insights arising from the analysis.Â In addition, students must also actively engage their peers by asking at least one question to at least two presenters during the session. Presenting students shall also be assessed on their ability to respond to audience questions.

Assessed tutorial/lab (Exercises, 5%, Individual). This task is to provide students with early feedback on their progress. The task will involve a set of theoretical and computational questions. Students will provide pen and paper solutions to the theoretical questions and use the R software package to solve the computational questions.

Take-home assignment (Exercises, 45%, Individual). The assignment contains various problems, ranging from typical exam questions to computational tasks. Diverse solution techniques can be used and students are expected to apply numerical and computational methodologies where appropriate. The inclusion of more advanced questions is designed to challenge students and their partial answers will also be considered and evaluated. All problems must be addressed individually, but help can be requested in class.

Final exam (Examination, 50%, Individual). The final exam is an open-book examination covering the material from lecture and tutorial/lab components. The questions will be theoretical in nature requiring pen and paper solutions, with successful responses demonstrating studentsâ grasp of concepts presented over the duration of the course.

In-Class Test (Exercises, 10%, Individual). You will tackle and solve theoretical and applied problems using Markowitzâs mean-variance portfolio optimization framework. This assessment emphasizes the mathematical and quantitative tools and techniques around this topic. As such, this task requires a critical understanding of the assumptions and mathematical methods involving these topics. Some computational work using Python may be required as part of this task.

Project (Project, 45%, Individual). In this assessment task, you will be given historical data on equities and construct optimal portfolios according to the portfolio optimization and construction frameworks discussed in class. Relevant frameworks and techniques include Markowitzâs mean-variance portfolio optimization framework, factor models, Arbitrage Pricing Theory, and tracking error variance minimization. You will also compare and contrast portfolios using portfolio performance and diversification indicators and risk measures. Your main deliverable for this assessment is a Python notebook detailing your implementation, analysis, and conclusions.

Final Examination (Examination, 45%, Individual). Through this activity, your knowledge and competencies on the techniques and concepts discussed throughout the subject will be assessed. This is an open-book examination and will cover all topics discussed during the term.

Assessed Tutorial (Quiz, 15%, Individual). The assignment will require students to determine and interpret risk measures in under various financial settings and probabilistic modelling assumptions. It will also require students to critically appraise and compare risk measures in terms of the axiomatic framework for risk measures.

Project/Problem Set (Project, 50%, Individual). The assignment will require students to determine and interpret risk measures for a set of real-world portfolios using a range of techniques and methodologies covered in the subject. This task uses authentic scenarios in the form of real-world portfolios and financial data and requires the use of software to perform the necessary calculations to generate the risk measures. Communication skills will also be critical to the successful completion of the assignment as students will be required to submit a written report summarizing the methodology used, stating the results of the analysis, and discussing the results obtained in a clear and concise manner.

Case Study (Presentation, 35%, Individual). The assignment will require students to determine and interpret risk measures for a set of real-world portfolios using a range of techniques and methodologies covered in the subject. This task uses authentic scenarios in the form of real-world portfolios and financial data and requires the use of software to perform the necessary calculations to generate the risk measures. Communication skills will also be critical to the successful completion of the assignment as students will be required to briefly present and discuss their answers to the case study questions and to respond to questions about their work.

Assessed tutorial/lab (Exercises, 5%, Individual). This task is to provide students with early feedback on their progress. The task will involve a set of theoretical and computational questions. Students will provide pen and paper solutions to the theoretical questions and use the R software package to solve the computational questions.

Assignment (Exercises, 45%, Individual). A set of set of theoretical and practical problems. Theoretical problems are statistical/mathematical in nature, requiring pen and paper based solutions. Practical problems are numerical in nature, requiring computational solutions implemented in R. This task is to be completed individually
Final Exam (Examination, 50%, Individual). Open-book exam.

Assignment (Individual) (Project, 50%, Individual). The individual assignment in this subject will have three parts. Due dates and assignment tasks will be announced on Canvas, so be sure to check the Canvas site for this subject regularly (at least once a week) for updates. Assignment Part 1 will be due (and feedback provided) before the census date; Parts 2 and 3 will be due later in the teaching period. The weighting of the three parts will be, respectively, 10%, 20% and 20% of the total marks in this subject. The assignment as a whole will assess disciplinary knowledge and will encourage enquiry and critical thinking through the combination of theoretical and practical problems, including implementation (using Python) of solutions on real financial market data. Students will need to communicate explanations and justifications of their solutions in a clear and concise manner.

Implementation case study and presentation (Individual) (Case study plus presentation, 50%, Individual). This task will test your knowledge and competencies in applying techniques in financial mathematics presented in this subject. It will be a practical, realistic problem posted on the Canvas site for this subject several weeks before the end of the teaching period. This will give you sufficient time to solve the problem and prepare a five-minute presentation which addresses the specific questions and criteria laid out in the problem statement. In the final assessment period (dates TBA), you will need to give your presentation before a panel of academics, as well as answer questions about your presentation. This task will be marked based on whether your presentation and answers to follow-up questions correctly and sufficientlyÂ address the specific criteria laid out in the problem statement.

Problem solving workshops and written reports (Laboratory/practical, 35%, Individual). Calculations, short responses and longer simulation-based case studied. Some of the tasks will focus on the core disciplinary content of the subject i.e. correct mathematical formulation and calculation and others will focus on the applicability of probability theory to problems in diverse areas including genetics, population biology, signal processing, financial option pricing, meteorology and game theory. Where appropriate, some use of common mathematical computing programmes (including Mathematica and Microsoft Excel) may be called upon. Additionally, each assessable workshop will include a short English language component.
In-class Test (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). Calculations and short responses to several questions including seen and unseen questions, definitions, and applications of concepts to specific problems.
Final examination (Examination, 50%, Individual). Open-book examination

Worksheet (Exercises, 50%, Individual). These exercises contribute to the development of disciplinary knowledge. Students will need to express mathematical ideas by writing proofs and drawing diagrams representing connections and mathematical objects. This will develop communication skills.
Progress Check (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). An in-class quizz for assessing and providing feedback on students' learning progress across Week 1 - Week 7 for the subject.

Final Examination (Examination, 20%, Individual). 1-hour summative exam. Completion of an hour assessment task to check your understanding and ability to solve problems using the tools learned throughout the subject. Will be delivered online via Canvas. Details to be provided on Canvas.

Progress snapshot (In session exam, 50%, Individual). In-class in Week 3 and 9 and take-home in week 6; see Canvas for dates, times and locations. Assessment task is designed to take a "snapshot" of student's learning, skills and understanding as they progress through the subject. Will cover theory, definitions, algorithms, methods, proofs, and calculations. Marked for correct workings and answers.

Summative test (Final exam, 45%, Individual). In class during week 12; see Canvas for dates, times and locations. Summative assessment of student's learning, skills and understanding at the end of the subject. Will cover theory, definitions, algorithms, methods, proofs, and calculations.Â Marked for correct workings and answers.
Presenting solutions (Interactive oral, 5%, Group, individually assessed). See Canvas for marking rubric.

Early Check-In (Exercises, 10%, Individual). In one of the early on-campus tutorials, students have to solve problems from the tutorials up to that point, hand-in their solutions for feedback and marking, and discuss their solutions in class. Preparatory material from Canvas is important for this task and it will enable students to assess their understanding of foundational concepts early in the semester.

Learning Assessment Check-Ins (Exercises, 50%, Individual). These are two sets of exercises spaced throughout the semester are based on the material from tutorials and lectures. The tests are equally weighted, each being worth 25%.

Final Exam (Examination, 40%, Individual). The final examination will be held during the examination period at the end of semesterÂ covering the whole content of the subject and its application to contemporary problems.Â

Modelling written report (Written submission, 20%, Group, group assessed). Each group of students will be assigned a simplified practical problem. The group will have to Formulate a detailed linear program Solve the model via specialist software Interpret the results in a written report with graphs and tables. The detailed instructions and assessment rubric will be provided on Canvas.

Reflection on the principles of ethical engagement with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples (Written submission, 10%, Individual). Reflection on how the principles of ethical engagement with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples would apply in the context of the problem assigned for Modelling Written Report

Class Tests (Quiz, 40%, Individual). Students are asked to apply the fundamental principles and concepts of mathematical programming in optimisation analysis and implement mathematical programming solution procedures manually in problem solving. There are two class tests: Class Test 1 will assess the topics discussed in weeks 1-4 inclusively. The weight of Class test 1 is 15%. Class Test 2 will assess the topics discussed in weeks 5-8 inclusively. The weight of Class test 2 is 25%.

Final Exam (Final exam, 30%, Individual). The final exam covers all the mathematical programming problems introduced in the subject. Students are asked to apply the fundamental principles and concepts of mathematical programming in optimisation analysis and implement mathematical programming solution procedures manually in problem solving. Each student is expected to generate her/his own solutions to the questions contained, abide by any examination rules as laid out on Canvas as well as the examination paper, and take responsibility for the successful file submission to the Canvas server.

Lab worksheets (Exercises, 20%, Individual). In each lab you will be given worksheet to complete. This will guide you through using RStudio in relation to the topics covered in the lectures that week. You will interpret the output you generate in RStudio to answer the analysis questions on the sheet. The lab worksheets allow you to engage in learning throughout the subject with low stakes assessments that also give regular feedback.

Assignment (Group Work) (Report, 30%, Group, group assessed). You need to use R/RStudio to answer all the assignment questions, including performing the necessary statistical analysis and writing up the conclusions in a clear, concise manner. Questions in the assignment will relate to material covered in lectures 1 to 8 (computer labs 1 to 7).

Examination (Examination, 50%, Individual). The exam gives students the opportunity to demonstrate their understanding of the modelling introduced throughout the subject. Information on the final examination will be released closer to the date. This is an open-book exam.
In-class test (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). To assess understanding of the theoretical material underpinning spanning all material prior to the student vacation week. Open book offline assessment.

Lab worksheets (Laboratory/practical, 50%, Individual). Four (equally-weighted) assessable worksheets to be completed during the final 40 minutes of the lab class during the weeks as stated in the subject schedule. These assess ongoing progress in the subject and provide frequent feedback and low stakes assessment. Open-book offline assessment.
Take-home assignment (Project, 20%, Individual). Take-home assignment covering material from the whole subject

Assignments (Exercises, 20%, Individual). There will be two assignments. The first assignment corresponds to the first half of the subject and the second assignment to the second half.Â These assignments will test your mastery of the fundamentals of the subject and your ability to solve some real-world problems whose solution involves differential equations.
Class Test (Mid-session examination, 30%, Individual). Complete 3 questions covering material up to and including the material from class on September 23.
Final Exam (Examination, 50%, Individual). Complete 5 questions. This will assess your mastery of the subject as a whole.
Class test 1 (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual)
Class test 2 (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual)

Problem Solving Assignment (Report, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students need to select a research topic on global optimisation, and must seek approval from the lecturer regarding the research scope and main tasks. The submitted report should include, but not limited to, a concise literature review; description and formulation of the global optimisation problem; development of novel algorithms and/or critique of the existing approaches; illustration of the applicability for real-world problems; comprehensive computational experiments to compare the performance of the algorithms; summary of main results and future directions.

subject_name: Machine Learning: Mathematical Theory and Applications
text: Computer labs (group) (Report, 20%, Group, group assessed). Implement and apply machine learning algorithms to real-world problems collaborating in groups. This assessment task contains a single task. Students will work in pairs to solve a set of theoretical and practical problems. The final product is a report in notebook format that presents the solutions. The work will be critically assessed by the lecturer, who will provide substantial feedback. See the program for deadlines. Students may be asked to explain or justify their solutions to ensure they have produced the work. Failure to do so will result in loss of marks and may lead to academic misconduct.

subject_name: Machine Learning: Mathematical Theory and Applications
text: Computer labs (individual) (Report, 40%, Group, individually assessed). Implement and apply machine learning algorithms, working independently and under time constraints (for the quiz part of the task). This assessment task contains two separate tasks. The first task is an in-class quiz early in the semester that assesses basic mathematical content that the students should be familiar with to succeed in the subject. The second task is a set of two computer labs of a similar nature to Assessment Task 1. For these computer labs, students are encouraged to discuss the work with each other, however, each student submits an individual report. The work will be critically assessed by the lecturer, who will provide substantial feedback. See the program for deadlines. Students may be asked to explain or justify their solutions to ensure they have produced the work. Failure to do so will result in loss of marks and may lead to academic misconduct.

subject_name: Machine Learning: Mathematical Theory and Applications
text: Final project (Quiz/test, 40%, Individual). This assessment task is a project to be solved individually under a time constraint of 5 hours. Students will be able to bring their solutions to Assessment Tasks 1 and 2 and reuse programming codes from those assignments. The final project is expected to take place after Week 12.

Assignments (Exercises, 60%, Individual). 5 assignment sheets will be completed out of class. It must be handed in during class by the date specified on the assignment. Assignments will be marked and returned during the following class. You must show working for each question on the assignment.
Exam (Examination, 40%, Individual). Final Examination

Job Application (Portfolio, 25%, Individual). To prepare students to apply for workplace roles. In this assessment task you will identify an industry role that you currently qualify for, such as an internship role. You will then complete a job application for that role which includes a resume and cover letter which addresses the selection criteria of the role. In class you will be given further guidance on how to write a convincing job application and an opportunity to get feedback from peers on your application before submitting it through a peer review process. This task includes a milestone assessment component that evaluates your academic and professional communication. You may be guided to further language support after the completion of this subject if your results in this milestone task indicate you need more help with your language skills.

Video interview (Reflection, 25%, Individual). To prepare students for a job interview. In class you will learn about the interview process and be given time to practice these skills with your peers with a practice interview reviewed by a peer. After preparing for the interview in class, you will be given access to industry software used for remote asynchronous interviewing. These tools are often used in industry for roles with large numbers of applicants as a first round of interviews. You will then be able to log-on to the tool at any point during Week 10 to complete the interview. In the interview you will be presented with a series of questions and for each you will be asked to record yourself responding to these questions. You are expected to have a microphone and camera for this assessment task. If you have technical issues or cannot arrange for this equipment you must contact the subject coordinator as soon as you become aware of the issue.

Working in Teams (Exercises, 35%, Individual). For students to become technically proficient in an industry-standard project management software and methodology. Project planning tools and techniques are regularly used in industry for planning, progress tracking and accountability of teams and team members. In particular in IT, Kanban boards are used to track agile teams and many digital tools have been developed to facilitate this. In small teams you will be given a workplace scenario to develop training material for your company. The project involves planning using a project planning tool and agile methodology. Your work in the scenario includes using the project planning tool to capture all planned and completed work. This task is moderated by SPARKPlus, a peer and self-assessment tool. All students are expected to respond to the SPARKPlus survey.

Individual Reflection (Reflection, 15%, Individual). To reflect Â on a topic or experience from the subject which was particularly formative to your understanding of industry. In this task you will consider your experiences and exposure to new topics this semester and identify one experience or topic which was particularly formative to your understanding of working in industry. You will reflect on this topic using the reflection framework presented in class, identifying what you have learned and future planned action. This is an opportunity to not just recount what you have been told but expand on your understanding of the chosen experience or topic. This task includes a milestone assessment component that evaluates your academic and professional communication. You may be guided to further language support after the completion of this subject if your results in this milestone task indicate you need more help with your language skills.

subject_name: Cloud Computing and Software as a Service
text: Research Essay (Essay, 10%, Group, individually assessed). A list of cloud-computing topics will be given by the lecturer. Each group needs to select one topic, conduct research on it and write an essay based on their findings. The group is expected to read at least 5 references relevant to the topic prior to writing the report. The suggested structure of the report will be discussed during the lecture.

subject_name: Cloud Computing and Software as a Service
text: Software as a Service (SaaS) Development (Project, 25%, Group, individually assessed). This task is based on the Cloud-based software development skills that are covered in the lectures and the labs. A case study pertaining to SaaS development will be given to the students. Students will work in groups of three each to engineer a prototype SaaS using the Force.com platform.

subject_name: Cloud Computing and Software as a Service
text: Report on Software as a Service (SaaS) Development (Report, 10%, Group, individually assessed). Students (working in groups three each) are expected to write a project report (the key descriptors of which will be discussed during the lecture) on the SaaS development exercise carried out as a part of Assessment Item 2.

subject_name: Cloud Computing and Software as a Service
text: Presentation (Presentation, 20%, Group, individually assessed). Students (working in groups of three each) are expected to deliver a presentation outlining their learning experiences with the SaaS development exercise (Assessment item 2). Suggested presentation outline will be provided during the lecture.

subject_name: Cloud Computing and Software as a Service
text: Final Assessment (Project, 35%, Individual). A case study pertaining to application development using Amazon Web Services (AWS) will be given to the students. Students will individually of three each to develop the application. Students will complete this assessment individually.

Plan and proposal (Report, 20%, Group, group and individually assessed). Based on the data mining problem and the group that you have formed, this task involves describing your group, the role of each team member, your proposal for solving the data mining problem and your plan for solving it. Assignments will be assessed based on the quality and plausibility of the proposal and plan and the completeness of team roles.

Mid-project update and presentation (Report, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). In this assignment you will give a progress report on your work in the project to the client. Your group will describe the results of your data exploration and give initial findings as well as an updated project plan. This will involve a report as well as a short formal presentation to the client. Assignments will be assessed based on depth of data exploration, quality of understanding of the data mining problem as expressed through the initial findings and the understandability, professionalism and depth of the client presentation.

Final project and presentation (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). Your group will deliver a report to the client describing the results of the data analytics investigation. Your group will give a formal presentation describing the project and results to an executive panel from the client organisation (think of it as the company board).

Quiz on subject (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). To provide students with an awareness of human-centred research methods as taught in this subject. Students are quizzed on their understanding of the subject matter, the way the subject itself is set up, and their responsibilities as ethical and people-focused researchers.

Poster on interviews (Report, 30%, Group, individually assessed). To provide students with the opportunity to put into practice and further develop skills in human-centred research. This includes literature research, developing relevant questions, performing interviews, qualitative data analysis, and communication of findings. The assignment requires students to work in groups of 3 or 4. They study and develop a research proposal, followed by contacting potential participants and performing in-depth interviews. Afterwards, students are encouraged to learn substantial methods for the analysis of data and its reporting. Online tutorials and class meetings give students the opportunity to receive guidance and feedback on their progress. SPARKPlus will be used to answer questions about groupwork after submission.

Short report on probe design (Report, 10%, Individual). To provide students with the opportunity to put into practice and further develop skills in human-centered research. Following the direction set out in task 2, this task approaches similar research questions with another qualitative research tool, namely probes. Students will learn its application and analysis, and communication of findings. The assignment requires students to independently design and develop a probe kit, explain the research goal of the kit and how each of the probe kit elements contribute to reaching this goal. Visual material, such as sketches or photos should be included of the draft probe design. A draft positive and respectful informed consent form needs to be attached. A description should be added of the participant the student has invited to participate in their research, without revealing their identity. Online tutorials and class meetings give students the opportunity to receive guidance and feedback on their progress.

Presentation of analysis, short paper and video on probe study (Combination, 50%, Individual). To provide students with the opportunity to put into practice and further develop skills in human-centered research. Following the direction set out in Assessment Task 2 (group work), this task approaches similar research questions with another qualitative research method, namely probes. Students will learn its application and analysis, and communication of findings. The assignment requires students to individually study and develop a research proposal, followed by contacting a participant and asking them some questions (intro interview), then handing them a self-made probe kit and after pick-up performing an in-depth face-to-face interview (exit interview). In the last tutorial before the Assessment Task 4 submission deadline each student will be required to present the outcome of their thematic analysis in-class.Â This is a compulsory item to be able to get marks for Assessment Task 4. Compared to Assessment Task 2, this individual task puts more emphasis on the quality of writing a paper and dissemination of findings in an academic way. Due to the visual and physical nature of the probes method, a video deliverable enables students to communicate that part of their work effectively. Students need to demonstrate awareness and implementation of positive and respectful ethical practices. This includes applying the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander (AIATSIS) Code of Ethics when working with and for Indigenous Australians; demonstrating that they have gained approval of free, prior, and informed consent; and attaching a completed ethics form.

Weekly Lab Activities (Exercises, 30%, Individual). Become familiar with the core concepts and algorithms presented in the lecturer and establish a baseline prototype to develop further through the other assessments. Lab activities will be provided on Canvas for students to work through each week. These will be scaffolded such that clear instruction are provided to achieve a lower grade bracket, while higher grade brackets will require students to investigate and self-learn to design and develop a solution.

Create an Unreal Engine Tutorial (Project, 20%, Individual). Explore the Unreal Engine further by choosing from a wide selection of engine features, self-studying that feature, and creating tutorial to teach it to other students. The Unreal Engine has a vast array of advanced features, from lighting, to animation, special effects, world builders, pre-built behaviour trees, and substantial code architectures. In this assessment, students will have four sub-tasks in order to explore these further: Choose one of these features and explore it in depth. This can be a system that is interacted with through the Unreal UI (e.g. world building), one that is through Blueprints (e.g material shaders), one that is through code (e.g. the Gameplay Ability System), or one that requires a mixture of these. Create a written tutorial in the style of the lab activities from Assessment 1. This activity should scale well, presenting foundational knowledge at the beginning and a reasonable challenge by the end. After submission, students will be given tutorial activities made by other students and be required to complete them and provide an anonymous peer review along with their completed project files. Each tutorial's creator will then need to verify and mark the completed tutorials submitted by other students.

Artificial Intelligence and Procedural Content Generation Prototype (Project, 25%, Group, individually assessed). Demonstrate a deeper understanding of artificial intelligence and procedural content generation in games, beyond that of the lectures and lab activities, and communicate this knowledge with others. Work in groups of two to establish a unique prototype that will be built upon in Assessment 3 and Assessment 4. This prototype should be an interactive technical demonstration, highlighting the challenges in coding advanced systems in game-like virtual environments, rather than being a refined game design. Start this unique prototype by creating one advanced system per group member. Each group member may choose to design and build either an artificial intelligence or procedural content generation system. This may extend upon the existing system created through the lab activities or may be entirely new. This prototype will be extended in Assessment 4 to include other features and combine the two systems. Therefore, the two systems should be designed to complement and work well together (while still being two distinctive contributions) and be designed with the requirements of Assessment 4 in mind. The Assessment 3 prototype does not need to produce a polished and engaging build. Instead, you will create a short video of your work to demonstrate the key features of the prototypeâs design, code and its execution and communicate these to staff and other students.

Final Multiplayer Prototype (Project, 25%, Group, group and individually assessed). Demonstrate advanced knowledge of C++ programming in the Unreal Engine by producing a substantial game-based technical demonstration by incorporating networked multiplayer techniques into the existing artificial intelligence and procedural content generation systems created in Assessment 3. Finalise your group's technical demonstration by building upon Assessment 3 and the lab activities to incorporate networked multiplayer and your knowledge from Assessment 2 into your prototype. The project should now resemble a complex, unified prototype that creatively incorporates multiple advanced topics into a playable interactive technical demonstration. This prototype should be refined in its technical implantation, visual presentation, and user interaction, such that it is ready to be used in future employment portfolios.

Project â Analysis, Planning, Architecture & Design (Project, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). Demonstrate the ability to analyse, plan, architect and design a software application. This assessment task will require a team of 4-6 students to analyse the assigned project case study problem; and produce, submit and present a group report containing Software requirements & development plan; and architecture & design (description and software prototype). The deliverables of this assessment task also include a compulsory oral/visual group report and prototype presentation (no slides) during the scheduled assignment assessment (showcase), and individual contribution logbooks. Any individual student who failed to attend and present in these showcases will receive zero (0) as a final individual mark. Additional information about this assignment and assessment tasks will be provided in the project brief.
Project â Implementation & Testing (Project, 50%, Group, individually assessed)

Online Quiz (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). Demonstrate the ability to understand the theory and practice of software development. It includes 5 online quizzes (quiz schedule will be published on Canvas).

Artefacts, reflections and workplace records (Portfolio, 100%, Individual). Students collect information and artefacts during their work placement. The information and artefacts should be: Written records of workplans and performance appraisals from the beginning, middle and end of their work placement Written records of critical incidents from their work placement. This may include photographs, observations, stories, and artefacts Reflections on their experience of the monthly huddles The artefacts need to be collected and curated in an eportfolio. These artefacts will be developed and submitted as assessment in the subsequent subject 41055 Engineering Workplace Review.

Cover letter & resume (Report, 25%, Individual). This is a task to build studentsâ capabilities in identifying potential employers and developing a competitive cover letter and resume. In this task, students will investigate potential organisations that they might undertake an internship with. They will develop a tailored cover letter and resume for one of the organisations.

Mock interview (Presentation, 75%, Individual). This is a task to build students' capabilities in articulating their experiences and value to a potential employer. In this task, students will video themselves answering questions as part of a mock interview.
Lab Assessments (Exercises, 30%, Individual). Building on the material presented in the preparation lectures, exercise and workshop exercises, the student will attempt a programming challenge.

Code Comprehension (Interactive oral, 25%, Individual). The student will be presented with a small section of code and asked to answer a small number of comprehension questions about that section of code. The questions will be made available before the assessment sessions. There will be four sessions, which, timetabling permitting, will be in Weeks 4, 7, 11 and 12. The sessions will be run during the workshop/lab classes. The sessions, in order. will be worth 5%, 5%, 7% and 8% respectively.Â

Project (Project, 25%, Individual). Building on the material presented throughout the subject, students will progressively build components of a single, substantial piece of software, meeting a design objective.
Exam (Examination, 20%, Individual). Answer questions posed by the examiner in a take-home, open-book exam format.

Extension (Project, 0%, Individual). The student will develop program(s) to solve a (series of) challenging free-form problem(s), requiring research into techniques that may be outside the scope of the subject, and thus at least some independent study.

AI technique demos (Presentation, 40%, Group, individually assessed). Assess studentsâ ability to articulate their understanding of artificial intelligence techniques used to solve simple practical problems based on examples provided in labs. In this assessment task, students will work in pairs to develop four AI technique demo videos. Detailed tasks and deliverables will be available in assessment task 1 specification in Canvas subject site.

AI Project (Project, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). Assess a studentâs ability to work in a small group, collaboratively develop a showcase of applying some selected AI techniques to solve an interesting real-world problem and effectively present the outcomes of the project. In this assessment task, each group will develop an AI application showcase by applying selected AI techniques to solve an interesting real-world problem and present the outcomes. The deliverables consist of two parts. One part is group-based deliverables which include a solution program with detailed annotations, a brief report about the AI technique used and how it is evaluated, and a video to present the project, including the problem to solve, how chosen AI techniques are used to solve the problem and evaluation. This part will be marked as a group and take 25% of the subject mark. The other part is individual-based deliverable which is a reflection report including self-reflection on the learning journey to complete this assignment and peer-reviews of group members in the context of this project. This part will take 5% of the subject mark.

Final Exam (Examination, 30%, Individual). Assess studentsâ ability of explaining and applying key concepts and common AI techniques in simple scenarios. Answer questions about key concepts and simple applications of AI techniques during an open-book exam. The question types include multiple choice question, multiple answer question, fill single or multiple blanks question, matching question, and true or false question.Â Â

Industry and Society Understanding and Analysis (Report, 20%, Individual). To understand the current industry and society needs with respect to NLP-related jobs and skills. This is an individual assessment where each student needs to search current job advertisements related to NLP, and analyse the skills needed for the jobs. The report needs to describe the identified jobs, the required skills and experience, and what business domains the jobs are needed for. The report will also need to have discussions outlining the studentâs current skills and experiences, skills needed in related industries and society, and the skill gaps the student needs to fill to meet the job requirements.

Quiz (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). To undertake a quiz. The quiz will consist of multiple choice and short answer questions testing the understanding of the basic concepts and algorithms covered in the subject.

Project Development (Report, 50%, Group, individually assessed). To develop a project report and a presentation. In Assessment 3, each group will propose a real-world problem that NLP methods can address. A project on solving this problem needs to be developed, with both theoretical and empirical analyses that show the advantages of the proposed idea. The report needs to include theoretical justifications on why the proposed idea is expected to solve the proposed problem. It will also need to include the workflow of the code and empirical analysis of project results on sample NLP data. Each group will also need to effectively communicate their project results in an oral defence, comprising a presentation followed by questions from the teaching staff and peer students.

Programming Assignment 1 (Project, 30%, Individual). Demonstrate the ability to implement a non-trivial algorithmic solution to a computational problem and justify the choice of solution through algorithmic and computational complexity arguments. Prepare a report detailing the design and its justifications. Take a given computational problem, examine the problem from a complexity stand point and apply known algorithms to solve the problem.

Algorithmic Research (Report, 30%, Individual). Demonstrate abstract understanding of algorithms (as separate from implementation issues) and convey this understanding to fellow students. Research a given algorithm, write a report on its algorithmic and complexity characteristics, and present findings to the tutorial. Fellow students will then evaluate their understanding of the algorithm against the benchmark of being able to develop an implementation.

Programming Assignment 2 (Project, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). Demonstrate the ability to combine simpler algorithms to produce a solution to a complicated computational problem. As a group, develop an algorithmic solution to a complicated computational problem by breaking the problem into soluble subproblems, justifying design choices through complexity and algorithmic assessment of the problem. Prepare a report detailing these considerations and developments.
Knowledge Quizzes (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). Promote understanding of algorithmic theory that supports the subject material. Complete practical or theory quiz before given deadline.

Curated professional practice portfolio (Portfolio, 50%, Individual). Interview (Presentation, 50%, Individual). Engineering Design Portfolio (EDP) (Portfolio, 100%, Group, group and individually assessed). To simulate the real-world of practice by curating a collection of artefacts to meet requirements. The Engineering Design Portfolio documents your curated individual learning journey within the Studio. It requires the development of artefacts supported by documentation of the design and decision-making processes. Further details will be provided on Canvas. The EDP will also contain your four artefacts and should include continuous reflection that synthesises your development and achievement of the subject learning outcomes throughout the Studio journey. The EDP will be assessed using a levels rubric at each submission and finally in the assessment period to determine the grade. Professional Persona : including name, discipline, and aspiration in the engineering industry and experience in the Mechanical Systems Design Studio 1. See Canvas for more details. 2. Four (4) artefacts : a. Artefact 3 (Second-Generation Design) : Informed by the team's re-design priorities as a whole, in this artefact the individual should document their re-design work on a major mechanical component. Artefact 4 (Presentation of the Second-Generation Design) : In this artefact the student should present an overall description of the final re-design as a whole and with specific focus on their part. Portfolio and Presentations (Portfolio, 100%, Group, individually assessed). To document the iterative learning process and artefacts that demonstrate the achievement of learning goals related to computing science. Students are expected to work in teams assuming the role of a professional colleague throughout the project phase. Although students work in teams, their submissions are assessed individually. The computing science portfolio and presentations are carefully designed and assigned as four components. Each component informs the next component so that tasks are expected to be completed in the order proposed to obtain optimal success in the studio. A performance level rubric is used to identify individual progress during the 12-week semester in view of students making individual improvements to their performance level based on continuous feedback and opportunities for personal reflection. The components include: Component 1: Project Initiative Groupwork: Group; Individually assessed Length: 1000 to 1500 words, reference is excluded. The intent of this component is to train the ability to construct a project team and initiate a project, with clearly defined topics and tasks, team responsibilities, and management strategies. Following the training of research essentials in Sprint 1, students are required to construct a project team with 4-5 members sharing similar interests and with complementary skillsets and conduct substantial research to define their research topics and problems. Each team must develop a project proposal with a clearly defined research topic and feasible methodologies, as well as functionated team responsibilities and a strategic plan of project management. Students are strongly encouraged to communicate with relevant academic researchers at UTS for topic-specified consultation and advice. The Project Initiative encompasses three deliverables: Project Proposal including a research topic, involved methodologies, and expected outcomes. Statement of Team Responsibilities including team roles and task allocations. Project Management Plan including project management strategies, risk analysis, and project timeline with milestones. Component 2: Project Progress Groupwork: Group; Individually assessed Length: 1000-2000 words, reference is excluded. The intent of this component is to train the ability to proceed a project with the implementation of essential research skills, e.g., introducing research topics, searching and collecting research literature, and implementing basic methodologies, and reflect a teamâs learning journey with evaluations. Following the training of academic writing in Sprint 2, each team is required to introduce their research topics with the appropriate use of critical thinking skills, propose a feasible search strategy and collect at least 3000 articles aligning with their topics, and start to implement bibliometric methodologies and tools to analyse the data with raw results. Students are strongly encouraged to communicate with relevant academic researchers at UTS for topic-specified consultation and advice. The Project Progress encompasses four deliverables: Introduction including the background information of the selected topic and the motivation of choosing this topic. Data Profile including search strategies and the descriptive statistics of the data. Raw Results including some results generated by involved methodologies and bibliometric tools, with a mixture of tables and figures. Project Management including the contributions of team members (linked with their responsibilities), the update of the project timeline with milestone achievements, and potential risks and challenges. References must follow the UTS APA referencing style, with an appropriate use of reference management tools. Component 3: Project Solution Groupwork : Group; Individually assessed Length : Deliverable 2: Project Portfolio (at least 3000 words). The intent of this component is to train the ability to develop a project solution with a multifaceted skillset of research essentials, academic writing, and success in research. Following the training of extensive skills for research success in Sprint 3, each team is required to develop a solution for their pre-defined topics, and deliver the results through a coherent and logical framework and with insightful discussion using critical thinking skills. The Project Solution encompasses two deliverables: Deliverable 1: Project Presentation Each team is required to give a presentation to report their solution to the class, around 20 minutes. The presentation must cover the following content: Introduction of the Research Topic Data Profile Analytical Results Critical Review Conclusions All team members are required to present a part of the project, particularly reflecting their own contributions. Deliverable 2: Project Portfolio Each team will report their project solutions in a Project Portfolio, including the following contents: Introduction Data Profile Analytical Results Critical Review Team Responsibilities and Evidence Conclusions The report must follow a coherent and logical framework and present results with an appropriate mixture of tables and figures. References must follow the UTS APA referencing style, with an appropriate use of reference management tools. Component 4: Reflection and Responsible Research Groupwork: Individually assessed Length: 1000-1500 words. The intent of this component is to train the ability to reflect on the progress of self-development and learning journey and development of the understanding of research ethics. Students are required to evaluate their activities in this subject with critical thinking skills and identify their gains and pains along with the entire journey of the subject. Students are required to discuss their understanding on research ethics and how they practiced responsible research in their individual assignments and teamwork. Students are also encouraged to propose a responsible research plan for their future career development in a research-based environment.

Portfolio and presentations (Project, 100%, Group, group and individually assessed). To gain experience of professional practice by applying discipline knowledge and skills to identify and provide solutions to complex problems with collaborative effort Four progressive tasks are required, and these will be assessed using Performance Level rubrics per task (i) Task 1: Project proposal, plan, and presentation. Students are required to pitch a project proposal including items: topic, aims, objectives; significance and methods; benefits; feasibility via identifying significant problems and designing solutions. (ii) Task 2: Progress report on initial solution implementation and analysis. Students are required to report progress and conduct peer-review both verbally and in writing on initial solution implementation and analysis. (iii) Task 3: Showcase final project and summarise in a research paper. Students are required to showcase final project and summarise into a research paper with refined solutions, verification and validation, impact, research paper, future direction. (iv) Task 4: Reflective journal. Students are required to record personal learning progress in reflective journals to demonstrate self-reflection on professional practice, problem-solving, discipline technique skills, project management, teamwork and collaboration.

Project proposal, plan, and presentation (Presentation, Group, group and individually assessed). The intent is to utilise discipline knowledge and literature review skills to develop and present a comprehensive and well-structured project plan. Conduct a group presentation which should address these points: A group agreed topic â it should be narrow, specific, and solvable. State the aims and objectives of the project. Related work in the selected topic. Applying literature review skills to find relevant, high-quality articles on the topic, from diverse sources and with a variety of research perspectives. Critically evaluate the sources, based on key criteria selected and with reference to the decided topic. Significance of the research topic, feasibility study of the research problem and solutions considering teamâs ability and skill sets. An appropriate project management plan that with clear work breakdown structure and equal workload allocation among team members, as well as an efficient communication plan on how and how often team members will update progress and discuss challenges. Presentation : Students individually will be required to work on the presentation and then meet and agree on one presentation they give submit. Evidence of their individual work will be appendix to the presentation slides. Each student is required to present during the presentation. Feedback will be given for presentation. Submission : Package the presentation slides as one pdf and submit to Canvas.

Progress report on initial solution implementation and analysis (Report, Group, individually assessed). The intent is to apply software and analytic skills to implement and critically evaluate solutions. Students work collaboratively to: Formulate a problem, and identify and propose solutions.. Implement solutions with appropriate tools. Conduct initial analysis about the solution(s) with details such as benchmark datasets, evaluation criteria, and comparison to baselines if any. Summarise into a report and disseminate with a presentation for peer-review. Reflection on performance of teamwork should be included in the presentation. Feedback from peer review should be incorporated to improve on final projects. Students are expected to replicate and execute the implementation on their own machine. The experimental results from their own run are reported, along with individual understanding, interpretation, and contributions. Each student is required to present during the presentation for peer review. Feedback will be given for both presentation and report.

Showcase final project and summarise in a research paper (Report, Group, group and individually assessed). The intent is to experience the iterative process in problem-solving and enhance skills in academic writing. Students work collaboratively to: Iteratively improve performance of a solution with incorporating feedback from previous task and other sources. Conduct more thorough analysis about the experimental results via assessing their validity. Summarize findings and insights from the experiments, and organise them in a way that supports the discussion. Verify research outcomes, significance, and impact, against the statements in the research proposal. Summarize the project into a research paper with at least these sections: abstract, introduction, related work, problem formulation, proposed solutions, experiments, and conclusion. Showcase the final project. Students individually will be required to work on the verification and validation of research outcomes (getting code run on their own computing devices and conduct experiments), discussion and conclusions and then meet and agree on a final showcase version they submit. Evidence of their individual work and collaboration should be appendix to the research paper. Submission : Package the showcase slides and research paper as one pdf and submit to Canvas

Reflective journal (Reflection, Individual). The intent is to self-reflect, manage project and teamwork. Regularly reflect on what has been set out to achieve in the weekly project work, how each task was approached, what problems were encountered, what feedback have been received and how have they been incorporated, what could have been done differently, and what have been learnt from the experience. The assessment should be submitted regularly via Canvas.

Practical Individual Project (Report, 20%, Individual). To ensure a firm ground for learning the advanced topics of the subject To allow students to self-assess whether/how the subject suits their learning objectives (this task will be done before the census date) To guide students to start with the course project (see Task 2) Implement a parser realising the function of a simple digital calculator (or similar functionalities at the same level of technical challenge); Write a short report on the implementation, linking to the concepts and methods learned in class.

Practical Group Project (Project, 30%, Group, group assessed). To ensure students master the theory of computation and understand how it is linked with practical computation. The project will be based on assignment 1, but significantly more sophisticated. Completing this project involves reviewing, mastering and applying a large part of the scope covered by this subject. Students need to apply the techniques learned during Week 3-8. Implement an interpreter or a compiler of a simple but practical programming language (or task of equivalent technical challenge that expands upon Assessment Task 1) Write a report on the implementation steps, technical problems encountered and solutions.

Theory Assignment (Project, 40%, Individual). The theory assignment assesses the students' understanding of the theoretical concepts underpinning standard models of computation. Demonstrate understanding of key theoretical concepts through developing solutions to long-form problems based on techniques and methods shown in the subject.

Weekly Quiz (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). There will be a quiz on most weeks. Each quiz is a fairly simple comprehension check. The aim is to ensure students are properly pacing their learning of potentially challenging concepts.

The report should document the process followed, and contributions by individual team members.
