Labs (Laboratory/practical, 10%, Group, individually assessed). Wireshark and hands-on Labs: Experiments, observations, and analysis There are twelve labs, including Wireshark, network hands-on, and project assessment labs, to enable students to actually observe the sequence of messages exchanged between two protocol entities and build simple networks. Students are expected to test the network connectivity, explain and analyse the observed data during the labs. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited.

Projects (Project, 10%, Group, individually assessed). Build design, development, and implementation skills. No GenAI. Project 1: Build a Web Server You will develop a simple Web server in Python that is capable of processing only one request. In the Companion Website, we provide the skeleton code for your server. Your job is to complete the code, run your server, and then test your server by sending requests from browsers running on different hosts. Project 2: Build your own network You will build your own network using Cisco switch and router. Your job is to initialise the switch and router, complete basic configurations in hosts, switch and router. You will demonstrate the network routing status and connectivity, and analyse the network traffic.

Assignments (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). Test conceptual understanding, problem solving skills and facilitate self-assessment. Students will be given a series of questions about the assignment topic and then required to submit their answers through an online quiz in Canvas. The questions will require students to do some background reading and perform some analysis and/or calculations to reach the answers. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited. Assignment 1. Network performance analysis. Assignment 2. Transport analysis. Assignment 3. Routing protocols.

Quiz (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). Test conceptual understanding, problem-solving skills and facilitate self-assessment. The quiz is in the form of multiple choice, short answer questions, plus system design and evaluation problems. It covers specified chapters, lectures, learning materials, and tutorials. Requires application of knowledge, techniques, evaluation, and resources to solve problems. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited.

Final Exam (Examination, 45%, Individual). Test concept understanding, problem-solving skills, overall assessment. The exam is in the form of multiple choice, short answer questions, plus system design and evaluation problems. It covers specified chapters, lectures, learning materials, and tutorials. Requires application of knowledge, techniques, evaluation, and resources to solve problems. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited.

Reflective ability assessment (Reflection, 30%, Individual). The purpose of this task is to evaluate how well students are learning to reflect. The task for students is: to demonstrate critical reflection expressed as high level competence in their personal reflection journal, and, to demonstrate building design reflection capability in their weekly design reflection journals.

Process assessment (Laboratory/practical, 20%, Individual). The purpose of this task is to learn to make and record process decisions. The task for students is to demonstrate: how they are learning about process and what they are learning about process, and by showing their contributions to process. This will be done by recording decisions and actions using the tools Jira and Confluence on a weekly basis. Note: There is a separate Assessment document (available at the beginning of each semester) which gives fuller details for each assessment task.

Product assessment (Laboratory/practical, 50%, Group, individually assessed). The purpose of this task is to learn how to build requirements and assess against those requirements. The task for students is to demonstrate that the client is satisfied, the outcomes specified for the project description have been achieved, and the product performs as expected. This will be done via team demonstration of their product at the end of the semester. Note: There is a separate Assessment document (available at the beginning of each semester) which gives fuller details for each assessment task. This assessment requires group work. 20% of this assessment marks will be group assessed and 80% of this assessment marks will be individually assessed. SPARKPlus will be used to assess individual contributions and individual marks.

Project Presentation (Presentation, 15%, Group, individually assessed). To develop studentsâ skills in collaborating on a complex problem and presenting project outcomes to stakeholders Throughout the studio students will work in teams to define a problem, generate possible solutions, select and justify suitable options, prototype and verify solutions in a complex inter-disciplinary context. In this task, students will present their project to stakeholders for feedback.

Project Report (Report, 35%, Group, group and individually assessed). To develop studentsâ skills in collaborating on a complex problem as well as documenting and presenting projects to real stakeholders Throughout the studio students will work in teams to define a problem, generate possible solutions, select and justify suitable options, prototype and verify solutions in a complex inter-disciplinary context. In this task students will report on the results of this work in a final project report which shows background research, problem definition and scoping, solution ideation, prototyping/solution development, and implementation planning.

Individual Portfolio (Portfolio, 50%, Individual). To develop studentsâ individual understanding and skills in the project context and to highlight their professional development as they collaborate on a complex problem In this task students will individually develop artifacts towards a professional portfolio to be submitted at the end of the subject. Artifacts to be included are negotiated with the subject coordinator and project context dependent but could include items such as background research towards the project and reflections on professional development. Student contributions towards the team project will also be included in the portfolio.

Project 1: Email spam filtering (Project, 30%, Group, individually assessed). For this assessment, each student will work on a real-world case involving email spamming using skills learning in this subject. The primary objective is to analyse the email dataset, extract meaningful features for spam activity, and identify spam emails. Using analytical tools and techniques such as regression models, Support Vector Machines (SVM), or deep learning methods. Students are required to submit a report including their methodology, analysis, and results. Students are also required to demonstrate their results onsite to the teaching staff.

Project 2: Intrusion detection (Project, 30%, Individual). In this assessment, students will apply practical cybersecurity techniques to simulate a virtual network environment tasked with defending against and launching cybersecurity attacks. This exercise aims to simulate real-world scenarios to develop their abilities to configure and analyse network intrusion detection systems (NIDS). Students are required to submit a report including their methodology, analysis, and results. Students are also required to demonstrate their results onsite to the teaching staff. Â

Project 3: AI attacks and defences (Project, 40%, Group, individually assessed). In this assessment, students are required to conduct an investigation centred on the examination of AI attacks and/or the corresponding defences. This is a group work. it is recommended that each member try a different method on the same topic and compare and consolidate the results together.Â Individual contributions must be clearly stated in the report. Each group are required to submit a consolidated report including their methodology, analysis, and results. Students are also required to demonstrate their results onsite to the teaching staff.

Security Assessment Report (Report, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). This assessment requires students to investigate the security management issues in corporate organisations in teams by evaluating the risk levels, potential impact of threats and vulnerabilities, and cost benefit analysis of control methods, to analyse the security objectives of businesses and requirements and propose justified contingency plans to manage security risks in a group report. The report must follow prescribed procedures and include the following components: IT environment description; Corporate environment description; and A plan for approaching the identification of security threats. (Group assessed 15%, individually assessed 15%.)

Security Management Report (Report, 40%, Individual). This assessment requires students to prepare a security management report based on the findings of their investigation by using knowledge of IT security policies, risk assessment and management process, to identify personnel security, training, security education needs, and associated legal and ethical awareness. The report should apply prescribed management and audit procedures and consist of: an overview of the IT security management case; list of risks, threats and possible countermeasures; analysis of findings and the supported bibliography; review and reflection on the findings and propose justified recommendations. Students should orally present reports in the last workshop and prepare to answer questions. (Report 25%, Presentation 15%)

Online Quiz (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). This quiz tests studentsâ appliance of risk analysis and management approaches to consolidate the application skills of minimizing the risks and procedures to security audit. Open book quiz.

An essay to conduct independent research on one of the latest system security topics. (Report, 30%, Individual). This assessment is for students to conduct independent research on one of the latest system security topics. Students will be required to follow the standard procedure to investigate research papers in the area of system security. Students must generate a proposal to address system security problems and present their ideas to their peers and the teaching staff in a 5-minute presentation. Students are required to submit a research essay of approximately 1500 words as well as present a 5-minute talk. This essay should consist of: a proper title and an abstract for a chosen topic description of the research problem and brief findings literature review and synthesis of findings using appropriate referencing

Demonstration and Validation (Practical test, 20%, Individual). This assessment verifies studentsâ understanding of weekly workshop content through hands-on demonstration and Q&A. At the end of each workshop, students are required to present their completed practical tasks to the teaching staff, demonstrate the functionality or outcomes of their work, and respond to questions that assess their technical understanding and problem-solving process. This assessment ensures students can apply system security concepts in practice and can clearly explain the techniques, tools, and reasoning behind their solutions. Students will be assessed on: â¢ successful completion and demonstration of workshop tasks â¢ accuracy and clarity of explanations provided during Q&A â¢ engagement with workshop activities and troubleshooting steps

Online Quiz (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). This online quiz will assess studentâs appliance of system security, internal mechanisms and broad Information Technology knowledge related to computer system security. Students must demonstrate an ability to relate, justify, analyse and respond to questions around system security, technical vulnerabilities, technical remedies and cyberspace security and safety under examination conditions. It includes 2 in-workshop Canvas quizzes of 30 minutes each (complete during the scheduled workshop session), which consists of discussion and application type questions for case analysis and problem solving tasks. Students will respond to a set of questions including multiple choice and short answer questions during the quizzes.

A project to identify security vulnerabilities and propose technical solutions to rectify them. (Project, 40%, Group, individually assessed). This assessment task is for students to identify security vulnerabilities by various attacks and hardened systems. The students will be grouped into defensive and offensive teams. The offensive team has to choose a subset of the top ten vulnerabilities listed on OWASP project website, identify these vulnerabilities in systems nominated by the defensive team and document their findings. Defensive team students will be tested on their ability to harden the system. Both teams are required to verify experimental outcomes and to propose solutions to remedy the identified vulnerabilities. Students are required to submit a technical report of approximately 2500 words and demonstrate their results onsite to the teaching staff. This report should consist of: an overview of the chosen vulnerabilities description of technical findings and supporting evidence in screenshots analysis of technical findings discussion and justification of potential remedy actions based on findings.

Report on privacy attacks (Report, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). 1. through the assessment of student application of standard practice of attacking 2. through the assessment of evidence of teamwork skills in evaluating and planning testing 3. through the assessment of student awareness of ethical codes of conduct whilst working in the corporate environment In this assessment task, student teams will investigate a realâworld privacy breach involving a corporate environment. They will evaluate the levels of privacy in terms of data breach. They are required to write a report to summarise those breaches.

Privacy preserving project (Case study, 50%, Individual). 1. through the assessment of student ability and competence in using appropriate Privacy preserving technologies to defence the proposed attacks. 2. through the assessment of student ability to reflect and critically analyse experimental testing results before making wellâinformed conclusions. Implementing and/or comparing a set of existing privacy/security algorithms on a specific problem domain to defence the attack in the first assignment.

Secure Programming and Vulnerability Assessment (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). To practice secure programming skills (e.g., C/C++) and investigate and understand real-world security vulnerabilities. Students will need to understand the root causes of the vulnerabilities and classify them into the corresponding bug types. Through the practices in quizzes, students are required to inspect and understand example vulnerability code fragments. Students will be given a source code that contains vulnerabilities â and will need to identify what line they are in and what kind of vulnerability they are as part of your report. In the quiz â students will be given, multiple choice and short answer questions that inquire about security vulnerabilities in a source code case study. Quiz is individually assessed.

Source Code Representation for Software Analysis (Project, 20%, Individual). To demonstrate how compilers represent various real-world source code fragments as an appropriate representation for software security analysis as a foundation for building software security tools. Students will need to understand source code representation and basic concept of software analysis and testing, including the knowledge of compilers, intermediate representation of source code, and how to compile and represent various real-world source code fragments as an appropriate representation for software security analysis. To demonstrate this understanding, the student will be working on LLVM compiler and SVF code analysis framework to develop a graph traversal on code graphs. Students are required to submit well-documented code implementation they have developed to output the desired results.

Software Verification and Testing (Portfolio, 15%, Individual). To practice and apply software security analysis techniques and start building automated source code analysis tools based on the code representation (in Task 2) to automatically reason about a programâs properties (e.g., control- and data-flows) or program execution states. In this task, students will apply source code analysis techniques to capture source code properties and verify the assertions embedded in the code. Students are required to submit well-documented code implementation they have developed to output the desired results.

Automatic Detection of Security Vulnerabilities (Project, 15%, Individual). To deliver and evaluate the effectiveness of the developed security analysis and testing tool (Task 3) in detecting and defending a range of vulnerabilities. In this task, the student will leverage and apply techniques to automatically perform assertion-based verification for code using static symbolic execution.

Vulnerabilities scanning, exploiting and penetration testing report. (Portfolio, 30%, Individual). To implement common computer security attacks, complete short exercises with common penetration testing software, and investigate common vulnerabilities and report on the results. In this task, the student will conduct penetration testing, including port scanning, session hijacking and password cracking. Students are required to submit a penetration testing report and a presentation video to demonstrate the results.

Critical Discussion and Inquiry Exercise: Exploring Given Topics (Exercises, 20%, Individual). To demonstrate the ability to engage in critical discussion, effectively communicate understanding, and express inquiry on given topics. This assessment task is intended to allow students to critically engage with the material covered in this subject throughout the session. Through pre-readings, collaborative discussions in the class, case studies, and reflections, students formulate their responses to questions designed to encourage reflexivity.

Data Storytelling Blog post (Essay, 10%, Individual). To critically discuss and reflect on Australian Indigenous knowledge systems and practices as examples of cultural information systems. Students are to write a data storytelling blog post that explore Australian âIndigenous knowledge systems and practicesâ as examples of cultural information systems. Students will explore and communicate how Indigenous knowledge can be conceptualised as cultural information systems, fostering an appreciation for the rich heritage and wisdom embedded in these traditions. This task aims to develop studentsâ skills in data storytelling, critical analysis, and effective communication while encouraging a thoughtful exploration of cultural diversity and information systems in the context of Australian Indigenous communities.

Data Warehouse Design (Case study, 15%, Individual). To enhance database design skills, specifying Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) processes and emphasize the pivotal importance of data quality and consistency throughout the design of a data warehouse. Students design a data warehouse for a fictional organisation. Students should outline the Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) processes required to populate the data warehouse with relevant data, emphasising the importance of data quality and consistency.

Dashboard Design (Case study, 15%, Individual). To enhance business intelligence skills through designing a clear and insightful BI dashboard, emphasizing key performance indicators (KPIs) and ethical considerations in data processes and decision-making. Students to design a comprehensive BI dashboard for a given business scenario. Students should consider key performance indicators (KPIs) and design a dashboard that provides meaningful insights to decision-makers. The emphasis should be on clarity and simplicity in dashboard design, including ethical considerations of how data is collected, processed, and utilised in decision-making processes and practices for a business intelligence system.

BI Analysis and Implementation (Project, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Develop a business intelligence solution that adds value and competitive advantage. Students are to develop a business intelligence conceptual solution for a real-case scenario. Business Intelligence life cycle will be used as a roadmap to understand how data and information transform into intelligence, and how different applications/technologies can be used to analyse and report data. This assessment task is divided into two components. (1) Report and (2) Presentation. At least 10% of these components are marked individually and distributed in both the report and presentation, i.e., 40% (30% group, 10% individually).

Problem definition and stakeholder analysis (Report, 10%, Group, group assessed). Students become familiar with the purpose of problem definition and stakeholder analysis. Students work in groups to identify a real-world problem, identify different stakeholders and analyse their respective decision-making environments using design thinking practices.

Data preparation and initial concept (Report, 25%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students practice ethical data harvesting, data quality and initial visual concept development Students work in groups to identify and ethically harvest data, apply contemporary data quality and data integration methodologies, and develop initial visualisations. Students work on group component (5%) and individual sections of their project (20%).

Visual data exploration prototype - presentation (Presentation, 15%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students demonstrate their visual data exploration prototype. In this task, students are expected to demonstrate the main features of their data exploration prototype. All group members are expected to actively contribute to their prototype demo and will be asked on-the-spot questions about different features of the prototype, including brief statement of the problem, the underlying data structures, data quality and integration practices and visual ethics, multidimensional model and data exploration features. Students present group component (5%) and individual sections of their project (10%).

Visual data exploration prototype - report (Report, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students develop capability in designing a visual data exploration prototype. Students work in groups to design multidimensional models suitable for non-technical stakeholders as well as implement a prototype using a commercial data visualisation software. Students report group component (5%) and individual sections of their project (25%).

Prototyping project reflection (Reflection, 20%, Individual). To reflect on the project in the form of key lessons learned. Following group presentations, each student reflects on the lessons learned from their own group project and the in-class presentations given by other groups. The reflection focuses on the central question: âIf given an opportunity to do this project again, what would I do differently?â The reflection is expected to cover the whole life-cycle of the project, starting from the analysis of stakeholder problems, problem-driven (rather than data-driven) visual data exploration needs of different stakeholders, identification and ethical harvesting of relevant data, data quality, integration, data modeling for the identified stakeholders, design and implementation of a data exploration environment all the way to project presentations and lessons learned.

Research Project (Project, 80%, Group, individually assessed). A research report outlining the motivation and background behind the problem choice, a brief literature review and a detailed description of the solution developed, the methodology used, the results and conclusions, and an outline of future extensions. The work will be given as a written report. The allocated mark given to each student in the team will be a normalised percentage of the allocated mark on the basis of each team memberâs contribution (as determined by their peers). The work will be graded on its quality as a well-informed solution for an industry problem, and on the quality of the written report. The marking scheme is given below.

Presentation (Presentation, 20%, Group, individually assessed). This item assesses a studentâs oral communication skills and ability to present arguments clearly and concisely to specialist and non-specialist audiences. Students will develop and present an industry-based poster video presentation based on their project.

Socio-Environmental Project Appraisal: Critical Analysis (Written submission, 30%, Individual). To demonstrate critical thinking and understanding of social, environmental and project management considerations in evaluating case studies of real engineering projects. Each student will individually assess an engineering project from the supplied case studies, considering project management, environmental, and societal aspects. Students will be expected to conduct extensive research on the selected project using reliable sources and to apply critical thinking skills. Students are required to submit an evaluation report, which will be assessed and the content will be used for Assessment Task 2.

Economic Project Appraisal: Critical Analysis (Written submission, 30%, Individual). To demonstrate the ability to evaluate theÂ economic perspective in case studies of real engineering projects. Following Assessment Task 1, Students work individually to analyse and appraise an engineering project from the same case study through an economic lens. Students will be expected to conduct extensive research on the selected project using reliable sources and to apply critical thinking skills. The task submission includes a written report and an Excel file.Â

Holistic Project Review and Recommendations (Combination, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Demonstrate critical thinking by analysing and critiquing engineering reports from systems-thinking and ethical perspectives. In groups, students will critique a real-world case study of an engineering project, and report their findings in a written report (20%) and an oral presentation (20%). Assignment task 3A: Written report (20%): Students are required to submit a written report that critically evaluates the project, with a focus on analysing trade-offs between sustainability dimensions (social, environmental, and economic), ethical and professional responsibility considerations, and provide well-justified recommendations for improvement. -The written report will be moderated by SPARKPlus to give individual results for each student .Â Assignment task 3B: Presentation (20%):Â In-class task; Â students present their findings and respond to questions from the tutor and peers. All students are required to participate in preparing presentation materials and present their work. The presentation isÂ 12 minutes, followed by 8-10 minutes of Q&A (total 20 minutes).Â - The mark breakdown for the presentation is 75% group work (15 marks) and 25% individual performance (5 marks).

Scoping Investigation: Project Context, Opportunities and Challenges (Written submission, 20%, Individual). This assessment requires students to investigate the project context to develop an evidence-based understanding of the factors that will influence the design of an engineering solution. Working individually within their project team, students analyse one aspect of the project context, including its opportunities, challenges, stakeholders and broader system environment. The analysis establishes the foundation for the engineering design work undertaken in Assessment 2, where individual investigations are synthesised into a collaborative design proposal and subsequently informs the detailed project developed in Assessment 3.

Interim Report and Presentation (Combination, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Report: Group assessed 20% Presentation: Individually assessed 20% This assessment builds directly on the project context investigations undertaken in Assessment 1. Student teams will consolidate the individual analyses completed by team members and use this evidence to develop and justify a preliminary sustainable engineering design proposal. Teams will investigate alternative engineering solutions, apply sustainability frameworks, undertake technical, environmental, social and economic analyses and use a structured multi-criteria decision-making approach to identify a preferred design solution. The assessment requires students to justify design decisions using evidence gathered in Assessment 1 and critically evaluate alternative solutions before progressing to the detailed engineering proposal developed in Assessment 3. Â

Final Report and Presentation (Combination, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Report: Group assessed 10% Presentation: Individually assessed 30% This assessment builds on the preliminary engineering proposal developed in Assessment 2. Student teams refine their proposed engineering solution by incorporating feedback received throughout the design process and developing a detailed final sustainable engineering proposal that addresses all requirements of the Request for Proposal (RfP). The assessment requires students to justify design decisions in different project phases through detailed sustainability analysis, while demonstrating systems thinking. Individually, students progressively demonstrate their understanding of the team's engineering proposal through the Engineering Design Reviews conducted during tutorial sessions in Weeks 10 and 11. The final client presentation in Week 12 requires each student to individually defend the team's engineering design by explaining and justifying key design decisions, technical analyses and sustainability considerations, while reflecting on how feedback, collaboration and iterative design informed the evolution of the final engineering solution and their professional capability development.

RFT Proposal Critique (Written submission, 20%, Individual). You will evaluate multiple tender responses against an RFT, applying critical thinking and project management principles to recommend the best proposal. You must conduct a comprehensive analysis that demonstrates your ability to assess complex engineering proposals against the specified evaluation criteria. Your evaluation will require you to critically analyse each proposal's technical merit, project management approach, compliance with professional standards, and overall suitability for the project requirements. You will identify risks, assess value for money, and provide a justified recommendation with supporting evidence. This assessment develops your skills in interpreting technical documents, applying critical thinking to complex decisions, and communicating professional recommendations to stakeholders.

Contractor Response to RFT (Written submission, 35%, Group, individually assessed). This assessment challenges you to develop a comprehensive contractor response to a complex engineering RFT requiring multidisciplinary integration. Working in multidisciplinary teams (4-6 students), you will collaborate to create a professional RFT response document that directly addresses tender evaluation criteria, demonstrates technical capability, presents competitive commercial proposals, and meets professional procurement standards.Â This component is worth 35% and completed as a group.Â The groups mark is moderated by SPARKPlus and each student gets an individual mark.

Consortium Charter and Peer Review Portfolio (Creative project/portfolio/showcase, 10%, Individual). You will individually develop an assessment that demonstrates your personal accountability for analysing project information, applying relevant project management and engineering theory, and exercising professional judgement. This individual component focuses on integrating into a consortium, contributing to a shared charter, and providing structured peer feedback to partner firms to evaluate feasibility, identify key risks, and communicate a justified position aligned with client and project needs. Although the work takes place within a group, you are assessed individually. This component is worth 10% and completed individually.

Presentation Portfolio (Presentation, 35%, Group, group and individually assessed). You will build a presentation portfolio throughout the semester, demonstrating your professional communication skills across multiple contexts. Your portfolio consists of a final management presentation worth 30% by default, with opportunities to "lock in" up to one third of these marks (10%) through in-class presentation activities. When you participate in in-class presentations, those marks are secured early and reduce the weight of your final presentation accordingly. For example, if you earn 10% through in-class activities, your final presentation becomes worth 20% instead of 30%. This approach allows you to practice and build confidence while reducing the pressure on your final assessment. You can choose to do only the final presentation for the full 30%, or engage with in-class opportunities to distribute your marks across multiple lower-stakes presentations. The portfolio approach recognises that communication skills develop through practice and provides multiple opportunities to showcase your abilities in professional engineering contexts.

Project checkpoint presentations (Presentation, 15%, Group, group and individually assessed). Every few weeks over the semester, you will present in-class updates on your project progress, including your understanding of the project brief, the context and complexity of your project, your proposed solution, and more. You will receive feedback on your progress that you can then incorporate in to your final project report and presentation.

Reverse Project Brief (Written submission, 20%, Group, individually assessed). Purpose : Demonstrate your understanding of your allocated project briefÂ by analysing it from multiple angles and clearly communicating that understanding back to your project partner. Working in your group, you will complete a structured response to your allocated project brief using the template provided. This is your opportunity to demonstrate a clear and well-reasoned understanding of the brief and its context.Â This is a group task, but will be moderated by SPARKPlus feedback to calculate your individual mark.

Project Report (Written submission, 20%, Group, individually assessed). This written submission supports and complements your project presentation, providing the project partner with your analysis and proposed response to the project brief. You will to demonstrate your understanding of: the project brief and its complexity relevant cultural considerations you have incorporated into your design process and proposal You need to describe and advocate for your project proposal (i.e. what you are proposing in response to the project brief and why it is worth your project partner pursuing), including sustainability analysis using one of the approaches we have reviewed (e.g. Life-cycle analysis; triple-bottom-line; SDGs, or cost-benefit analysis). Additional details such as drawings or calculations can be included in an appendix. You will also have to briefly summarise how you have incorporated feedback from the Reverse Project Brief and from the in-class project checkpoint presentations. The audience for the submission is the project partner, and the writing is expected to demonstrateÂ an understanding of respectful communication with the diversity of Indigenous stakeholders.

Project Presentation (Presentation, 20%, Group, individually assessed). This assessment is a presentation aimed at your project partner (represented by your tutor). Your aim is to convince them of the merits of what you are proposing in response to their project brief. You will need to demonstrate your understanding of: the project brief, the project context and complexity,Â key stakeholders and associated cultural considerations Â You also need to describe your project proposal, including sustainability analysis business case any key assumptions or limitations recommendations for next steps and/or implementing your proposal Â Â

Job interview on collaboration (Interactive oral, 25%, Individual). To demonstrate your development of collaboration skills, you will participate in a mock job interview with one of the teaching team. In the interview you will be asked different questions about how you have achieved the relevant subject learning outcomeÂ SLO4:Â Collaborate in diverse interdisciplinary teams and with stakeholders to achieve problem solutions.Â You will need to draw on examples from your experience in the subject.

Combined Module Tests (Exercises, 25%, Individual). This assessment consists of three separate online tests conducted via UTS Canvas under restricted open-book conditions. Each test evaluates the content covered from either the start of the session or the conclusion of the previous test up to the week of the current test. During the tests, students are permitted to use one double-sided, A4-sized sheet of handwritten notes . No other printed or digital materials are allowed, including Canvas lecture slides, tutorial handbooks, and external websites. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited.

Skills Based Assessment (Laboratory/practical, 35%, Individual). The Skills-Based Assessments (SBAs) are designed for students to demonstrate their practical understanding of network security. This individual, restricted open-book assessment is conducted in class during students' scheduled tutorial/lab sessions using Packet Tracer software. Assessment questions will be released via Canvas at the specified assessment time. During the assessment, students are permitted to use one double-sided, A4-sized sheet of handwritten notes . No other printed or digital materials are allowed, including Canvas lecture slides, tutorial handbooks, and external websites. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited.

End-of-session Quiz (Quiz/test, 40%, Individual). This individual, restricted open-book test consists of short-answer questions conducted via UTS Canvas. The test will be completed in class during the scheduled session time and covers the concepts and knowledge studied throughout the semester. During the test, students are permitted to use one double-sided, A4-sized sheet of handwritten notes . No other printed or digital materials are allowed, including Canvas lecture slides, tutorial handbooks, and external websites. The use of Generative AI tools is strictly prohibited.

Labs (Laboratory/practical, 20%, Individual). To practice cryptographic algorithms and tools. Use security tools to run cryptographic schemes and perform cryptographic analysis and attacks through eight labs throughout the session. In every lab, a specific task and lab guidance will be given to students. Labs are normally completed in class time. Students are required to individually complete the lab tasks guided by lab notes, and then submit a lab report after the lab. The lab reports are assessed by tutors based on lab progress and answers to lab questions. Feedback on the labs will be provided by tutors in class and on the reports.

Quizzes (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). The Quizzes are designed to motivate continuous learning, analysis and the recall of the technical knowledge relevant to the subject concepts. Two in-class quizzes will take place during the labs to consolidate studentsâ technical knowledge of topics covered in class. Each quiz will cover all material covered in classes that precede it. The quiz is open book. Feedback on the quizzes will be provided in-class, after the quiz.

Implementation project (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). To critically analyse cryptographic problems through hands-on implementation of cryptography concepts, and to practice cryptographic techniques in a collaborative manner. Cryptographic specific project topics, such as implementing cryptographic algorithms, developing cryptographic attacks and configuring cryptographic systems, will be provided to students. A group of students (normally three) will be required to research appropriate practical techniques and carry out hands-on work to complete their chosen task. Students must also reflect on how these techniques are used more broadly in society to help individuals and organisations manage issues such as digital identity, security and information privacy. The assessment will cover group work and individual contribution. The group project will be assessed by tutors in-class based on the task completion and questions on the tasks. 40% project marks are for the group assessment and 60% project marks are for studentsâ individual work. The group component of the mark covers the overall project and how team members have worked collaboratively to implement their chosen overall task. During the assessment, the groups need to present the group work, such as codes and commands, and their results to tutors. Each student will be asked questions about the project task individually, and this will form the basis of individual assessment. In-class feedback on the project will be provided by tutors, both formative (during the project development phase) and summative (during in-class assessment).

Cybersecurity Capstone Portfolio (Portfolio, 100%, Individual). To document the iterative learning process and artefacts that demonstrate the achievement of learning goals related to cybersecurity. Students are expected to work in teams assuming the role of a professional colleague throughout the project phase. Although students work in teams, submissions are assessed individually. The Cybersecurity Capstone Portfolio is designed around a series of component parts. To meet the pass performance level of the portfolio, all components must be included. A performance level rubric is used to identify individual progress during the teaching session in view of students making individual improvements to their performance level based on continuous feedback and opportunities for personal reflection. The components of the portfolio include: Component 1: Individual Learning Contract Agreement Groupwork: Individual The intent of this component is to identify and document project direction, and set personal goals for the project duration. Each team member will create an Individual Learning Contract (ILC), and have it agreed to by their academic mentor(s). The ILC will be created in Canvas as an online assignment using a template provided. The ILC should describe activities that will enable each team member to gain additional knowledge and skills that will enhance the studentâs contribution to the team and product. Each team member is expected to select at least two technical and two non-technical learning activities, generally different than their peers. Component 2 Personal Design and Learning Journal Groupwork: Individual The intent of this component is to record and reflect on individual learning, design process, experiences and feedback received while working on the team product. Â Each student creates a Personal Design and Learning Journal (PDLJ) and records their learning, experiences and reflections on a regular basis. Students must keep their journal using a professional record-keeping tool as used in industry or research. The first purpose of the PDLJ is to document your individual contribution to the team product development by including evidence of work done and reflections on what worked, what didnât work and what you might do differently in future while working on the product development. The second purpose of the PDLJ is to document your progress against your own ILC goals set near the start of the session. You must curate evidence of your individual learning regularly throughout the session that demonstrates how you progressively achieve the goals articulated in the Individual Learning Contract (ILC). As well as receiving feedback from academic mentors, students may also be asked to share their progress with other students for peer feedback in some weeks. Participating in giving and receiving peer feedback, and reflecting on and documenting feedback, forms part of this task. Â Each team member must be able to demonstrate a history of regular contributions throughout the session. It is a requirement that the PDLJ be submitted at regular intervals. Feedback will be provided (either by staff or peers) for PDLJs submitted on time by the deadlines on Canvas. In the overall assessment, the PDLJ will be considered together with other artefacts in the portfolio in determining an individualâs final grade according to the performance level rubric. Component 3: Team Product/Prototype Proposal and Pitch Groupwork: Group, group and individually assessed The intent of this component is to define the scope of the cybersecurity capstone project and to negotiate the scope and outcomes with the product owner and mentor. Project teams submit a written proposal for their product/prototype and have it agreed to by their product owner(s) and academic mentor(s). The proposal should include agreed deliverables and a timeline for the work to be carried out. The length of the proposal should be sufficient to fully describe the proposed Product, deliverables and timeline. A template with suggested section headings will be provided as guidance. This component is group assessed (all team members will include the same written proposal in their portfolio). Teams must also âpitchâ their product proposal in an oral presentation. All members of a team must participate in the pitch. This component is individually assessed. Component 4: Team Product/Prototype Delivery Groupwork: Group, group and individually assessed The intent of this component is to demonstrate your ability to deliver a cybersecurity capstone project to an agreed scope. In doing so, each team member also demonstrates their capacity to solve problems, create solutions, develop design specifications, implement the product/prototype, work in teams, communicate professionally and manage time and tasks. There are three sub-parts to this component: A presentation delivered in class (roadshow) that describes what was produced, including a demonstration where appropriate. The presentation is individually assessed. The product itself and a report and video that describes the product development process and outcomes. The size of the report will depend upon the complexity of the product and the number of students in the team.Â The video should be approximately 3 minutes, and the intended audience is your future employer.The report and video is group assessed (one submission per team), but individual grades may be moderated based on team memberâs overall contribution and evidence curated in their individual PDLJ. A communication log of meetings with the product owner, which clearly presents the meeting schedules, attendees and summary of discussions. This will typically be part of the final report. This part is also group assessed (one communication log per team), but individual grades may be moderated. All students must be present in class for the final presentation/demonstration, and all students must have contributed to the project throughout the session, including meetings with the product owner. The report should document the process followed, and contributions by individual team members. Â

The lab reports are assessed by tutors based on lab progress and answers to lab questions. Feedback on the labs will be provided by tutors in class and on the reports.

Each student will be asked questions about the project task individually, and this will form the basis of individual assessment. Â

Research project (Literature review, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). To research cryptography theories, and to communicate cryptography knowledge to specialists. In this research project, a group of students (normally three) are required to complete a literature review on selected recent advances in cryptography, including applications, projects, technologies and social impact, and write a report based on the review. A suggested report structure will be provided online. The topic list will be available from week 1. Students need to choose their topics by the end of week 5, and the report is due at the end of session. Each member of the team will be required to research a different but related area within the chosen group topic, and write a section based on the research for the individual contribution. The group report should include each studentâs individual contribution, as well as an overall summary of how the different individual sections relate to each other. Each studentâs individual contribution to the project will account for three quarters of the project marks (30%) and the group component will account for the remaining one quarter (10%). Students are encouraged to create an early outline of their report, and draft versions throughout the session, to receive feedback from tutors in class. Feedback on marking of the report will be available after final results are released to students, on request.

Team Progress Report (Report, 10%, Individual). This assessment is to provide opportunities for students to communicate with team members and coordinate individual progresses in a team basis, reflecting the teamâs learning experience, project development, teamwork, and individual contributions. Team Progress Reports are required to be submitted weekly, from Week 2 to Week 11. Team progress reports will be an important worklog for a team, recording the progresses of team construction and development, including allocating team responsibilities, learning and problem-solving experiences, project logs, teamwork and individual contributions, etc. Importantly, team progress reports will be the evidence of teamwork and individual contributions for AT4.

Product 1: Analytics project plan and design (Report, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). This assessment is to train students to integrate domain-specific knowledge and business problems, and related data and resources with analytics/machine learning methods and processes to design desirable solutions. Through this task, students will develop skills of critical thinking and analysis of appropriate state-of-the-art analytics technologies to address challenging real-world business problems and objectives. Part 1 of Product 1 (15%): An Analytics Project Plan and Design report The report is required to follow a professional template of project reports, and address the following items: Background Business objectives Analytical goals and tasks Data and resources Analytical system architecture Analytical methods Experiments and evaluation methods Implementation design Expected outcomes Timetable with milestones Risk management References Part 1 of Product 1 is group work, and all team members are expected to work as a team and will receive the same marks reflected by the Analytics Project Plan and Design report. Part 2 of Product 1 (15%): Project Plan Presentation A presentation to present the teamâs analytics project plan and design, including the major contents of your report (Part 1 of Product 1). The Part 2 will be scheduled before the due date of Part 1, and please appropriately elaborate Part 2âs feedback given by the audiences to Part 1. Each team member is required to deliver a part of this presentation, reflecting their contribution to the project. We will individually assess each team member, according to their presentation performance and team contributions.

Product 2: Project analytical report (Report, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). This assessment is to train students with enterprise all-round and hands-on thinking, ability to effectively synergize cross-disciplinary knowledge, processes, skills, and experience to implement a project plan and design (Product 1) into analytical solutions to address enterprise challenges and innovations. Students are expected to make sense of enterprise data, evaluate results, improve the analytical design and strategies, deploy actionable analytical results, and communicate with stakeholders. Students will learn to develop industry-standard analytical systems, solutions, documentation, and communications. Part 1 of Product 2 (25%) : A Project Analytics Report This report is required to summarize the activities, results, and findings in the analytical report with a professional template of industry project reports. The content of the report includes: Background including confirmed business objectives and analytical goals System Architecture and Models including implemented analytics/machine learning methods Experiments (for method selection, testing, and development) System Interface including data, user interface, results, and recommendations Deployment Plan Business Impacts References Part 1 of Product 2 is group work, but we will individually assess each team memberâs contribution through a SPARKPlus-based peer evaluation. Part 2 of Product 2 (15%): Project Showcase A showcase with all team members to present the teamâs analytics project report, particularly the implementation of the developed data analytical tool/system (Part 1 of Product 2). The Part 2 will be scheduled before the due date of Part 1, and please appropriately elaborate Part 2âs feedback given by the audiences to Part 1. Each team member is required to deliver a part of this presentation, reflecting their contribution to the project. We will individually assess each team member, according to their presentation performance and team contributions.

Self-Reflection and Peer Review (Reflection, 20%, Individual). This assessment is to provide opportunities for students to report and justify their individual contributions to the team, with self-reflections of their learning experience, self-development, and teamwork experience, and peer review the contributions of other team members. The Self-Reflection and Peer Review is to an online assessment, including two parts: 1. Self-Reflection on the own experience of students, including Completion of team responsibility (highlighting challenges, efforts to handle the challenges, the lessons learned from the efforts, and future improvements) Team collaboration experience (enjoyable moments, barriers, resolutions, etc.) Self-development and learning experiences 2. Peer Review other team memberâs commitment and performance in the team from the following aspects: Commitment to team responsibility Team collaboration (attitudes, manners, communication styles, etc.) Evidence quoted/cited must be from AT1 Team Progress Reports.

Project Proposal (Report, 15%, Individual). This assessment task prepares students in their search for finding a potential new technology that could match their company context and generate a competitive advantage. This assessment item focuses on the description of your organisation and technological innovation that you want to use in assignments 2 and 3. This task will allow the students to construct a research proposal on conducting a technology and innovation management project at an organisation level. The students could choose their own company or any hypothetical start-up company. The students are also free to choose any technological innovation such as industry robots or chatbots to find information and relate to the company they want to apply.

Management of a technological innovation (Report, 45%, Individual). This assessment task helps students implement their knowledge of technology management activities and tools in a company context. The student should document a critical analysis of their organisationâs current TM processes and practices/capabilities like an audit exercise. Then, the student will discuss how to implement a new technological innovation within the organisation. This task will allow students to see the link between technologies and TM activities. Adopting tools to analyse the implementation of technological innovation will facilitate students to observe the gaps in current TM practices. Then, the student will develop solutions to overcome the observed gaps. The student is encouraged to engage and interview their organizationâs executive leaders to make this a practice-based assignment. They will use materials presented to them from module-2 to module-4

Assessing potential implications of a new technology (Report, 25%, Individual). This task aims to guide students to research all potential impacts of new technology and develop a mitigation strategy to overcome any negative effects generated by this new technology. The student will be able to evaluate the impact of technological change by analysing and presenting the potential impact of technological change on stakeholders (such as employees, customers, and society) of an organisation. The analysis will cover both the positive and negative effects of technologies. Then, the student will focus on designing solutions to overcome any adverse effects of technological changes on personal, organizational, and societal levels.

Pitch for the new technology (Presentation, 15%, Individual). This assignment allows students to develop their presentation skills in a compelling business pitch where they communicate why and how new technology should be deployed in their companies. The student will effectively communicate all aspects of introducing a technological change at the company, consolidating previous findings (Assignment 1, 2, and 3). This presentation will mimic a business pitch for top senior management. The student will present the advantages and disadvantages of new technology for the company, followed by a plan for how the new technology could be successfully implemented.

subject_name: Digital Strategy: Aligning Business and Technology
text: Current state executive brief (Reflection, 15%, Individual). Business and industries are in different stages of theirs journeys towards a digital future and are facing a variety of challenges along the way. In times where digital technologies supercharge life cycles and competitive environments, it is important for business to stay on top. This assessment item focusses on an initial assessment of an organisation with respect to its digital progress. This assessment task therefore provides you with an opportunity to apply your understanding of these considerations to a specific case. Please consider a business of your choice. This could be the company you work for or another company of your choice (possibly in an industry you are passionate about and for which you have some background knowledge and some information that is publicly available). This will be the organisation you work with for all assessments. Be sure to look ahead at the other assessments before deciding on an organisation to work with. Some criteria for selecting your company: You need to be able to access information about your company's current digital strategy. The company's current digital strategy needs room for improvement. If they already have an innovative digital strategy theyâre probably not a good choice to work with for this subject. The companyâs executive members are considering a large investment program to prepare the business for a digital future. As a newly hired digital strategy consultant, you are asked to provide an assessment brief, summarising the current position of the companyâs digital journey. In this short executive report, they are expecting brief answers to the following questions: Q1: To what extent does your organisation currently rely on digital technology? Where on the evolution of the 4 industrial revolutions do you see your organisation? Q2: What could be the potential opportunities going forward based in the free perfect and instant characteristics of digital information goods? Q3: What could be the potential challenges for your business of choice? What have you learned from challenges or successes other companies have had?

text: Digital strategy pitch (Presentation, 45%, Individual). Everyone knows by now that digital processes are essential. However, with the vast and growing array of digital capabilities available, it is paramount for a business to have a plan that matches digital initiatives with company goals â a digital strategy. The aim of this assessment task is to create and communicate a digital strategy for a specific business in order to avoid failure in implementation. Following the study of the assessment framework, the executive board is keen to get cracking. They have, however, understood that any digital initiative can only be successful, if it is embedded in a new digital strategy. They have now asked you to give them a pitch presentation, outlining key recommendations to a roadmap initiating successful and sustainable digital change. Based on your findings from the previous two assessment tasks, create and record a presentation to the board of the company that covers: Your understanding of the companyâs existing strategy and how and where it needs to adapt This includes the companyâs willingness to change (see AT1) A placement of your initiative within The existing strategic priorities the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals A plan to engage and communicate throughout the whole organisation introduce measured for governance and sustaining change specific to the digital nature of the initiatives Some key success measures A summary of recommendations and suggested next steps

A use case for AI in business (Report, 15%, Individual). This assessment item focusses on the initial identification of a use case for AI in a business environment. Businesses are facing a variety of challenges in the digital age and AI can be a possible solution to tackle those challenges. This assessment task provides you with an opportunity to apply your understanding of these considerations to a specific case. Please consider a business of your choice. This could be the company you work for or another company of your choice (possibly in an industry you are passionate about and for which you have some background knowledge and some information that is publicly available). The companyâs executive members are considering a large investment program to prepare the business for a digital future. AI could become one important pillar of this program. As a first step, the executives have asked you to conduct an initial exploration of possible use cases for AI across the business. They are expecting a brief overview in the style of a management summary addressing the following questions: What are the key challenges that the companyâs industry is facing in the current competitive environment of rapid digital disruption? Mini AI application examples (Project, 45%, Individual). Assess studentsâ ability to apply selected AI techniques to solve simple problems. Students need to choose THREE pairs of AI techniques to develop AI application examples to show how these AI techniques are used to solve three simple problems. The three problems include one search problem, one classification problem and one regression problem. For each problem, students need to develop two working solutions using two AI techniques. The deliverables of each example include a professional report and a working notebook/program in Google Colab.

Group project plan and design (Project, 35%, Group, group and individually assessed). This assignment equips students with AI thinking and critical analysis of various phases in undertaking AI projects, including defining problem statement, assessing and selecting proper AI techniques, and developing methodologies, solution architectures, processes and workflow, and evaluation criteria. The task trains students to integrate domain-specific knowledge, target problems, data sources with AI techniques to design desirable solutions. The design proposal integrates cross-disciplinary thinking, knowledge, and skills for data-driven evidence-based design to solve an interesting and challenging practical problem.Â This is a two-part assessment. In Part 1, students need to develop a detailed project proposal in a small group that addresses an AI application case with specific objectives, data resources, solution designs including AI technique selection and justification, milestones, evaluation, expected outcomes, and risk management, etc. The group also needs to produce a presentation video for end-users of their AI solutions. A template of project proposal will be provided in the assignment specification. Part 1 weights 25% of subject mark (i.e., 25 marks). In Part 2, students need to write an individual reflection report to present evidence that reflect what they have learned from this task, such as the AI application domain, challenges of the target problem and why selected AI technique can help, what contribution they have made to design the solution to the chosen problem and what roles they were able to take if their proposal would be implemented. Part 2 weights 10% of subject mark (i.e., 10 marks).

Project Requirements and Specifications (Essay, 25%, Group, individually assessed). To determine requirements and specifications on a project in the field of image processing and pattern recognition. This assignment will require each group of 2-3 students to produce a written document containing requirements and specifications for an image processing and pattern recognition project. The project topic should be granted approval by the lecturer. The specifications must cover: analysis of the problem, including the availability of one or more suitable, public datasets; selection of the techniques that the students expect to solve the problem. This will include various, plausible alternatives; motivation for the approach based on the knowledge acquired during lectures and independent readings; a performance evaluation methodology which will be used to assess the approachâs performance. This will require conducting experiments on the chosen dataset(s) with the various alternative techniques and collate their performance; a list of references; the contribution of each student to the group will be described in a short table in the report.

This assignment will require each group of students to implement the project described in their Assignment 1. The project will be developed as a Matlab program. The contribution of each student to the group will be described in a short table in the report. This assignment will consist of a written report on the outcomes of the project.

This task will involve each student presenting a critical review of an academic research paper related to the topic studied in Assessment Tasks 1 and 2. Weekly Task (Laboratory/practical, 30%, Group, individually assessed). Practising engineers are expected to design andÂ validateÂ the physical layer performance ofÂ wirelessÂ networks. By designing and modellingÂ antennasÂ in wireless systems, students develop essential engineering skills, including the use of advanced simulation tools to evaluateÂ wave propagationÂ behaviour. This task focuses on a series of design and electromagnetic modelling exercises using HFSS. Emphasising the critical role of physical layer technologies such as antennas, propagation environments, and wave propagation characteristics, this project equips students with a deep understanding of how physical constraints and design choicesÂ impactÂ overall network performance. GuidedÂ hands-on lab activities will support students in applying theoretical concepts to practical simulation tasks, reinforcing their subject knowledge, problem solving, and research capabilities.Â

Design Project (Project, 20%, Group, individually assessed). This design project requires students to apply electromagnetic theory and simulation techniques to solve real-world wireless engineering problems through the use of electromagnetic modelling tools. Focusing on the physical layer of 4G and 5G networks, students will design and evaluate components such as antennas, propagation environments, and wave interactions to assess key performance metrics including radiation patterns, gain, and bandwidth. By abstracting practical challenges and validating designs through simulation, students will demonstrate their ability to translate theoretical knowledge into functional engineering solutions. Students may use generative AI tools, such as Microsoft Copilot, to support specific tasks in this project, including reviewing simulation models, generating technical descriptions, clarifying complex concepts, drafting documentation, and improving report clarity. Any use of AI must be clearly acknowledged in the final report. Students are expected to critically review and validate all AI-generated content to ensure accuracy and uphold academic integrity. The project culminates in the submission of a professional wireless design report and encourages teamwork by reflecting the collaborative and competitive nature of real industry environments. Cybersecurity Challenge Studio Portfolio (Creative project/portfolio/showcase, 100%). This subject is assessed through a single Portfolio. The purpose of this assessment is to document the full challenge process, evidence, and outcomes of the selected stream, and to present a professional, evidence-based account of what was completed, how the work wasÂ validatedÂ or evaluated, and what the scope, assumptions, and limitations are.Â Students must select one stream in Weeks 1â2 (Industry stream or Research stream), and the Portfolio requirements are aligned to the selected stream.Â The Portfolio must be professionally written and include step-by-step evidence, analysis, and reflection. Students must provide professional evidence of their work, such as screenshots, logs, experimental outputs, code, records of progress, and other relevant artefacts. Screenshots and other submitted evidence must include the studentâs identification details (for example, student ID/number) where required by theÂ subjectÂ instructions.Â The Portfolio also includes a recorded presentation and demonstration that communicates the problem, approach, key technical steps, evidence of outcomes, and limitations in a manner suitable for a professional audience.Â Assessment requirements differ by stream, as follows.Â Â Â Industry stream Â Students in the Industry stream complete a practice-to-project portfolio structured through four milestones.Â Milestone A: Learning contract completion and Hands-on training Â selection and execution In Weeks 1â2, students select a set of hands-on training tasks based on the signed learning contract.Â Tasks carry different point values based on difficulty and may be subject to selection limits for lower-difficulty tasks. Students must construct a task combination that meets the trainingÂ requirement. The Portfolio must document the key steps, technical process, evidence, and analysis of the completed work. A progress check is due in Week 5.Â Milestone B: Student-designed project development Â Students develop a project derived from their selected training direction and applyÂ appropriate securityÂ standards and/or methods to support security-by-design and validation. A complete project and Portfolio draft is due in Week 10.Â Â Milestone C: Cross-group penetration testing and professional testing documentation Â Each group is paired with another group, with both groups testing each otherâs systems or solutions through security testing activities such as penetrationÂ testing, andÂ producing professional testing documentation. This documentation must include scope, approach, evidence, findings, and recommendations. Evidence from Milestones AâC must beÂ consolidatedÂ into the final Portfolio. This is not a competitive milestone; studentsâ performance will be evaluated on the quality and professionalism of their testing documentation. This milestone is due in Week 12.Â Â Milestone D: Recorded presentation and demonstration Â StudentsÂ submitÂ a recorded presentation and demonstration. The presentation must clearly communicate the challenge, approach, key technical steps, evidence of outcomes, and limitations in a manner suitable for a professional audience. The presentation should also propose potential ways to address the limitationsÂ identifiedÂ in Milestone C. This milestone is due in Week 14.Â Â Â Research stream Â Students in the Research stream complete a research-to-evidence portfolio structured through four milestones.Â Â Milestone A: Learning contract completion, paper selection, method analysis, and implementation/replication with comparative experiments Â In Weeks 1â2, students select a target paper based on the signed learning contract, either provided by staff or sourced fromÂ appropriate venues. Students then analyse the research background, motivation, feasibility, and assumptions of the selected work, and implement or replicate the proposed method(s). Comparative experiments must be conducted against relevant baselines or related methods, including evaluation across different datasets or settings whereÂ appropriate. A progress check is due in Week 5.Â Â Milestone B: Limitations analysis and improvement proposal Â StudentsÂ identifyÂ limitations of the selected work and propose a justified improvement or extension. WhereÂ feasible, the proposal should be supported by evidence such asÂ additionalÂ experiments, ablation studies, or a clear analytical or mathematical derivation. A complete Portfolio draft is due in Week 10.Â Milestone C: Cross-group peer analysis Â Each group is paired with another group to conduct reciprocal peer analysis of each otherâs work. Students critique and analyse the other groupâs work toÂ identifyÂ weaknesses, limitations, and the research-to-practice gap. WhereÂ appropriate, groups may apply alternative datasets or settings and/or different adversarial models or attack strategies to evaluate usability and security properties. Findings from this milestone must be incorporated into the final Portfolio. This milestone is due in Week 12.Â Â Milestone D: Recorded presentation and demonstration Â StudentsÂ submitÂ a recorded presentation and demonstration. The presentation must clearly communicate the research problem, approach, key technical steps, evidence of outcomes, and limitations in a manner suitable for a professional audience. The presentation should also propose potential ways to address the limitationsÂ identifiedÂ in Milestone C. This milestone is due in Week 14.Â Â Â

text: Lab portfolio (Laboratory/practical, 50%, Group, individually assessed). To demonstrate capability in responding to realistic cybersecurity incidents. Throughout the session, students will complete a series of lab activities relating to security operations (SecOps) and incident response. Each lab will present students with a realistic cyber attack scenario, and students will engage hands-on with the processes of incident response such as incident detection, impact assessment and strategies to contain or eliminate the threat and recover systems and data. While completing each lab, students are expected to keep lab journal notes which are collated to become the lab portfolio which is submitted for assessment. In some weeks there may be a lab worksheet provided that needs to be completed, while in other weeks the lab notes may be more freeform, with students documenting their observations, actions and outcomes. Further guidance will be provided in class and on Canvas. Some labs are completed individually, while others may be done in pairs. In both cases, each student must individually prepare their own lab notes, and copying or sharing notes between students is not permitted. Students submit their lab portfolio mid-way during the session for feedback (10% weighting), including labs completed up until that point. Students are also invited to seek individual feedback from tutors on their lab portfolio content in other weeks during the lab classes, as required. The final lab portfolio submission is worth 40%, covering all labs completed during the session.

subject_name: Cyber Threat Intelligence and Incident Response
text: Case study report (Report, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). To demonstrate a holistic approach to cyber threat intelligence and incident response, integrating research skills with contemporary industry practice in designing a response to a case study scenario. For this task, students work as a team of 3-4 students to prepare a written report based on a case study that will be provided. The overall requirement is for students to design a response strategy that addresses the case study provided. In their design, teams are required to address all aspects of cyber threat intelligence and incident response processes covered in the subject, and contextualise their application to the provided case study. The design presented should reflect current industry practice. In addition to technical capability, designs must also demonstrate an awareness of the social, environmental, economic and ethical contexts of Security Operations (SecOps) as they apply to the provided case study. Teams are also required to engage with contemporary research and literature in cyber threat intelligence and incident response in preparing their report, and reports must include an appropriate reference list in APA format. Individual contributions will be evidenced in the group report. In marking, 15% of the weighting is based on groupwork and 15% based on individual effort.

The remaining 25% of the assessment will be based on the quality and completeness of each studentâs individual work, including task execution and responses to tutor questions regarding the progress of project..
