Presentations (Presentation, 20%, Individual). To interpret a chosen emerging AI topic through an oral presentation with insights gained from algorithm implementations and literature studies. Students are required to choose one of the four implementation topics and conduct an individual presentation to reflect their learning journey with an appropriate logical line and presentation structure. An understanding of the topic with appropriate literature review Insightful understanding of at least one representative algorithms and extensive discussion about the industrial applications of the chosen AI topic/techniques. Appropriate presentation skills are required.

Knowledge Quiz (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). To demonstrate an understanding of computational intelligent theory and operation Quizzes are presented as single/multiple choice, 2-4 questions per week for ten weeks. These are from slides and recommended research papers. These are completed in or after class and students receive feedback during class.

Lab Practice (Laboratory/practical, 35%, Individual). To apply computational intelligence algorithms to public data to solve problems The goal of this assignment is to develop your hands-on skills in performing learning from data, as well as further understanding of the practical technical details of the learning procedure. You will implement a simple algorithm from scratch. In the report, you will need to identify and discuss a problematic issue in the present implementation

Final Project (Project, 45%, Individual). Design a fuzzy inference system to solve a given problem Students will use the algorithm learnt in the class to solve the problems in the final project. Students will (1) demonstrate the understanding of the given problem and datasets; (2) introduce the related work of the given problem and related algorithms; (3) design the solution(s) to the given problem, explain the solution(s), simulate the model(s), evaluate the outcomes and discuss the findings.

Weekly quizzes (Quiz/test, 40%, Individual). For students to benchmark their understanding of concepts presented within the weekly subject sessions Complete weekly online multiple-choice quiz covering the content studied in the prior week. Two attempts will be permitted.

In-Lab critiquing (Exercises, 30%, Group, individually assessed). This assessment task contributes to the development of quantum computing knowledge and its appropriate application, as well as contextualising professional and communication skills within the quantum computing discipline. Examine and critique quantum protocols, algorithms, and proofs. During each lab session, the students will be tasked with orally critiquing presented quantum protocols and proofs. Within groups, the students will develop an argument and elect a representative to deliver the argument to the class. Students will be assigned to self-assess their contribution as well as that of other group members via feedback survey.

In-Lab presentations (Presentation, 30%, Group, individually assessed). This assessment task contributes to the development of quantum computing knowledge and its appropriate application, as well as contextualising professional and communication skills within the quantum computing discipline. In teams, the students will explain specific quantum algorithms and concepts to the rest of the class. Emphasis is placed on effectively communicating new ideas using a variety of teaching and learning tools. Students will critique themselves and each other via feedback survey. A portion of the grade will reflect the quality of the feedback given.

Learning portfolio (Exercises, 30%, Group, group assessed). To synthesise how humanitarian engineering relates to and can inform other aspects of engineering practice through engagement with readings and related content. Students are expected to respond to prompts based off the previous weekâs work before each three-hour class from week 2 to week 7. Students will share these answers with peers during the class for the purpose of engaging in collaborative discussions to synthesise prescribed content from the previous week thereby relating it to their personal and then professional development. Each week students will use a collaborative online tool to combine their pre-class answers into a group submission. Regular formative feedback will be provided on student iterative learning progress so they can gauge their strengths and areas for improvement. In Week 8, student teams will submit their final learning portfolio, collating all their responses and demonstrating how they have incorporated formative feedback. Self- and peer-assessment of individualsâ engagement with criteria relating to collaboration or collaborative actions and behaviours will be used to moderate the team mark.

Humanitarian engineering project (Project, 45%, Individual). To communicate findings related to a humanitarian engineering topic of personal interest in more depth via written and oral modalities. Students will choose a topic of interest from a short-list of given topics in humanitarian engineering to explore and research in more depth. They will build on and explore topics covered already in class, in particular on the key concepts, skills and knowledge developed in the Learning Portfolio. Students will prepare a brief presentation supported by visual aids to communicate to peers in class. Students will be required to give each other feedback on their presentations and then incorporate feedback in preparing a written report. It is expected students will include information beyond what was covered in class and synthesise multiple perspectives.

Learning reflection (Reflection, 25%, Individual). To have a heightened awareness of how their perspectives on socio-technical thinking, co-design, and humanitarian engineering more generally, have shifted over time. Students will have opportunities to reflect on their own learning over the semester, in particular about how their perspectives on socio-technical thinking and co-design (two key tenets of humanitarian engineering) have changed over the semester. In week 1 and then in week 12 students will complete the same scenario-based task in class designed to elicit their design considerations and approach. Students will compare their responses as a prompt for reflection on their learning across the semester using the Rolfe framework (What? So what? What next?). Students will document the significance of those changes in light of their learning experiences over the semester, and how they might use what they have learned going forward in their studies and career.

Professional Learning Plan (Report, 10%, Individual). To develop a plan for their professional development based on available learning modules and approved external studies. This plan will align their development with their prospective career path. Learners will begin by finding a job they would like to apply for, allowing them to analyse the skills required and identify the gaps between their current knowledge and the skills needed. With this information, and with reference to the capabilities required of all IT professionals, they will create an achievable learning plan to address these gaps. The learner will identify activities from the learning plan for which suitable learning modules or approved learning paths are available and detail which they will engage with throughout the session.

Case study analysis and reflection on practice (Case study, 30%, Individual). To develop an understanding of Indigenous Australian engagement in the IT profession and how to ethically with and for Indigenous Australians. Part A (50%): Based on a case study outlining an ethical dilemma or similar, students develop a process for response or action aligned to the AIATSIS ethical framework. Part B (50%): Students must reflect upon how they will implement this learning within their own future professional practice.

Professional Learning Portfolio (Report, 60%, Individual). To show evidence of achievement of learning plan through their completed professional development activities. In so doing, learners will justify and demonstrate how they addressed the gap between their existing knowledge and future professional practice. Learners will prepare a report justifying the choices made in professional development learning and associated evidence of professional learning achievement. This will reference their learning plan and the learning they have undertaken. They will reflect on their progress and develop a set of goals for continuing their development.

Knowledge quizzes (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). To apply Python fundamentals and libraries for data processing and visualisation. The student will undertake two quizzes during the semester. Quiz 1 covers fundamental concepts in Python programming, while quiz 2 focuses on applying Python libraries for data processing and visualization. The student will take these quizzes during the workshop in class, and the questions may include multiple-choice questions, code-writing questions, and code-tracing questions.

Individual project task A â Data Processing (Report, 30%, Individual). To design, implement, and execute data processing tasks using Python-related packages. This assessment evaluates students' capacity to acquire the skills necessary for designing, implementing, and executing programs that perform data importing and processing tasks using Python-related packages on practical case studies. Students must design and implement a Python program using Jupyter notebooks for data processing. They must find a dataset, develop a working program to load data into appropriate formats (i.e., data frames), display statistics, and identify the data quality issues. Each student needs to create: A Jupyter Notebook, A Word document report that describes the main outcomes of the assessment, and A 7-10 mins video demonstration to describe results and challenges.

Individual project task B â Data Visualisation (Report, 40%, Individual). To design, implement, and execute data pre-processing and visualisation tasks using Python-related packages. This assessment task builds on Assessment Task 2. The student will continue working on the same raw dataset used in Assessment Task 2. The student needs to design strategies for data processing and data visualisation to address the target problem using Python and relevant packages. In this task, students must resolve data quality issues using Python and relevant Python packages. Also, they must answer specific business questions using data summaries and visualisations. It is expected that they will use Jupyter notebooks for implementation. The student will be evaluated to acquire the skills necessary for designing, implementing, and executing programs that perform data manipulations, pre-processing, and visualisation tasks using Python-related packages on real-world problems. Each student needs to create: A Jupyter Notebook, A report to explain the outcomes of the analysis, highlight interesting results, and discuss any challenges encountered, and A 10-15 mins video demonstration to describe the results and challenges.

Quizzes (Quiz, 20%, Individual). To apply Python fundamentals and libraries for data processing and visualisation. The student will undertake two quizzes during the semester. Quiz 1 covers fundamental concepts in Python programming, while quiz 2 focuses on applying Python libraries for data processing and visualisation. The student will take these quizzes online on Canvas, which may include multiple-choice, code-writing, and code-tracing questions.

Python Project (Laboratory/practical, 40%, Individual). Evaluate students' capacity to use acquired skills of Python programming learnt in the course. These include understanding the business problems and their exploration from the given dataset using a variety of techniques using Python programming language. Finally, to present them to the stakeholders using visualization techniques. Choose a public dataset/Kaggle competition/custom dataset from the resources provided or find your own. Students must design and implement a Python program using Jupyter notebooks for data processing. They need to develop a working program to load data into appropriate formats (i.e., data frames), display statistics, identify and fix the data quality issues. Once the dataset is cleaned, necessary pre-processing and visualization should be presented in a professional manner to explain the findings. Deliverables: A. An initial Abstract report (10%). B. A Jupyter notebook (35%).

Python Project documentation and oral assessment (Combination, 40%, Individual). Evaluate students' capacity to document and pitch their findings effectively. Students are required to write a detailed report of their projects explaining any interesting outcomes and challenges encountered. Moreover, they need to record a video demonstration to display the running code and results documented in the report. Deliverables: A. A Word document report that describes the primary outcomes of the assessment (20%). B. Video demonstration to describe results and challenges (15%).

Review Report (Report, 40%, Individual). To develop studentsâ cognitive ability, to improve research and writing skills, and enhance student knowledge and enthusiasm about renewable energy technology. Students are required to select one topic from Solar, Wind, Geothermal and Energy storage and write a critical summary of the literature relevant to the topic. They should identify the key work in the field, and outline where strengths and weaknesses within the literature lie. The Guidelines of report are available on Canvas. Feedback will be returned to students within two weeks after submission.

Research Report and Presentation (Report, 30%, Group, group assessed). To gain insight into green technology with respect to technical, environmental, economic and social-cultural criteria by examining all theoretical and operational principles through actual case-studies, to work as a team and to improve literature-review-based research and presentation skills. Students will be divided into groups and assigned a topic which they need to make a detailed assessment report for some case studies of one targeted renewable energy. The report will include a literature review, information analysis and discussion. The guidelines for report and presentation will be posted on Canvas. Feedback will be returned to students within two weeks after submission. Students will then present their evaluations in front of teaching staff and answer questions from the Audience (15 minute presentation for each undergraduate student group and a 20 minute presentation for each postgraduate student group).

Online Quiz (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). To assess students' knowledge of renewable energy technologies (the need, fundamental science and engineering concepts) and energy policy. University guidelines will be strictly followed for all exams. Students are required to complete an online quiz that covers the subject contents in the subject outline. Students will be given a time limit of 24 hours to complete the online quiz. Once started, students have 90 minutes to complete all questions. Students will be expected to answer true/false, conceptual multiple choice and calculation questions in the online quiz. Detailed information can be found on Canvas two weeks before the quiz.

Weekly exercises (Exercises, 40%, Individual). To demonstrate programming knowledge and ability by designing and implementing small programs or adapting existing programs. For each exercise the student will be presented with sections of code, and instructions for alterations they are required to make to the code to achieve some specific goal. The student will be able to make these alterations and run the code directly within the learning environment and will receive immediate feedback showing whether they have successfully achieved the required goal. This provides early and frequent feedback about studentâs ability to demonstrate that they have acquired key knowledge and skills. Individual exercises are marked as either having been completed satisfactorily (for which a student earns full marks) or not (for which a student earns zero marks). There is no limit to how many attempts the student can make for each exercise. All exercises for each week are weighted equally, meaning that if a student successfully completes half of the required weekly exercises, they will receive half of the available marks for this assessment task. Weekly exercises are released at 8am Monday each week, and are due by midnight on Sunday each week. Standard penalties (see below) apply for any work that is submitted after the deadline. The exercises are released online and students may complete them in their own time. However, it is strongly recommended that students attend and attempt the exercises within the weekly scheduled labs where teaching staff will be available for consultation.

Assignment (Project, 30%, Individual). To demonstrate ability to design and implement a large object-oriented structure that follows a specification. In this assignment, students will build a large class structure that follows a specification. This will allow students to demonstrate their programming skills in a broader context than is provided in the weekly exercises. Students will submit their assignment for automated marking using the same online learning environment used for the weekly exercises. However, to successfully complete the assignment students will need to write entire classes and class structures themselves, rather than making isolated alterations to existing code.

Lab engagement and knowledge demonstration (Exercises, 30%, Individual). To use knowledge of programming to make high-quality contributions and achieve suitable outcomes. During the weekly labs students will be expected to engage actively and demonstrate the knowledge they have gained. Both engagement and knowledge demonstration will be measured. Engagement will be measured as the extent to which students complete quizzes, volunteer for tasks, and actively contribute to group exercises. Knowledge demonstration will be measured as studentsâ ability to answers quiz questions correctly, complete tasks correctly, and make high-quality contributions.

Labs (Laboratory/practical, 14%, Individual). The labs, both assessed and non-assessed, provide practice in programming. The task is to code a well-designed solution to a small specification. The output of this task is a program of one or more classes.

Programming assignment 1 (Project, 35%, Individual). This programming assignment provides practice and tests for the topics of system design and list operations. The task is to develop a well-designed OO system that uses lists. The output of this task is a solution of one or more classes.

Programming assignment 2 (Project, 25%, Individual). This programming assignment provides practice and tests for the topics of system design, GUIs and MVC. The task is to develop a well-designed OO GUI system that uses the MVC framework. The output of this task is a program of one or more classes.

Timed LMS exam (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). Students are required to complete an LMS exam within a time frame to consolidate the factual knowledge taught in the subject. Answer 20 multiple-choice and fill-in-blank questions. The quiz is open book but restricted from accessing external webpages and application programs.

Advanced Challenges (Quiz/test, 6%, Individual). Engage in advanced challenges which aim to improve competency in programming. The task is to code a well-designed solution to an interview level specification. The output of this task is a program of one or more classes.

Project (Project, 20%, Group, group and individually assessed). This practical task allows students to demonstrate their understanding and develop the essential skills required to design and implement an IoT-based solution. Working in groups, students will design and develop a small-to-medium complexity IoT application. The main project assignment involves all key phases of system development, focusing on understanding the problem space, key requirements (application drivers), system architecture, system design, and implementation. This also includes builds/scripts/code, resource utilisation, and critical risk mitigation. The total assessment weight is split equally, with half representing the group's output and the other half reflecting individual contribution. Detailed guidelines regarding team formation, marking criteria, and specific boundaries for generative AI usage for this project will be available on Canvas.

Labs (Laboratory/practical, 20%, Group, individually assessed). Through this task, students will be able to learn, practice and demonstrate sensor/actuation connectivity, data acquisition, storage and visualization, as well as, specific coding skills required to complete various tasks defined in the main project. The lab work will allow students to become familiar with IoT technologies. During labs, the students will be learning how to use IoT application programming tools, as well as, how to use the IOT hardware, microcomputers, sensors and actuators and other electronic/ electromechanical devices. Different marks may be assigned to labs, depending on task complexity. Details on GenAI usage will be available in Canvas, and explained in lectures.

Short Quizzes (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). This assessment task is designed to evaluate the student's understanding of key concepts, definitions, and issues covered in the preceding lectures. It consists of three short,Â equally weightedÂ quizzes conducted via UTS Canvas under open-book conditions. Each quiz comprises approximately 20 questions, including multiple-choice, true/false, fill-in-the-blank, and multiple-answer formats. During the quizzes, students are permitted to refer to official Canvas course materials (including lecture slides, tutorial handbooks, readings, and resources provided by the teaching team). External digital files, unauthorised third-party websites, communication platforms, and Generative AI tools are strictly prohibited.

Final Exam (Examination, 30%, Individual). This individual, open-book final exam consists of multiple-choice and short-answer questions conducted via UTS Canvas. The exam evaluates core conceptual understanding, system analysis, and design skills, focusing specifically on IoT system analysis and design problems covered across all lectures, tutorials, and lab sessions. During the exam, students are permitted to use official Canvas course materials (including lecture slides, tutorial handbooks, readings, and resources provided by the teaching team). External digital files, unauthorised third-party websites, communication platforms, and Generative AI tools are strictly prohibited.

This task is divided into three components: - 30% for a report (Business Plan) - 10% for team presentation in Week 10 (individually assessed via SPARKPlus) - 10% for poster presentation in Week 12 (individually Assessed via SPARKPlus)

In this task, students will work with their team to identify areas for investigation then individually investigate and evaluate information to become familiar with the context of their group project, critically evaluating information and sources to synthesise their research into a clear and concise written summary. Students will be assessed on both the desktop study itself and the documentation of the processes taken to produce it. Task A: Mindmap presentation: 5% Task B: Desktop study: 20%

Groups will be provided formative experiences to share their progress throughout the subject and develop a design proposal presentation to communicate their process and design. To utilise computer modelling and analysis tools to design and optimise a steel structure for the proposed building. This task involves creating a comprehensive model of the building, performing structural analysis, and designing the steel components to meet the specified requirements. Teams are to prepare a preliminary (draft) written report as per the criterion outlined in the Project Brief and specifications grading rubric made available on the brief project release (for students to gauge their performance level). There are 2 parts for submission. Part 1: Addressing feedback based on questions raised during Oral presentation Project briefs Part 2: Conceptual design report incorporating the feedback containing Building Description General Overview: Provide a brief description of the building, including its purpose, size, and any unique architectural features. Structural System: Outline the chosen structural system for the building (e.g., moment-resisting frames, braced frames, etc.). Site Information Location: Details about the building site, including geographic location, soil conditions, and any relevant environmental considerations. Design Loads: Specify the loads considered in the design, including dead loads, live loads, wind loads, seismic loads, and any other relevant loads based on local codes and standards. Computer Modelling Software Used: List and briefly describe the software tools employed for modelling and analysis. Results Interpretation: Present and interpret the results of the analysis, including: Displacement profiles Internal force distributions Stress and strain distributions Critical Sections: Identify and discuss critical sections and elements in the structure. Steel Design Design Codes and Standards: Specify the design codes and standards followed (e.g., AS 4100 for steel structures). Member Design: Detail the design process for the steel members, including: Selection of steel sections Calculation of capacities (bending, shear, axial) Check against design criteria (strength, stability, serviceability) Connection Design: Outline the design of connections, covering: Bolted and welded connections Connection detailing Verification of connection capacities Optimisation Design Iterations: Discuss the iterative process used to optimise the design for efficiency and cost-effectiveness. Alternative Solutions: Present any alternative design solutions considered and the rationale for the final design choice. Sustainability Considerations Material Efficiency: Discuss strategies for minimising material use without compromising structural integrity. Environmental Impact: Evaluate the environmental impact of the chosen design and materials. Lifecycle Analysis: Provide an overview of the lifecycle analysis for the steel structure

Photo Travel Diary of a Journey (Project, 15%, Individual).
