Transport Planning Evaluation Report (Report, 35%, Individual). To evaluate a studentâs ability to apply the theoretical concepts of traffic engineering and develop solutions to real-world operational problems within a transport network (focused on public transport). Students are required to generate an evaluation and recommendations report related to a case study of a real-world transport planning problem. The case study will focus on a comparison between different transport modes. Students will need to assess the transport and land use impacts to define and design potential solutions. Students will be required to submit a report responding to the brief provided. Online submission made through Canvas.

Transport Operations Technical Report (Report, 15%, Individual). To evaluate and apply the fundamental aspects of transport engineering with a particular focus on traffic engineering and modelling. Students solve a local traffic problem reflecting the design and decision-making methodologies used by a traffic engineers in practice. Students will undertake a data analysis exercise which assesses the conceptual understanding of the material covered in Weeks 7 to 9 of the subject. Students will be required to process traffic data related to a local problem and conduct further analysis to provide recommendations and a solution to the problem. Online submission made through Canvas.

Transport Modelling and Operations Report (Report, 35%, Individual). To evaluate and apply the theoretical concepts of traffic engineering and develop solutions to real-world operational problems within a road network. Students are required to complete a report that is related to the subject content delivered in Weeks 7 to 11. The project will involve students applying the 4-step planning process to evaluate the current and future transport conditions of a specified study area. Students will be assessed on their ability to apply the fundamental components of traffic flow theory and transport modelling. In addition, upon evaluating conditions, students will be required to develop traffic management solutions to alleviate issues identified through data analysis and additional contextual information related to the study area. Students will need to present the modelling methodology, results and traffic management solutions in a report format, similar to what is expected in professional settings and will be assessed on technical accuracy and clarity in presentation. Online submission made through Canvas.

Required topics quiz (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). This assessment task encourages students to engage and learn the subject progressively. To engage in tutorial discussions effectively students need to demonstrate their understanding of the topic by answering a quiz on the relevant topic. Watch the lecture, complete the quiz. Lectures and related material are provided online so that students can study the material at a time that suits them. A quiz is provided for each topic to enable students to check their progress toward mastering the topic.

Elective topic quiz (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). This assessment task encourages students to study, understand and apply the means of developing specialised software architectures. There are four specialised software architectures suited to particular problems. Choose any two of them, study them, then answer their respective quizzes.

Team project (Project, 45%, Group, group and individually assessed). Work in a team to develop an architecture for a specific system in a given context. The project is a group assignment to be completed in small teams. You are expected to develop a software architecture for a non-trivial system using the techniques learned in this subject.

Peer review (Laboratory/practical, 20%, Group, individually assessed). Develop and practice the professional skill of reviewing and critiquing the work of peers. Each group will present their work in progress to another group for their review and critique. Reviews are completed using a review form (currently Google forms) and submitted on completion. Peer reviews are conducted in the tutorial room.

Quiz (Quiz/test, 10%, Individual). The quiz consists of a small number (10 - 20) of multiple choice questions. The quiz will explore the extent of your knowledge and understanding across the weekly topics. The questions will be taken from: * The Lecture slides and Readings for weeks 1 - 6. * The Labs for Lectures 1 - 6. To answer the questions correctly you need to understand the question topic. To do this you will need to attend the weekly lecture/discussion sessions, perform the weekly lab and discuss the lab questions with your group and read the weekly readings. There will be a quiz Q&A document released two weeks before the quiz. There will be a practice quiz a week before the quiz.

Assignment (Project, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). The assignment is designed for students to demonstrate their skill in researching digital forensic topics in a real world environment. Students will practice their skills in collecting evidence from a digital device for later analysis by a forensic specialist. This assessment is a review of a Forensics topic of current interest and aims to add knowledge to the material provided in class. The topic is chosen from a list provided. Students need to research the topic online, download and explore some apps/tools and prepare a report and short presentation. Students need to provide detail in depth so that others can replicate the work. Students need to submit a Proposal to confirm the assignment topic and plan in the middle of the semester. By the end of the semester, students need to submit a Report and give a Presentation. There will be a proposal guide and report guide in the assignment introduction. Feedback will be provided via Canvas.

Skills tests (Demonstration, 40%, Individual). Skills Based Assessments (SBAs) are designed for students to demonstrate their skill in locating forensic evidence on a digital device. Students are given an image file acquired from a suspect's laptop and asked to assess if allegations of failing to comply with company policies regarding the use of company time or intellectual property are proven. Topics are taken from the weekly labs.

Weekly skills test (Laboratory/practical, 20%, Group, individually assessed). For students to demonstrate mastery of weekly lab concepts. Students are given a small assignment to complete in each week's lab class. Students can complete the assignment in class or in their own time. There will be 10 weekly tasks, each worth 2%. Students upload their answers for tutor feedback prior to the next lab class.

Learning Contract (Project, 10%, Individual). To create a plan i.e. a learning contract, to develop a prototype digital device using an FPGA. Develop a learning contract for this course using the following process: 1. Decide on project; 2. Create specifications for the deliverable; 3. Create a timeline for the work needed; 4. Document potential risks and how these might be dealt with; 5. Document materials and intellectual property (IP) needed for the proposed work. Throughout the first few weeks of class we will be looking at aspects of the learning contract.

Mid-project presentation and report (Project, 30%, Individual). To provide a progress update and gain feedback on project progress. Students will prepare a presentation and accompanying report on the progress of their project against the goals and plan in their learning contract. 20% of the marks are for the presentation and 10% for the report. Criteria for the presentation and report will be published online.

Final project report and presentation (Project, 60%, Individual). To present final prototype, demonstrate use and deliver report on project. Students must deliver a presentation and submit an accompanying report outlining the outcomes of your project paying particular attention to what was agreed in the learning contract. A demonstration of the developed prototype must also be provided during the presentation and documented in the report. 40% of the marks are for the report and 20% are for the presentation. Criteria for the report and presentation will be published online.

Individual learning contract (Portfolio, 30%, Individual). To provide an opportunity for guided self-learning of topics related to embedded systems. At the start of the teaching session, students create an individual learning contract (ILC) and then have it agreed to by their academic mentor(s). The ILC should describe a series of activities that will enable the student to gain knowledge and skills in the area of embedded systems, particularly to enhance the studentâs contribution to the team and the product to be developed. Students generally complete this individual learning independently and outside of class time, and check in regularly with their academic mentor to update progress, receive feedback and identify any challenges encountered. Assessment of the ILC will take place in three phases: ILC setup and agreement at the start of session ILC maintenance and monitoring during the session ILC finalisation at the end of session Students document their individual learning in a portfolio.

Embedded systems project (Portfolio, 50%, Group, individually assessed). To demonstrate the ability to design, implement, test and evaluate a product based around an embedded system. Students work in teams to design and implement an embedded systems product. Each group must prepare a portfolio documenting their contributions, design decisions and insights relating to the product throughout the teaching session. Weekly updates are expected, with each update building on and extending the previous work in the portfolio. By the final submission at the end of session, the portfolio should be a complete record of the work undertaken. Students must submit their portfolio for assessment and feedback a minimum of 5 times during the session, but may submit up to a maximum of 10 times. The individual mark of each student will be determined based on the individual contribution to the group submissions.

Final report (Report, 20%, Group, group and individually assessed). To demonstrate professional written and oral communication skills in documenting and describing an embedded systems product. Teams of students prepare and present a final report describing the product that was implemented. The report should describe design choices, technology choices, and the implementation and testing strategy. A separate section should provide an evaluation of the product, to identify benefits and limitations of the approach chosen, what you learned along the way and what you might do differently in a future embedded systems design. As a team, students also need to deliver a short presentation of their implemented product to their peers and teaching staff. The presentation is to include technical aspects of the product design as well as a reflection on how collaboration as a team impacted on the quality of the product. All team members should contribute to the presentation. The audience for both of these deliverables is industry professional engineers.

Quiz (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). The quizzes are designed to motivate continuous learning, analysis and recall the technical knowledge relevant to the subject concepts. There are two quizzes, each worth 10% of the total mark for this subject. The quizzes will be held during tutorial/lab sessions.

Skills Based Assessment (Laboratory/practical, 30%, Individual). The skills based assessment is for students to demonstrate practical skills in identifying and resolving network security issues as might be found in practice. Students will undertake a skills based assessment to test their skills learned from the lab and tutorials.

Final Exam (Examination, 30%, Individual). The final exam will explore the extent of student knowledge and understanding throughout the subject. The final exam will cover short answer-type questions. The material examined will cover Lectures Week 1 to Week 11.

Lab Submission (Laboratory/practical, 20%, Individual). For students to demonstrate hands-on learning of cybersecurity concepts. In most weeks, marks will be allocated to individual lab components which will be announced to students in the lab handout on UTS Canvas. There will be eight (8) different lab tasks.

Environmental law & planning scenario analysis (Report, 30%, Individual). This assessment task aims to assist students to consolidate and refine their ability to analyse environmental and planning legislation. This assessment task consists of two interlinked components: Task 1a Environmental Law (worth 15% of total assessment value) and Task 1b Environmental Planning (worth 15% of total assessment value). In Task 1a, students will select and critically analyse an environmental law case or dispute involving development planning. A suggested list will be made available to students online on Canvas. When writing this report and presentation, students are encouraged to draw similarities and adapt approaches from precedent cases or court decisions as reported in literature. They will demonstrate understanding and ability to apply environmental law to a specific and simple case. In Task 1b, students will be required to conduct risk-cost-benefit analysis of a proposed development plan and write a report. A suggested list will also be made available to students online on Canvas. They will identify relevant environmental and planning legislation and policies, interpret their meanings, objectives, and implications with respect to the proposed land use or development. They will also demonstrate and interpret the inter-connection between planning and environmental law, and propose solutions to relevant planning problems.

Environmental planning case analysis report & presentation (Report, 40%, Individual). In this assessment task students will develop problem solving, critical analysis and communication skills to resolve conflicts between development and environmental conservation and apply these skills in the planning process. In this assessment task (worth 40% of total assessment value), students will present a written report and a verbal presentation to discuss the relevant environmental legislation and propose strategies to resolve legal conflicts. Students will be presented with a hypothetical scenario relating to an actual location or environmental law case in Australia. This assessment task consists of 2 stages (stage 1 and stage 2). In stage 1 (worth 5% of total assessment value), students are required to submit an outline of their case report. Students will receive feedback prior to the final submission of their case report. In stage 2, students are required to submit their case report (worth 25% of total assessment value) and a pre-recorded presentation (worth 10% of total assessment value).

Online quiz (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). In this assessment task students will interpret the implication of contemporary environmental law in the context of land use and development planning. The online quiz will be open book. Students will apply their skills developed from the subject to gather information for environmental planning, interpret the meaning and implication of environmental law, assess the interaction between environmental law and other law discipline, and evaluate the impact of emerging issues and new technologies on the evolution of environmental law. These will be demonstrated through a series of short answer and multiple choice questions. This assessment will cover subject content in Blocks 1 to 4.

Decision Diagnosis and Bias Analysis (Written submission, 20%, Individual). Students will select a real-world case study from a credible source and apply judgment and decision-making frameworks to analyse three key decision-making situations. They will identify the cognitive biases and heuristics influencing each decision, evaluate their impact on the decision-making process and outcomes, and recommend practical, evidence-based mitigation strategies. In addition to the written analysis, students are required to submit supporting appendices, including a Bias Identification Table, a Source Evaluation Table, an AI Use Declaration, and an Academic Integrity Statement, to demonstrate their analytical reasoning, critical evaluation of evidence, and responsible academic practice.

Designing Decision Support Systems (Written submission, 40%, Individual). This assessment develops students' ability to design, justify and evaluate decision support systems for complex real-world problems. Building on Assessment 1, students will critically evaluate the decision-making situations identified within their case study and determine which two decision situations would benefit most from structured decision support. For each selected situation, they will justify the most appropriate decision support approach, develop and apply the selected approach, interpret its outputs and critically evaluate its effectiveness.Unlike Assessment 1, which focused on understanding how cognitive biases influence decision making, this assessment focuses on designing decision support solutions that improve the quality of human judgement.

Group Decision-Making Report and Presentation (Combination, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Report: Group assessed 30% Presentation: Individually assessed 10% Report: This assessment builds directly on the work completed in Assessments 1 and 2. Student teams will select one case study from those previously analysed by group members and collaboratively develop an integrated organisational decision-making strategy for the selected case. Drawing on the cognitive bias analysis and decision support approaches developed in the earlier assessments, teams will synthesise and extend this work by applying group, strategic, leadership and agile decision-making frameworks to address a critical organisational decision problem. Teams will justify the integration of cognition-driven, model-driven and data-driven approaches, critically evaluate their effectiveness and develop evidence-based recommendations that reflect professional decision-making practice. Presentation: Students should demonstrate an individual understanding of the approaches used and explain their own contribution to the group's analysis.

Individual Charter (extended) (Report, 20%, Individual). Students are expected to prepare an extended project charter on a provided template. Further details of the project specifics will be available on canvas by week 2.

Group Project (Project, 70%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students will work in groups of up to six people to develop a detailed project management plan of an engineering project. The plan will consist of multiple parts as follows:Â A team charter: stating how the team will work together (group mark: 10 marks)Â A project charter: stationing the objectives and details of the project (group mark: 10 marks) Interim deliverables submitted as the team learn the various topics.(0 marks) A final report: Individual students in the group will be responsible for finalising the information in their chosen sections of the report. (individual mark: 50 marks) Further details of the project specifics will be available on canvas by week 2. Â

Reflections (Report, 10%, Individual). Each student will submit an individual critical reflection report. The report will include studentâs self-assessment and evaluation of their learning and performance in the subject.

Project Identification and Context Analysis (Written submission, 35%, Individual). Students will individually identify a significant public engineering or infrastructure project from publicly available sources and prepare a concise analysis of the project. The analysis will examine the projectâs objectives, purpose, and expected beneficiaries; describe its technical characteristics and implementation; and analyse the broader social, economic, political, and environmental context in which the project operates. Students will also consider the opportunities and constraints that may affect the project's successful implementation. This assessment provides the foundation for the comprehensive financial and economic evaluation undertaken in Assignment 2.

Project Financial and Economic Evaluation (Project, 30%, Group, group assessed). Following the investigations undertaken in Assignment 1, students will form groups and select one engineering or infrastructure project for comprehensive evaluation. Working collaboratively, they will undertake a comprehensive financial and economic (socio-economic) evaluation of the selected project. Using publicly available data and appropriate evaluation techniques, students will identify, classify, quantify, and assess project costs and benefits; undertake financial and economic cost-benefit analyses; calculate key viability indicators; evaluate project risks and uncertainties; and provide evidence-based recommendations regarding the projectâs financial and economic viability. The assessment requires students to integrate engineering, financial, economic, social, and environmental considerations to support informed investment decision-making. Â Individual marks may be adjusted based on peer evaluation using SPARKPlus to reflect each studentâs contribution to the group work.

Executive Investment Pitch (Interactive oral, 35%, Individual). Building on the group work completed in Assignment 2, each student will individually deliver a 3-minute Executive Investment Pitch to a simulated decision-making panel, followed by a 2-minute interactive question-and-answer session. Students will communicate the outcomes of the projectâs financial and economic evaluation succinctly and persuasively to a non-technical audience. The pitch should clearly justify the recommended investment decision, demonstrating why the selected project is viable from financial, economic, social, and environmental perspectives. During the question-and-answer session, students will defend their recommendation, justify the underlying analysis and assumptions, and demonstrate their individual understanding of the groupâs financial and economic evaluation. The interactive oral assessment will be conducted during Week 12. As this is an individual assessment, attendance is mandatory, and students are expected to attend their allocated tutorial.

Journal (Journal, 30%, Individual). Students will be required to peruse reputable media coverage of issues/problems affecting either domestic or international contexts and explain how they believe a systems thinking approach is helping or would help address the complexity of one of those contemporary issues/problems. The deliverable for this assessment is a weekly 1-page (maximum) report which will be peer marked and discussed during tutorials.

Group Project (Project, 70%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students will be required to join âengineering consulting firmsâ which have been approached by a client to assess and enhance the sustainability of a particular aspect of project that deals with the built environment, energy, water or waste management, or a combination of two or more of these. The details of the project, group dynamics, conditions, requirements and constraints can be found in the detailed project description available through Canvas. The project is made up of the following deliverables: Part A - Final written report - students, applying systems thinking and broad research, will analyse the problem and propose an engineered solution which will be contained in a comprehensive written report (SLOs 1, 2, 3, 4) Part B - Weekly research reports â students will produce reports on the research that their team has conducted as their contribution to their group effort (SLOs 1, 2) Part C - Presentations in the form of pre-recorded videos â Initially, to peers, so that the cohort can assess all the different proposals and craft, with a combination of the best, a comprehensive proposal for the client, then to the client (SLOs 3, 4) Part D - Peer assessment â students will provide a peer assessment which will be used to evaluate individual contributions to team delivery (SLO 3)

Topic and Case Study Analysis (Report, 20%, Individual). For students to predict and avoid failures due to human factors, design flaws, materials failure and extreme conditions. Students study the topics provided and select one based on their interest and background. Then, they identify and describe two engineering failures related to their topic that occurred previously. For each case study, students set the boundaries, identify stakeholders, define the inherent risk, describe the causal chain, and explore if the case studies affected or were affected by Indigenous communities.

Risk Management Plan (Report, 30%, Group, group assessed). For students to apply risk management principles and processes conforming with AS ISO 31000: 2018 in a case study Students prepare a risk management plan in accordance with AS ISO 31000: 2018 for one of the case studies investigated in assessment 1. Students need to: Define the system boundaries carefully; Establish the context clearly in accordance with the standard; Clearly state the risk tolerability criteria employed; Show evidence of consideration of alternatives for risk management; Include a discussion; and Consider aspects beyond the texts and subject materials.

Quantitative Risk Assessment and Decision Making (Report, 50%, Individual). For students to research their topic, assess, evaluate, and treat risks using quantitative risk assessment and risk-based decision-making techniques in a case study. This assessment is authentic and requires students to apply what they have learned and higher level thinking to solve complex problems in a similar way that they would do in professional practice. Students study their topic to understand the elements and parameters involved. They learn and apply appropriate quantitative techniques to conduct a risk assessment to verify the magnitude of the risk exposure in terms of deaths/injuries/damages/costs in one of the case studies prepared in assessment 1. Then, they explore different risk treatment options and select the best option(s) considering the time, cost, quality and scope constraints using a risk-based decision-making technique.

Assignment 1: Research on Market and Innovation (Combination, 40%, Individual). Within your chosen market and industry, describe the existing competition and innovation. Explore the technological innovations in the market and challenges that market is facing from all social, environmental and financial perspectives. This task is divided into three components: 10 for a presentation in the class 15 for a live document of progress and reference integrity 15 for a final report Focus of the live document is on your regular progress and your engagement with relevant academic and industry reports.

Assignment 2: Innovation Concept Development Project (Combination, 60%, Group, group and individually assessed). Work in teams to develop a comprehensive report of a concept for a product or service innovation to tackle an everyday problem. This includes problem scoping, solution ideas and selection, customer requirements and product or service features, product or service design, innovation strategy and business model, applying suitable idea generation and evaluation methods. This task is divided into three components: - 20% for team presentation on Week 10 (individually Assessed via SPARKPlus) - 10 % for live document of progress and reference integrity (individually Assessed via SPARKPlus) - 30% for a report (Concept Development) Presentations will be delivered by your team on week 12 in your tutorial classroom.

Group activities and project (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students will be required to join one of 6 groups each of which is divided into 5 teams of 5-6 students each. The aim of the groups is to come up with a sustainability initiative and high-level execution plan for UTS to implement within a 1 to 2-year period. The details of the project, group dynamics, conditions, requirements and constraints can be found in the detailed project description available through Canvas. The project is made up of the following deliverables: Part A - Initial pitches and selection â each student will pitch to their own team the initiative they want their team to work on. Teams will choose a winning pitch. The winning pitch author will become the team leader through the process of crafting a vision and strategy to underpin the initiative (SLOs 1, 4) Part B - Weekly research and artefact production â students will take turns in leading/managing the weekly work required to adequately perform all the necessary research and produce the necessary artefacts to ensure that their teamâs initiative is the one chosen by the group they belong to (SLOs 1, 2, 3 4) Part C - Presentations (SLO 1, 4) Initially, to their own group for selection Then, to the rest of the groups for final selection Finally, to the UTS Sustainability Engagement Manager Presentation in the form of pre-recorded videos.

Case study analysis (Exercises, 25%, Group, group and individually assessed). Each week students will be given a short video or text dealing with some aspect of leadership and responsibility. During the tutorial time, each team will analyse the material provided and answer a set of questions. On alternate weeks, each team will be required to either report to the rest of the cohort in a class discussion or to the teaching team in the form of a one-page written report due by the end of the day.

Weekly reflection and posting on discussion board (Reflection, 15%, Individual). Each student will be required to identify 2 persons they consider leaders from their own perspective - at least one of the chosen leaders must be a person that all the rest of the class either already knows or has the possibility of knowing about, e.g. Gandhi, while the other one can be a person in that studentâs life, only known to them. The task is to analyse the leadership of those persons from the perspective of each of the weekly topics discussed during the lectures and tutorials. The deliverable for this assessment is a weekly online posting of maximum 250 words on the discussion board of each team, which will be discussed and peer marked.

Weekly journal (Journal, 10%, Individual). Students will be required to peruse reputable media coverage of issues/problems affecting either domestic or international contexts and find an example of âgoodâ leadership and an example of âbadâ leadership. Students must explain what makes each case either âgoodâ or âbadâ leadership. The deliverable for this assessment is two submissions, each with 3 weekly 1-page (maximum) reports which will be peer marked and discussed during tutorials.

Online Problem Sets (Quiz/test, 30%, Individual). Online Problem Sets focus on applied financial concepts and models to which students must apply analytical skills and understanding of finance influences on business. They consist of a combination of multiple choice, numerical and case study questions. The aim of the Online Problem Sets is to help students develop study habits and address the learning objectives of each week. The Online Problem Sets represent self-directed online resource utilisation within a digital platform. Students are required to engage with the subject material and demonstrate mastery of technical and theoretical knowledge weekly by testing their understanding. Marks will be awarded on the level of mastery achieved prior to the commencement of each week. There will be 10 weekly Online Problem Sets undertaken during the seminar testing each student's skills developed and knowledge constructed of the subject content. These problem sets act as a feedback loop for students to gauge their progression and understanding of the material presented and highlights which learning objectives students need to improve weekly.

Group Assignment (Report, 20%, Group, group assessed). Students are required to prepare a financial model for a particular firm in order to analyse the current and future performance using various models and techniques. This assignment is based on collaborative work among group members for the creation of a financial model for your business. Your group is required to produce a financial model (using the guidelines available in Canvas) of your business. It is based on the work that has been, and is being, undertaken in the seminar, online material on UTS and other information which must be researched and /or resourcefully created. For the group assignment, students will be assessed as a team, which means each group member will normally receive the same mark. No complaints about group operation will be considered after the assignment has been submitted. Please see the assignment section of Canvas for full details.

Online Video Presentation (Presentation, 40%, Group, group and individually assessed). Students have to present the analysis and valuation of their case study in the seminar in order to draw conclusions about the feasibility of expansion/ replacement investment. Communicating in a face to face environment is an important skill for studentâs business career. Presentations are based on and reflecting industry experience and real-world contemporary issues. Each group is required to produce a 15-minute presentation. The presentation is to be delivered in PowerPoint or an alternative digital visual presentation method (e.g., Presi, Keynote etc.). Students are required to submit their analysis and valuation of the case study online. Students will work in teams and will submit a joint presentation and will allocate the effort across the members of the group. Students are encouraged to come to an agreement on the allocation and procedures for disagreement should anyone not contribute. All group members must contribute to the production of the presentation equally and record themselves presenting. Assessment marks will be allocated according to both coherent analysis and presentation style. In addition to communicating in a face to face environment, students are required to develop their online communication skills by recording a video presentation. You need to explain an aspect of contemporary financial topics both accurately and creatively in the video presentation. Please see the assignment section on Canvas for full details.

Peer Review (Report, 10%, Group, group assessed). Students are required to review the presentation of two other groups and assess them in order to give them constructive feedback. This assessment develops and assesses collaboration and critical thinking skills among students. Students are required to peer review each other in the presentation assessment. Each group will peer review and provide constructive feedback on two presentations. Failure to participate by any member in peer reviews will result in zero (0) marks for this component of assessment.

Research and Analytical Report about Point-of-Use/Point-of-Entry Systems (Report, 35%, Individual). To assess students' ability to understand and evaluate current point-of-use/ point-of-entry (POU/POE) protocols for decentralised water treatment systems. Students are required to undertake research on methods of decentralised water treatment systems that are used in a modern setting. They are then required to undertake technical, social and economic analyses of a chosen system and compare it with other systems available in the commercial market.

Technical Report on Design of Decentralised Water and Wastewater Systems (Report, 35%, Individual). To demonstrate the ability to apply knowledge related to designing decentralised water/wastewater treatment systems. Students are required to design two decentralised treatment systems to specified criteria. This is an open-ended design assessment. Students can assume the data; however, it should be noted clearly, justifiable and well-referenced.

Exercise Set on Decentralised Water and Wastewater Systems Practices (Exercises, 30%, Individual). To assess students' ability to understand and evaluate decentralised systems that are representative of current practices in Australia and overseas. An exercise set will need to be submitted for this assessment task. Students will be required to explain the decentralised water and wastewater processes, demonstrate design procedures and provide practical recommendations on the decentralised systems in Australia and overseas.

Review Quizzes (Quiz/test, 15%, Individual). Regular quizzes are held each block to give students feedback on the progress in understanding key concepts and procedures. A 60 minute online quiz will be held on the dates and times specified in the Program.

Laboratory Test (Laboratory/practical, 25%, Individual). Lab activities allow students to link theory and practice using industry standard tools and techniques. Students will capture packets using the 'wireshark' software, and analyse the composition, flow and timing of packets and frames in a very similar way to what a professional telecommunication engineer would do in configuring and troubleshooting a real-world network. In the lab exam, students will demonstrate their capabilities to analyse traffic, identify faults and measure network performance in a simulated network environment. Students will retrieve an obfuscated Mininet lab exam script via Git, which they will execute in their virtual machine image. Using this script, you will need to complete a series of tasks on the emulated network, including (but not limited to) traffic analysis, route analysis, port scans, and various types of performance testing. Performance metrics may include measurements such as latency, jitter, packet loss and throughput. You will be expected to describe exactly how you performed each test that you used and provide a technically accurate interpretation of the results. The task will be a restricted open-book exam.

Final Exam (Examination, 40%, Individual). This provides an opportunity for students to demonstrate their individual understanding of key concepts and procedures as would be used in an industrial setting The final exam will be conducted in the form of supervised online exam for onshore students; offshore / remote students will be assessed via an oral exam/interview to be conducted via Zoom.

IP Addressing Test (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). To assure that all students passing the subject have a minimum level of understanding of critically important concepts such as IP addressing, subnetting and supernetting. Take the online IP addressing test at the time specified in the Program. You may have up to three attempts at this task. You will receive the highest mark exceeding 80%; if you fail to reach the 80% threshold by the third attempt, you will receive a mark of zero for this task.

Design, Implementation and Documentation (Report, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). Project Teams should provide WSN Architecture/Design and possibly a mock-up UI. Consideration should be given to use of Open Source hardware/software and COTS components (hardware toolkits, IDEs, Frameworks, DBMS, libraries, and middleware, etc.) This assignment is the main project development package that includes a design documentation providing final architecture/high level and low level designs; and test/integration plans; and any documentation related to implementation for the assigned project .The assignment should be completed by cooperating small teams of approximately 3-4 students and integrated by the Team as a seamless Team deliverable. You will be assessed individually and as a Team. 10% will be assigned to individual work and 20% to groupwork. You are required to identify each team memberâs contribution in your written report.

Project Presentation, Demonstration (Demonstration, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). Demonstration of the prototype WSN application. Delivery of the project's artefacts and the final report. This assignment is a Team presentation and demonstration which includes a discussion on the deliverable plus its conformance to the major functional abstractions/components identified. The assignment should be completed by cooperating small Teams of approximately 3-4 students and integrated by the Team as a seamless Team deliverable. You will be assessed individually and as a team. 20% will be assigned to individual work and 10% to groupwork. All team members are required to participate in the presentation and demonstrate their achievements. Each team has a total of 10-15 minutes to present the project and all team members should participate, we will then dedicate 5 minutes for questions and answers. Students are encouraged to conduct real environmental experiments (e.g. measuring the soil moisture content using sensors, generate and analyze data).

Quizzes (Quiz/test, 40%, Individual). For individual students to evaluate their learning and understanding of the key concepts based on the given materials (lecture notes and handbook). 3 short quizzes are designed for individual students. Students are required to answer different types of questions. There will be no negative marks for incorrect answers. Quizzes are paper-based and will be held in class, during the lecture time. Quiz 1: 5% Quiz 2: 15% Quiz 3: 20%

Conceptual Catchment Model (Report, 20%, Individual). To highlight the perceptual and conceptual issues associated with catchment modelling. Students must design a conceptual model of water flow through a catchment and to write a a supporting explanation describing and justifying the generic processes and flow paths included in their model specifically for the problem provided.

Model Calibration (Presentation, 20%, Individual). To consider the suitability of a model for the intended purpose. Students will analyse the calibration of a prepared catchment model through comparison of recorded and simulated data. Students should propose suitable approaches to improve the calibration. Outcomes of this analysis are to be presented as a briefing to a line manager.

Hydrograph Generation (Report, 20%, Individual). To be able to predict runoff hydrographs from a catchment and to understand and interpret these hydrographs. Students must predict the runoff hydrograph from a catchment using an alternative process models. These alternative predictions are to be compared and a report prepared presenting the two hydrographs and reasons for any differences (if any) between the two alternative process models. Students will predict the runoff hydrograph from a catchment using an alternative process. Students should compare the original and alternative predictions. Outcomes of this analysis are to be presented as a report to a senior engineer. The outcomes should include reasons for any differences (fi there is any) and a comparison between the two prcoess models.

Capstone (Integrative) Report (Report, 40%, Individual). To apply developed concepts in the preparation of a catchment modelling solution to address a new problem. Students are required to apply concepts that they have developed in the three first assignments to prepare a catchment modelling solution to address a new problem. Students must prepare a report detailing the results of their analyses. This assignment is to be prepared as a project proposal to a client requesting a solution to their problem.

Assignment 1: Basic Neural Networks and Fuzzy Systems (Report, 20%, Individual). To analyse basic concepts within neural networks and fuzzy logic by solving real-world problems. Students are required to answer three questions related to Perceptron training, basic fuzzy theory and basic fuzzy control system. For each question, students are required to provide the explanation, discussion, reasoning, working steps and source code if appropriate. Marking scheme of this assessment is available in Canvas.

Assignment 2: Advanced Neural Networks and Fuzzy Systems (Report, 20%, Individual). To apply advanced theories of neural networks and fuzzy logic by solving real-world problems. Students are required to answer two questions related to multilayer neural network and its learning algorithm, and the use of convolutional neural networks. For each question, students are required to provide the explanation, reasoning, working steps and source code if appropriate. Marking scheme of this assessment is available in Canvas.

Reflective Essays (Essay, 10%, Individual). Aims to reflect and apply the knowledge you have learned in the seminars by lecturer/guest speakers. Each student is required to write two reflective essays (any two of the topics by lecturer/guest speakers in this subject). The talks will be held in weeks 10-11.

Major Group Project (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). Develop and implement a basic trainable neural network or a fuzzy logic system for a typical control, computing application or biomedical application. Students are required to conduct a research group project. There will be two assessment seminars and oneresearch paper submission. In the first seminar, students in each group are required to present the specification of their project. It is expected that they will have finalised the functional block diagram and demonstrated the feasibility of the system or software. In the second seminar, students in each group are required to present the methodology, testing and results of their project. Furthermore, students are required to write and submit one research paper based on the findings and results of the project. The research paper is individually assessed.

Assessment Task 1 â Quality Planning and Analysis Report (Written submission, 35%, Individual). Students are required to prepare an individual written report on a topic related to Quality Planning and Analysis , selected from a list provided by the teaching team. The report should demonstrate a critical understanding of the selected topic by integrating relevant quality management concepts, contemporary research, and practical industry perspectives. The report should include the following components: Introduction and Problem Context â Introduce the selected topic and explain its significance. Literature Review â Critically synthesise the relevant literature using at least 5 high-quality academic references . Analysis and Discussion â Apply and discuss appropriate quality planning and analysis tools and techniques relevant to the selected topic. Current Challenges and Improvement Opportunities â Identify key challenges, gaps, and opportunities for quality improvement. Conclusion and Recommendations â Summarise the key findings and provide practical recommendations. The report should demonstrate evidence-based analysis, and effective academic writing, supported by appropriate referencing throughout.

Assessment Task 2 â Quality Planning and Analysis Group Project (Combination, 30%, Group, group assessed). This assessment is designed to provide students with an opportunity to apply the quality planning and analysis concepts, tools, and techniques covered throughout the subject to a practical, real-world scenario. Working collaboratively, students will analyse a product, service, or work system and develop a structured quality improvement approach using appropriate quality management methodologies. As the focus of your project, the group may choose one of the following options: Design and production of a product (e.g., household appliances, electronic devices, clothing and footwear, transportation equipment, etc.); Design and delivery of a service (e.g., healthcare, education, hospitality, tourism, logistics, etc.); or Design and execution of a work or project (e.g., construction of a house, bridge, road, or other engineering works). Throughout the project, students are expected to apply appropriate quality planning and analysis tools, where relevant, such as DMAIC, Kano Analysis, Quality Function Deployment (QFD), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Cost of Quality (CoQ), Design for Quality (DfQ), Statistical Process Control (SPC), Lean Manufacturing, and other continuous improvement techniques covered in the subject. The assessment comprises two components: Group Report (20%) Weighting: 20% Submission: One report per group Length: Approximately 5,000 words (excluding references and appendices) The report should demonstrate the systematic application of quality planning and analysis tools to investigate the selected case, identify quality-related issues, evaluate findings, and develop practical recommendations supported by appropriate evidence. Group Presentation (10%) Weighting: 10% Duration: 6~7 minutes per group. The presentation should clearly communicate the project objectives, analytical approach, key findings, recommendations, and practical implications. All group members are expected to contribute to the presentation and demonstrate an understanding of the project. Â

Assessment Task 3 â Quality Improvement Solution (Combination, 35%, Individual). This assessment provides students with an opportunity to individually investigate and present how quality planning and analysis principles are applied within their discipline or a selected industry sector. Students may choose a topic related to manufacturing, construction, computer science, logistics, healthcare, or another relevant field, and critically examine how quality management contributes to improving organisational performance, product or service quality, process efficiency, customer satisfaction, and continuous improvement. Students are expected to demonstrate the application of appropriate quality planning and analysis concepts, tools, and methodologies discussed throughout the subject, such as Six Sigma, DMAIC, Kano Analysis, Quality Function Deployment (QFD), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), Cost of Quality (CoQ), Design for Quality (DfQ), Statistical Process Control (SPC), and Lean Manufacturing, where relevant to the selected topic. The assessment comprises two components: 1. Individual Presentation (20%) â Each student will deliver an individual presentation of up to 6~7 minutes . The presentation should communicate the student's analysis in a clear, logical, and professional manner and include the following: Introduction and Industry Context â Introduce the selected product, service, or work system and explain its industry relevance. Application of Quality Planning and Analysis Concepts â Demonstrate the application of relevant quality planning and analysis tools, techniques, and engineering principles to investigate the selected case. Key Challenges and Improvement Opportunities â Critically discuss the major quality-related challenges identified and propose practical improvement opportunities supported by appropriate analysis. Conclusions and Practical Implications â Summarise the key findings, present evidence-based recommendations, and discuss their implications for engineering and industry practice. 2. Individual Written Submission (15%) â Students will submit an individual technical report of approximately 2000 words (excluding references and appendices) that supports their presentation. The report should clearly describe the engineering problem, present the quality planning and analysis methods and tools applied, interpret the findings, and critically discuss their practical implications and limitations.Â Â

Supply Chain Analytics (Written submission, 20%, Individual). Use data analysis with Excel to define the problem. This is a scenario-based task where you are provided with company customer complaints data to define the problem, analyse and propose solutions to. Your deliverables include spreadsheet (excel) analysis and a report.

Engineering the Value Chain (Written submission, 55%, Group, individually assessed). The detailed requirements and any support material for this Assignment are set out on Canvas. This is a Group Assignment where the weights are allocated as per follows: Group component : 30%Â Individual component : 25%. Assessment feedback - Report returned with marks (summative). In groups of three, students apply value chain analysis to a top Australian organisation. You will research the organisation and the value chain options, benefits and risks. Each group will need to submit a managerial report based on the extensive analysis conducted on the case study provided. A 5-minute video-clip is to be submitted also by each group member highlighting the problem, solution methodology and findings to the company managers (this will be individually assessed).Â

Presentation (Presentation, 25%, Individual). The presentation assesses each studentâs individual understanding and application of operational and supply chain management concepts. Students are required to submit a concise slide deck and participate in an in-person presentation which also includes Q&A. Each student explains and demonstrates their understanding of application of operational and value chain concepts. Â

Communicating Concepts in Data Ethics (Essay, 50%, Individual). Concept map and article Part 1 Concept Map/Visual Representation Students will draw on concepts covered in Module 1 to produce a concept map/visual representation (with ~250 words of text) that describes the complexity of an ethical issue of their choice (e.g. it might be: concerns about privacy, discrimination or fairness when behavioural data from computer-equipped cars is shared insurance companies; crime statistics and behavioural data being used in ways that result in the over-policing of volunerable and marginalised populations; data from streaming services and its relation to media production and tastemaking; personal health data and privacy etc). The concept map/visual representation should show an understanding of the exact type of data and processes involed in the situation (Week 1). It should also include a clear statement of the stakes (e.g. why should we be concerned about this?) and make reference to, or compare, at least two of the ethical theories covered in Module 1 such as social contract theory, utilitarianism, virtue ethics, kantian ethics, deontology and consequentialism (Week 2). Part 2 Article/Think Piece Drawing on feedback from Part 1, students will write a short article explaining the ethical problem outlined in Part 1 in simple terms understood by a general audience. Students should use a real world example or a hypothetical to illustrate key points and expand on key ideas from the concept map/ visual representation by conducting their own desk research. The revised concept map/ visual representation should appear in the article/think piece as a figure with figure legend and a clear connection to the article's narrative. All sources used and referred to must be appropriately referenced either in APA style and/or with hyperlinks. A list of references must also be provided. In text references and the reference list does not count towards the word limit for this task. Further details are provided on the subject's Canvas site. Examples of previous work will be provided.

Response to Hypothetical Scenario (Case study, 50%, Individual). Students select a case from a range of provided hypothetical scenarios involving data malpractice in different industries (e.g. banking, healthcare, policiing etc) to work on. Each case asks students to assume a stakholder identity and write a response from that particualr point of view. Information on the style and format of the response varies for each of the cases and information will be provided at the end of Week 4. Students will formulate a response to the hypotehtical scenario that includes: a) situating the case within an appropriate legal and regulatory context (i.e. showing they understand what laws and regulations apply) and a clear articulation of data types and processes involved in the scenario. b) an interpretation of actual or potential forms of malpractice inherent in the case expressed through an appropriate code of ethics along with a discussion of the strengths and weaknesses of exisiting codes of ethics. c) a set of recommendations for better day to day practice and/or the potential reform of data-related policy, regulation and law. A list of references must also be provided. In text references and the reference list does not count towards the word limit for this task. Further details are provided on the subject's Canvas site. Examples of previous work will be provided.

text: Quiz (Quiz/test, 20%). Students will complete an online quiz designed to test knowledge and literacy about key definitions and concepts drawn on in the subject.

subject_name: The Ethics of Data and AI
text: Essay (Essay, 30%). Students will draw from material presented in weeks 1-6 that covers examples and debates on ethical issues relating to applications of AI technology and the fundamental biases arising in their design. Students will write a reflective essay which discusses scope, limitations, and future considerations of an application of AI technology in the Australian context. Students are expected to consider the Australian cultural context and the question of creating ethical AI from an Indigenous perspective in their response.

subject_name: The Ethics of Data and AI
text: Case Study (Case study, 50%). Students choose from a range of provided hypothetical scenarios involving different forms of risk and malpractice. They conduct a critical analysis of the discussing how there has been a significant breach of regulation or evidence of questionable ethical conduct. The case study will include discussion of the nature of non-compliance or malpractice expressed through the terms set out by appropriate laws, codes of ethics, regulatory frameworks and academic debates and make recommendations for best practice.

Conceptual understanding and inquiry (Exercises, 35%, Individual). This task provides you with an opportunity to consolidate your learning about the major concepts addressed in the online learning materials and workshop activities. There are five exercises which comprise short answer questions, which are submitted after certain workshops during the session. Please see Canvas for instructions, requirements, and due dates for completing this task.

Evaluating scientific perspectives in addressing global issues (Report, 35%, Individual). You will read and evaluate two scientific journal articles relating to one of the global issues covered in this subject. You will identify and describe the drivers for the research presented, the research questions, aims and methods of inquiry, the outcomes, benefits and significance of the major findings, and explain how the research in the two articles relate. You will also identify and explain how the research of both articles relates to or addresses the UN Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDG). This assessment task is submitted as written answers to questions (not a scientific report or essay) and submitted via Canvas. See Canvas for complete assessment task details.

Critical reflection (Reflection, 30%, Individual). The critical reflection draws upon your learning experience in this subject. You will use the 5R framework for reflection to complete this task. Your critical reflection is an in-depth reflection on a specific aspect of the subject, such as a particular workshop activity, global issue, or scientific journal article that you have encountered in this subject that has had an impact on your learning, challenged your understanding or increased your awareness of an issue. You may draw on or refer to your earlier reflections submitted as part of the online modules. However, this task is a new original piece of academic writing that you will tie to related scholarly literature. See Canvas for complete assessment task details.

Multiple Choice and Short Answer Quiz (Quiz, 40%, Individual). The quiz will be composed of 25-30 questions and includes a combination of multiple-choice, true/false, matching, fill-the-blanks, and scenario short-answer questions using the resources supplied in the modules.

Reflection on Animal Ethics (Reflection, 60%, Individual). Reflective task: From the perspective of the subject content, write a 1-page reflective essay, critically analysing a research case study.Â Explain how the design of the research study can be changed to have a more ethical and humane design. The essay should discuss: * What does the term âanimal ethicsâ now mean to you compared to the other views expressed by certain groups of people, eg scientists, animal cruelty groups, etc, * The research study briefly, * What aspects of the study could be improved from the perspective of ethics and humane treatment of animals? * How legislation protects animals, and * Whether/how the subject has influenced your views relating to the use of animals in research. This essay should communicate if your personal opinions have changed regarding the use of animals in research, how legislation and regulations enforce ethical and humane treatment of research animals and their well-being such that you could identify and explain ethical versus unethical use of animals in research.

Assessment Task 1 Quizzes (3 at 15% each) (Quiz/test, 45%, Individual). These quizzes are part of the assessment for this subject and follow each module. The short quizzes (with multiple choice and short answer questions) are each worth 15% of the total mark and are designed to test your understanding of the concepts presented in each module. The quizzes will be delivered through Canvas and you will receive immediate feedback on your answers. You have one attempt at each quiz.

You will include a short biosketch of your research experience. The marking rubric will be provided. Your mock research application will be assessed on content, format, grammar, sentence structure and referencing and application of correct structure and style of writing.

These tests will be taken online in Canvas and students will be expected to display understanding and application of relevant knowledge to scenarios and case studies.

Laboratory Induction (Presentation, 60%, Individual). Students to develop a laboratory induction session targeted towards new employees to the workplace, incorporating the following elements Recorded induction presentation Reference handbook summarising presentation 10 question quiz based on content delivered in presentation and reference handbook

The short quizzes (with multiple choice and short answer questions) are worth 45% of your overall mark. They are designed to test your academic writing skills and understanding of the concepts presented in each module. The quizzes will be delivered through Canvas, and you will receive feedback on your answers.

Policy briefing (Report, 55%, Individual). Using the ' Opportunities for an expanded algal industry in Australia' report and your literature search, you will produce a three A4-page policy brief (excluding any diagrams, boilerplate and references) using the template provided on Canvas. Your policy brief will discuss two possible applications of algae, including any of the applications discussed in the Australia21 report, for instance, using algae for pharmaceutical or therapeutic development, treatment of waste water, or rehabilitating the Great Barrier Reef. You will state the preferred option. The marking rubric and sample policy briefs are provided, and you will submit your report via Turnitin.

subject_name: Risk Assessment and Management for Science

You will have to try and anticipate all associated risks that may eventuate depending on the research project, including the consideration of risk assessments for the use of a hazardous chemical.

subject_name: Science Business Models and Intellectual Property
text: Intellectual Property Research Report (Report, 30%, Individual). Choose a project/idea where new intellectual property has been identified. The project/idea can be chosen from the list supplied, or be one that you have a personal interest in or familiarity with. You will prepare a short written report covering three areas below (300 word limit for each). Search for and summarise existing products and patents that relate to the research project/idea. This is aimed to showed novelty in the intellectual property relating to your project/idea. Propose steps that will help to develop the research finding from project/idea to product. This should address the key question of what needs to be done for the research findings and intellectual property to be commercialised â what is the current state of the research and what are the next steps to develop this research? For example, is the project at a concept stage where more experimental work needs to be done? Is it developed to the stage where prototype building of a product is needed? Is the experimental work laboratory based, and clinical trials are needed to prove efficacy? The suggested next steps should be feasible (using established and accessible methods, techniques, equipment), and should include costing and timelines. Research industries and identify businesses or companies who could act as industry partners to commercialise your intellectual property, and justify why these partners would be most appropriate. Your justification should consider the benefits (e.g. social, economic, environmental, health benefits) of your project/idea to the overall industry and to the specific industry partner(s) identified. This will also involve researching the industry/company strategies, costing your project and the revenue streams of your industry partner(s) of interest to ensure that it is within their budget scale, and discussing how intellectual property will be managed amongst the various parties involved in the commercialisation process.

subject_name: Science Business Models and Intellectual Property
text: Constructing a Business Model (Project, 30%, Individual). You will use your knowledge of the nine key business model concepts and your chosen project/idea to populate each of the nine key concept boxes on a business model canvas with inputs that reflect your understanding of each key concept and which work together to create a cohesive business model. Bullet points or short sentences are expected. You will also provide an appendix (500 words maximum) explaining why you made each decision.

subject_name: Science Business Models and Intellectual Property
text: Pitching your business model (Presentation, 40%, Individual). You will use the research & information you generated for assessments 1 & 2 to create a PowerPoint slide deck of 5 slides and a 3-5 minute oral presentation that pitches your business model to an appropriate audience (a potential investor). This will be pre-recorded, not live, and to be submitted online in Week 11. This assessment is split into two parts, 3a) Submission of your pitch and slide deck for peer review (can be draft or work in progress at this stage) and completion of peer review for one other student; and 3b) submission fo your final pitch and slide deck in Week 12. When performing your peer review, you will be providing feedback to one other peer via the allocated discussion board and using the marking rubric.

Developing your ideas (Project, 50%, Group, group and individually assessed). You will be provided with feedback to allow you to adjust your work for the second task. The second page will provide a brief elaboration that considers factors relevant to the biopharma and biomanufacturing context, which may influence the development and commercialisation of the proposed product.Â

Pitching your idea (Presentation, 30%, Group, group and individually assessed). Your task is to develop a pitch of the new product using a power point presentation that is exciting, convincing and based on sound scientific and business principles. Your final project pitch will be presented to a mock panel of potential investors with expertise in the appropriate areas. The final project pitch will be 10 minutes duration and 5 minutes of question time. You will be assessed on the content in a group manner, and presentation delivery on an individual basis.

Quizzes (Quiz/test, 20%, Individual). Students will be completing two quizzes in weeks 4 and 12. These quizzes will test students knowledge of key learning objectives covered in labs and lectures and provide feedback to the student in regards to their progress in the subject. These questions may take the form of scenario or knowledge based depending on the complexity of the assessed topic. Note that the quiz-1 in week 4 will be formative while the quiz-2 will account for 20% of marking.

Computer Lab Classes (Laboratory/practical, 30%, Group, group assessed). Each week students will be completing different activities during the computer laboratory classes. Note that three labs will account for 10% of marking each, while all the others will be formative.

Practical Examination and Expert Report (Report, 50%, Individual). Students will be required to complete a case scenario during a computer lab class and based on the investigation and findings will prepare an expert report. This will require students to apply the knowledge of key learning objectives covered in labs and lectures and their ability to bring this together in the form of a report. They will also need to apply an inquiry oriented approach and demonstrate a strong degree of problem solving skills to identify, analyse, process and report on the findings of their investigation. This task includes a milestone assessment component that evaluates English language proficiency. You may be guided to further language support after the completion of this subject if your results in this milestone task indicate you need more help with your language skills.

Quiz (Quiz, 30%, Individual). This online quizÂ assesses studentsâ understanding of material covered throughÂ the asynchronous online content and computer laboratory activities. The quiz will include a mixture of question styles, such as multiple-choice questions, short-answer questions, and scenario-based or reasoning questions requiring students to apply key concepts to selected digital and cyber crime contexts. This assessment task is to be completed individually . Please see Canvas for detailed assessment task information.

Computer Lab (Practical test, 40%, Individual). This multi-part assessment requires students to engage with selected digital traces in digital and cyber crime contexts, with emphasis on skills such as identification, interpretation, communication and critical forensic reasoning. This assessment task is to be completed individually . Please see Canvas for detailed assessment task information.

Group cybercrime topic project and presentation (Project, 30%, Group, group assessed). The project requires students to explore the topic and communicate key considerations relating to digital traces. This assessment task is to be completed in group . Please see Canvas for detailed assessment task information.

Lab-based Sessions (Combination, 50%, Group, individually assessed). Course Engagement (Combination, 30%). There are several aspects to this assessment task as set out below. Assessment Task 1A Pre-class preparation and shared activities (5%) This component rewards your preparation before classes, particularly the extent of your engagement with the Canvas modules, including readings and lectures, and any specific pre-class activities in the module (apart from the quizzes). Active and constructive participation in this context means: Asking questions and responding to questions informed by the readings and other quality sources; GeneratingÂ discussion and contributing to collaborative discussions with peers; Engaging respectfully with the views of others; Demonstrating willingness to consider and engage with alternative viewpoints; and Where relevant, admitting to a lack of understanding or areas of confusion. For further details make sure you read the information on Assessment Task 1A in the Assignments tab on Canvas. Panel  Presentation (Presentation, 40%, Individual). Panel presentation For this assessment you'll prepare a 5 â7Â minute presentation on one of 10 weekly topics. There will be a panel of five presenters each week. The presentations will be moderated by the lecturer. There will be an opportunity for the lecturer and your peers to ask questions about your presentation. You'll need to select your topic and sign up for the relevant week early in semester. Your due date will depend on your topic area. Because there is no uniform due date, applications for short extensions will need to be made by email to the subject coordinator.Â For this assignment you will need to prepare a Power Point presentation and a script including a bibliography.Â The Power Point presentation will need to be uploaded to Canvas before class.Â The script for your presentation, including your response to the lecturerâs questions will be due one week after the presentation eg, if your presentation is in week 3, your script is due the same day in week 4 at 11:59 pm. Word limit 1500 words not including the bibliography.Â Â We'll discuss the arrangements in the first class.Â Â Importantly, you may not do your presentation on the same type of IP as Assessment 3.Â Further details on this assessment,are available under Assessment Task 2 in the Assignments tab on Canvas.

Mock Trial (Moot) (Project, 40%). The Moot will require students to form into pairs. Three student pairs will be involved in each Moot. These student pairs will play different roles (and perform different work). The first pair will act as the legal representatives of an employee, or a group of employees (the Employeeâs Representatives). They will be required to: Prepare written submissions (2,000 words) one week in advance of the scheduled Moot. In these submissions, the Employeeâs Representatives will need to address the legal and factual issues relevant to their clientâs position; and Present their clientâs case in a mock trial to be conducted in class (for 7 minutes each); and Answer questions posed by the Judges in the mock trial. The second student pair will act as the legal representatives of the employer (the Employerâs Representatives). They will be required to: Prepare written submissions (2,000 words) one week in advance of the scheduled Moot. In these submissions, the Employerâs Representatives will need to address the legal and factual issues relevant to their clientâs position; and Present their clientâs case in a mock trial to be conducted in class (for 7 minutes each); and Answer questions posed by the Judges in the mock trial. The third student pair will act as the adjudicators (the Judges). They will be required to: Prepare questions for the Employerâs Representatives and Employeeâs Representatives in advance of the Moot (after reviewing the written submissions of each of these representatives); Ask questions to test and critically evaluate the submissions of the parties Representatives in the mock trial; and, Within one week of the mock trial, draft a decision and appropriate orders in which the legal and factual issues of the case are analysed and resolved (2,000 words). Half of each studentâs mark for the assessment will be based on the written submissions (in the case of the Employerâs and Employeeâs Representatives) and the written decision in the case of the Judges. This mark will be shared by each student pair. The other half of each studentâs mark for the assessment will be based upon that studentâs presentation in the mock trial.
