Designing an experimental plan (Literature review, 30%, Individual). In biology, every sample is different. Plant cells are different from bacterial cells which are different again from mammalian cells. When trying to perform proteomics on these samples, each has to be treated in different ways. In addition, the analysis techniques used in proteomics generate different types of overlapping data. In this assessment, you will choose a sample and describe how you would best analyse the proteome of that sample to gain understanding of how proteoform abundance changes lead to changes in biology. In the process of producing an appropriate workflow, you learn about different proteomic techniques and what kind of data they produce. For you to gain an understanding of the principal concepts of proteomics and how the techniques and technology can be applied, you choose a specific topic related to your work or interests or be provided with a topic. Potential topics should be pitched to teaching staff for discussion, refinement and approval. After extensive reading of the current published literature, you will design a workflow that would produce the most comprehensive and useful dataset, referencing the relevant literature. The methodology MUST be tailored for the specific problem, NOT a list of generic methods, and use the most up to date techniques and instrumentation available. The workflow should consider the following (which is not an exhaustive list and can be extended): Sample preparation and extraction methods most appropriate for the sample and intention of the study. Proteoform or peptide fractionation methods. Analysis (mass spectrometry) methods. Potential bioinformatic analysis methods. The most important criteria is that you must show a critical analysis of what your proposed method can do and what it can't do (analyse proteoforms?) and describe alternatives that would make up for that short coming.

Assessment of practical and analytical skills (Laboratory/practical, 35%, Individual). Understanding the process of an experiment and the effect of methodological choices on the sample and data produced is essential for generating robust and insightful data and findings. As such, this subject has a great emphasis on practical skills and thus you must demonstrate that you understand the potential methods you could use to generate data that is not confounded by methodological induced artifacts or simply does not fit the purpose of the study. You will be asked to complete a number of tasks prior to and during your attendance in class. These tasks are designed to encourage you to read the practical methodology before class and come prepared with prior knowledge of the experiment or questions to fill the gaps in your knowledge. These tasks will take the form of: Multiple choice and short answer quizzes. Scientific calculations. Data acquisition and analysis tasks that will assist with your final report. This is a competency based assessment that will show your ability to perform an experimental workflow. Objectives: To develop skills and understanding of proteomics techniques and analytical skills. A list of tasks will be detailed on Canvas.

Practical report (Report, 35%, Individual). A career in research-based science, whether it be in academia or in industry, is being able to design experiments, performing those experiments, analyse the data produced and communicate it in the context of previously published literature. This task will assess your ability to interpret the data that you generate in the practical component of the subject and communicate the results. The most prevalent form of scientific communication is the peer-reviewed journal article and you will present your results in the form of a manuscript ready for publication, thus learning the important skills of data interpretation and presentation. You will write a short technical report in a form consistent with proteomic journals covering the techniques, results and interpretation of your proteomics experiment in the practical classes. The discussion must include critical analysis of your ability to perform the experiments correctly. The report should be in the format of a short communication to a journal; divided into Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion and Conclusions.

Interculturality in the Hood (Report, 40%, Individual). Spaces of intercultural encounters are found everywhere around us and are the building blocks of daily local encounters. The aim of this assignment is for you to research, engage with, and map interculturality in your neighbourhood as a local space of intercultural encounters, connections and diversity. You will create a presentation or report that introduces intercultural spaces in your neighbourhood and then engage with intercultural encounters in this area and reflect on your relation and positionality to them. This will include large and small cultural, contested, Indigenous, multicultural and hybrid spaces. You are to prepare a deliver a recorded video presentation describing and discussing a neighbourhood you are familiar with and that features five spaces which in some way signal or identify interculturality, including Indigenous and contested spaces. You should explain why these places are significant for intercultural encounters and how you personally connect to, or are positioned within, these spaces. You will justify the choice of specific spaces of intercultural encounters that also locate yourself in that setting. The task requires a critical examination of the interactions within each chosen place/space, relating them to intercultural concepts discussed in the lecture series. You should critically reflect on the complexity of intercultural encounters in each space and link them to intercultural concepts learnt about in this subject. This assignment encourages you to engage deeply with your local environment, offering a personal and analytical perspective on intercultural connections and the spaces that foster them. In addition to the subject and further readings, you should refer to at least two references that focus on your Hood/suburb or neighbourhood and that provide historical information about its cultural and demographic makeup.
